This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for solving a high-dimensional non-linear problem - the Schrödinger equation. Specifically, we analyze the eigenvalue problem of the Schrödinger equation in multi-dimensional spaces using two-layer neural networks. By assuming that the networks are trained with random data and taking the average behavior, we derive mathematical formulas that predict generalization loss and select these outcomes. Additionally, we test the theoretical predictions in a high-dimensional (around 100) eigenvalue problem, demonstrating that they accurately forecast generalization loss. Crucially, our findings reveal that the convergence rate of generalization loss is inversely proportional to the square of the eigenvalue number. This rate is the same as the convergence of the network's approximation to the ground state in the Schrödinger equation. Furthermore, we observe that the network's convergence to eigenfunctions of higher integer numbers is impacted by geometric properties of the domain in which the eigenvalues are computed. These findings are validated in a 104-dimensional problem and the network's generalization is compared with the finite element method - a traditional, non-neural approach to solving the Schrödinger equation. The test reveals that the high accuracy of the network at approximating eigenvalues and eigenfunctions extends to a 104-dimensional setting, where it surpasses the finite element method in terms of computational efficiency. The integration of the network's predictions into the finite element method allows for a substantial reduction (around 8 times) in computational resources required to compute eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in multi-dimensional spaces. The breakthrough of this study has the potential to pave the way for the widespread application of neural networks in solving dimensional problems. The code used to conduct the numerical experiments and the theoretical derivations is publicly accessible at a specified repository. This research was funded by ANI and NSF. Homogenization outcomes for thin films, initially uniform but subject to periodic constraints in the basal plane, are well established in literature. In contrast, this note focuses on thin films whose lattice structure differs from the underlying substrate, leading to a disordered arrangement in the thin film's cross-section when subjected to periodic constraints. We derive a general expression for the effective properties of these films, averaging the impact of individual periodic cells. Ultimately, the convection dynamics within these films can be efficiently computed using standard numerical methods. In a specific example, we analyze a thin film with a square lattice, rotated 45 degrees, against a periodic substrate substrate, where the interaction energy follows a Lennard-Jones model. The results show that the effective transport properties of these films depend on the strength of the adhesion between the film and substrate, as well as the type of loading applied. When the film and substrate have strong interatomic forces, the convection patterns within these films become more complex, under external loading. Additionally, the study reveals that the effective transport properties of these films exhibit unique and load-dependent trends. In particular, high external loading can lead to an increase in the film's effective permeability, while also altering its effective elastic properties. Furthermore, the study suggests that the type of loading applied has a significant impact on the film's effective transport properties. In particular, high external loading can result in significantly larger differences between the film's and substrate periodic lengths. In a related development, the study also explores the convection patterns within these films, under various external loading. The paper explores the properties of a massless Dirac field within a specific type of spacetime model, focusing on whether the model's energy-momentum tensor meets the established mathematical criteria for physical feasibility. The consideration of local scaling symmetry leads to the determination of an invariant sector within the energy-momentum tensor, along with two dynamically significant scaling parameters, which facilitate a in-depth examination of the sector's characteristics. The analysis reveals that the sector possesses only one independent component, which explains why the energy-momentum tensor has one independent degree of freedom. Additionally, the paper discusses solutions where the scalar products of the Dirac field are constant over time and examine some implications of these solutions in quantum theory, considering relationships with Schrödinger pictures and the particles' statistical properties. Conclusions drawn from the study lead to further research questions, focusing on the effects of introducing a non-zero mass to the Dirac field. The investigation also raises broader theoretical questions about coupling the Dirac field to other fields in the context of local scaling symmetry, along with potential applications in quantum gravity. The answers to these questions will be the subject of forthcoming publications. The results presented in this paper first appeared in preprints dated between 2020 and early 2021. For over a decade, computer-aided detection of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) has played a significant role in estimating the likelihood of cancer recurrence and patient survival following surgical removal of a non-metastatic tumor mass. The main obstacle to implementing TIL detection has been resolving the dual goals of capturing detailed information about individual cells and covering the entire histopathological slide. Recently, a new approach has emerged for TIL detection, using cell clustering based on semantic segmentation masks, which treats this task as a categorical classification problem. We present the first federated learning solution for this problem, allowing multiple institutions to collaborate on training without compromising patient confidentiality. Our solution employs a multi-instance learning technique to handle varying numbers of cells per image, and uses a weighted cross-entropy loss function to prioritize discovery of novel categories. We tested our approach using a large publicly available TIL detection dataset and compared the performance of our federated learning method against traditional training methods. Our results indicate that training on a smaller dataset gathered through federated learning yields comparable or superior performance to training on a comprehensive dataset gathered through data aggregation. Moreover, our federated learning method allows multiple institutions to collaborate on training without compromising patient confidentiality. Our solution can be adapted for use in other computer-aided diagnosis applications that rely on cell clustering. We anticipate that our solution will facilitate collaborative training among institutions, and encourage other researchers to join this effort by contributing their datasets and models. We also propose a comprehensive dataset for TIL detection, dubbed Pathology-ML, and invite the research community to collaborate with us in developing a robust, patient-anonymous dataset for TIL detection. Our source code is publicly available, allowing other researchers to replicate our results and adapt our approach for their own use. We intend to continuously update our code and dataset as new techniques emerge, and welcome contributions from other researchers. In the future, we aim to apply our federated learning approach to other histopathological image analysis tasks, and study its efficacy in detecting cancer via TILs. Cavity magnomechanics provides a means to investigate the interplay between magnons and phonons in a fully quantum-mechanical framework. This study examines the magnomechanical system comprising a one-dimensional cavity cavity, a two-dimensional magnetic material flake, and a thin diaphragm that acts as a mechanical resonator. We analyze the time-evolution of the entangled states formed by magnons, phonons, and photons within the cavity. The system's time-dependent quantum states can be effectively managed through optical input-coupling, allowing for the generation of entangled states between magnons and phonons, as well as unentangled states between photons and the other two degrees of freedom. These outcomes show that a new type of quantum-state fabrication is possible by leveraging the magnetoelastic coupling effect in cavity magnomechanics. Moreover, we investigate the effects of various parameters on the entanglement generation and provide guidance for optimizing performance in experimental implementations. This research paves the way for advanced applications in quantum information processing and magnomechanics by exploiting two-dimensional magnetic materials. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the quantum ground states and their properties in magnomechanical systems. The results presented here are general and can be applied to different types of two-dimensional magnetic materials, as well as other configurations with distinct geometries. The theoretical methods employed in this study can be translated to experimental protocols, as described in detail, thereby facilitating the realization of entangled states in cavity magnomechanics. The entanglement properties examined here may also be applicable to other systems, such as superconducting qubits and nitrogen-vacancy centers, within cavity cavities. The research has potential future applications in quantum key distribution, quantum teleportation, and other information processing tasks. The analysis in this study provides new insights into the system's quantum properties and their relationships with magnons, phonons, and photons. Furthermore, it sheds light on the behavior of two-dimensional magnetic materials within cavity magnomechanics and explores the effects of magnon-phonon interactions on quantum states. Current approaches to quadrupedal locomotion learning through reinforcement learning often necessitate complex and problem-specific trajectory controllers. This has led to a limitation in adapting these methods to varied environments and task settings. This study presents an alternative solution, employing an evolutionary trajectory controller that can be universally applied across different environments and tasks. The evolution-based approach controls the evolution of the policy network's trajectory controller, allowing it to adapt to specific objectives. The proposed framework demonstrates efficacy in learning diverse quadrupedal gaits, including those similar to a trot and walk. Notably, this approach requires significantly fewer interactions with the environment in comparison to traditional reinforcement learning methods. The results of this study indicate that the underlying structure of the policy network's trajectory controller can be generalized across different environments and tasks. The advantages of this approach include reduced dependence on task-specific trajectory controllers and the ability to control multiple aspects of quadrupedal movement. The nature of hot winds emitted by low-luminosity active galactic nuclei is primarily understood as being powered by radiation-driven acceleration, yet the process by which they are initiated remains uncertain, especially in regards to low-ionizing continuum radiation. Recent studies utilizing high-resolution X-ray spectrometry have provided essential insights into these hot winds by allowing for spatially-resolved observations. This research focuses on the low-luminosity AGN within the galaxy NGC\ 7213, conducting an in-depth analysis of its Fe XXVI and Fe XXV K-shell lines within the Chandra spectrum. Our findings indicate that Fe is predominantly in the low-ionizing state within the wind emanating from the central region, particularly from a circular area with a radius of approximately 0.5-1 km. This supports the concept of hot winds being driven by electron ventilation, although it contradicts the standard radiation-driven wind model. This discovery is now formally reported for the first time. A diagram illustrating the Fe ionization stages as a function of distance is provided, along with numerical data essential for further exploration of this phenomenon. This research may hold implications for the understanding of hot winds within the AGN framework in general and it is possible that similar hot winds may exist in local galaxies that host low-luminosity AGN. As such, its potential significance for the understanding of local galaxy evolution cannot be disregarded. Numerical data referred to in this study include Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 2. A systematic approach is developed for model-free reconfiguration of nonlinear control systems using reinforcement learning techniques. Building on a model predictive control framework, a novel policy-based reinforcement learning method is proposed, which comprises two key components: an offline learning stage and an online reconfiguration process. Initially, a target policy is learned using model-free reinforcement learning algorithms via periodic offline learning sessions, each informing a database of experienced trials. During online reconfiguration stages, the system's current state is matched with similar states stored in the database, guiding the controller to guide the system to a safe state, where model predictive control takes over to achieve optimal performance. The efficacy of this approach is validated through simulations of a Boeing 747 longitudinal autopilot system reconfiguration. Additionally, theoretical underpinnings and key implementation details are provided, along with discussions of experimental design and potential extensions. The developed concept of experienced trials offers a versatile framework applicable to various model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, offering new avenues for research in adaptive control theory. The proposed methodology holds significant promise for the implementation of self-reconfigating systems in safety-critical aerospace applications. The SiD Detector is one of the validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically optimized for precision hadronic cross-section measurements. Due to issues with the detector's high luminosity factor, researchers have explored modifications to enhance its effectiveness. Two possible modifications, focusing on the vertex acceptances, are presented in this study. Firstly, extending the vertex tracker's acceptance from 0.8<T<1.3 to 0.8<T<2.5 can be achieved with minimal technological changes, significantly reducing threshold uncertainties in the process. Secondly, replacing the calorimeter with a more advanced technology could potentially broaden the acceptance without considerable technical modifications. Both proposed modifications are evaluated in terms of measurement capabilities for top quark mass and QCD coupling, demonstrating the potential for significant enhancements. In the case of top quark mass, both modifications yield comparable outcomes, with the first leading to a 1.5% improvement in sensitivity and the second resulting in a 3% improvement. As for QCD coupling, the first modification yields a 2% improvement, whereas the second results in a 4% improvement. Both modifications critically depend on the efficiency and accuracy of the underlying detector components. While the first modification presents relatively straightforward implementation challenges, the second requires more in-depth changes to the detector design. Nonetheless, both modifications present promising avenues for optimizing the SiD Detector's performance. Furthermore, these modifications can serve as a starting point for assessing similar modifications in other detector concepts. In addition to the measurements, this study also provides an overview of the modifications' implementation costs, indicating a relatively low financial requirement for the first modification and a more substantial investment for the second. Both modifications demonstrate the potential for addressing current concerns surrounding the SiD Detector's design, specifically with regard to threshold uncertainties and event reconstruction biases, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of detector optimization for future precision measurements at the ILC. Ultimately, this could prove invaluable in the development of the detector for the CLIC, where similar modifications may prove essential. As for the optimal design of the SiD Detector, the final decision on modification will rely on a thorough cost-benefit analysis, considering both technical and financial aspects. In the context of the design process, this study contributes to a broader discussion on the design of the SiD Detector by addressing current concerns surrounding event reconstruction biases and threshold uncertainties. As for the final design of the detector, the modification will be based on a comprehensive evaluation of the technical viability and costs. We conducted a deep study of globular cluster Tonantzintla 2, which is located at the heart of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy's core. Our analysis involved a deep spectroscopic image produced through MOSDEEP on the Magellan Baade Telescope, covering an area of approximately 3 minutes squared on the cluster's center and having a resolution of around 16,000. This extensive dataset comprised 123 individual spectra across 13,300 km/s at a 99% confidence threshold, containing 91 known cluster stars along with 32 new ones we discovered. These new stars were identified as members based on their colors, being previously unknown, with a significant number of them being new GC members: 20 were GC stars, 7 could not be classified, and 5 were likely not GC members. A detailed analysis of abundance was carried out for multiple elements, revealing a range from -0.4 to -1.9 for GC stars and from -0.6 to -1.3 for the new stars. Their mean metallicity was calculated as -1.61 ± 0.07, with metallicity dispersion and richness both estimated at 0.10 and 0.02, respectively. Additionally, we calculated an abundance spread of 0.46 ± 0.07 for this cluster. Our data showed strong evidence for minor elemental abundance discrepancies among the new stars. A comparison with other clusters revealed notable variations in these elemental abundances. This led to the conclusion that these discrepancies could be attributed to an early supernovae-enriched material present during the formation of this cluster. Moreover, we discovered an abundance trend that correlated positively with the strontium to europium ratio, specifically in the new stars. This phenomenon might be the result of a rapid oxidation process involving the transfer of electrons from strontium to europium, which in turn could be connected to the r-process material present during the formation of these stars. An analysis of the abundance of other elements revealed that these elements exhibited early supernovae-related patterns and were consistent with an early formation of the Sagittarius galaxy through a smooth, homogeneous process. This led to the conclusion that these elements were present in the cloud from the very beginning and were distributed uniformly after supernovae explosions. Furthermore, we calculated an age of 12.87 ± 0.29 million years for this galaxy based on abundance analysis. Our research introduces EarthNets, a comprehensive satellite image dataset, covering the entire globe from 2010 to 2020, offered through Amazon Web Services (AWS) Education initiatives to support AI training. This dataset is derived from the 16-meter resolution satellite images provided by DigitalGlobe, equivalent to a pixel density of approximately 50 objects per pixel. EarthNets is divided into 18 categories, spanning 131 classes, and includes time-series data for 314 areas, spanning from a month to 10 years in duration. To standardize data processing, we've developed the EarthNets toolkit, enabling seamless integration with AWS SageMaker for training and model development purposes. This research aims to promote AI development for observing the Earth through collaboration with over 50 organizations, and making associated data available through the EarthNets platform.

A step-by-step construction method is developed to formulate a simplified dynamical equation for a two-dimensional active nematic's direction, describing its behavior outside of equilibrium with a particular directional order. By applying a specific transformation, the simplified dynamical equation can be reinterpreted from an order parameter perspective that varies over time, similar to the Robert's model used to study liquid crystals in equilibrium. We analyze and investigate the stability of this simplified model through a systematic change in parameters, identifying critical points where new terms become relevant in the original active nematic model. These critical points introduce additional complexities, such as a two-way feedback loop and a second direction-order variable, giving rise to complex patterns and behaviors in the active nematic direction and the new variable space. We apply a mathematical technique to decouple these complexities, interpreting the effects of parameters through a broader understanding of the nematic model's components and interactions. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive description of the active nematic direction's behavior and its associated dynamics, offering insights into its observations in real-world active nematic experiments. We also propose a theory, supported by numerical simulations, that the observed stable, right-leaning spinning structures in two-dimensional active nematics may actually be indicators of a larger class of structures, encompassing not only spinning structures but also other patterns in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional active nematics. We conclude by highlighting the common thread running through all patterns in this larger class: the underlying structure, which gives rise to observed right-leaning spinning structures and other patterns, is essentially the same as the structure that governs liquid crystals in equilibrium. Furthermore, this larger class of structures and their interpretation may also apply to other phenomena beyond active nematics, potentially expanding the understanding of the underlying mechanism behind observed right-leaning spinning structures and other patterns. Road networks are often characterized by sections with consistent speeds and varied road types, interconnected with nodes representing intersections where speeds typically differ. This research introduces the RegiOnal Anomaly Detector (ReAD), a novel approach that identifies irregularities in road networks based on the uniformity of speeds along with regional analysis. ReAD leverages a dynamic partitioning method to subdivide the road network into more precise areas where similar road types exist, allowing for the detection of both local and broader irregularities. By comparing its performance to existing methods on real-world datasets, ReAD outperforms or matches the results while using reusable code and an open-source platform. Additionally, ReAD's complementary structure and parameters enable effortless adaptation to various problem formulations, such as detecting regular instead of irregular areas with minimal modifications. Moreover, the paper explores the method's extendibility to predict speed limits on roads, showcasing the framework's versatility and applicability to distinct transportation problems. Ultimately, ReAD is expected to contribute to the development of advanced road network analysis techniques. The paper's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/yangzh2010/ReAD. Snapshots of the code execution are also shared at https://yangzh2010.github.io/ReAD. html. ReAD has been registered in the UMAP gallery at https://uml.map/ ReAD.

This study evaluates several theoretical input values for the pion vector form factor, a crucial element in the process of a muon interacting with a pion through the vector current, as part of investigating the $(g-2)$ anomaly in muons. We consider various representations of the pion electromagnetic form factor, including vector and scalar combinations, as well as the Kroll-Nelsen theorem which relates the scalar to the vector combination. We use various approaches to determine the extent to which different inputs contribute to the $(g-2)$ anomaly in muons, as well as examine their impact on the calculation when performed directly versus using approximation techniques such as Urech's in medium to high Q^2 situations. Finally, we take into account systematics associated with the pion vector form factor at low Q^2 through the use of partial summing techniques in finite temperature and density conditions. We find that at low to medium Q^2, direct calculations tend to yield more precise results than Urech's approximation, a difference which could impact the $(g-2)$ anomaly calculation. Furthermore, at high Q^2, direct calculations tend to yield more conservative estimates than the Kroll-Nelsen theorem, a difference which could also affect the $(g-2)$ anomaly calculation. Ultimately, contributions from the pion vector form factor to the $(g-2)$ anomaly in muons are on the order of 10E-12, a difference which could approximately 2 orders of magnitude smaller than current experimental uncertainties associated with this value. Additionally, at high temperature and density conditions, contributions from the pion vector form factor to the $(g-2)$ anomaly in muons are on the order of 10E-15 to 1E-14, a difference which could approximately 4 orders of magnitude smaller than current uncertainties associated with this value in these conditions. Higher temperature and density conditions would yield contributions that are two orders of magnitude smaller than these values, a difference which could approximately 6 orders of magnitude smaller than current uncertainties associated with this value in these conditions. The relationship between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding halo mass has been studied extensively, with recent findings suggesting that more massive galaxies are embedded in larger halos. We aimed to determine how this relationship changes over time by analyzing data from the CANDELS survey, which includes galaxies at two distinct ages: around 1 billion and 3.4 billion years. Our analysis shows that younger galaxies tend to be linked with smaller halos at similar masses, implying a tighter correlation between stellar and halo mass as galaxies age. This trend holds true across various galaxy types, with the most massive elliptical galaxies exhibiting the most pronounced increase in halo mass for every unit increase in stellar mass over this time period. We propose that the significant mass growth of these massive galaxies in the past few billion years may be attributed to a phase of anti-correlated star formation and gas accretion, following an initial period of rapid star formation following galaxy formation. This new perspective on galaxy evolution has important implications for modeling mass assembly and the development of galaxy structure. Our study's findings are consistent with the theory of mass assembly may be dependent on galaxy morphology, with implications for understanding the evolution of large, yellow dwarf stars, as well as the potential role of galaxy mergers in shaping this relationship. Our data are insufficient to rule out the possibility that the observed trend is influenced by selection biases, particularly as they relate to visible light and galaxy morphology, and this issue should be addressed in future studies. Currently available cosmological simulations fail to capture the complex, time-dependent dynamics of galaxy mass assembly, instead relying on simple scaling laws that can predict the broad outlines of this process, but may not be sufficient for predicting specific galaxy characteristics. Further research is needed to develop more realistic models of galaxy mass assembly that can accurately predict both the broad, universal trends and the more subtle, time-dependent dynamics of this process. In the future, more advanced simulation models will be necessary to develop more accurate theories of galaxy mass assembly that can be tested through a combination of observational data and theoretical predictions. We also recommend that future research focuses on analyzing the relationship between galaxy mass assembly at a wide range of ages, from when galaxies first form to when their stars have completely dissipated. Additionally, more attention should be given in research to understanding the distinct evolutionary paths taken by different galaxy types, particularly as regards their mass assembly over time. In order to understand galaxy mass assembly over time, we must employ observational techniques such as deep, multi-wavelength surveys as well as indirect techniques, such as analyzing data at different scales

To utilize speech data effectively, it is essential to identify voiced segments, which are typically achieved through pitch detection. This process, however, can be complicated by various factors, including speech codes that alter speech patterns. These modifications can mislead traditional pitch detection methods, which rely on the fundamental frequency being stationary within voiced segments. As a result, these methods often produce inaccurate results, which in turn hinder numerous applications, such as voicing detection. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an unsupervised voicing detection method using a specific type of predictive filter, which analyzes both the current and past speech data to identify voiced segments. When combined with an optimized threshold technique, this method is capable of accurately detecting voiced segments, even in speech codes. To validate its performance, we compared this new method with traditional pitch detection methods on a significant dataset, which includes natural and altered speech recordings. Notably, our research found that this new method outperformed the traditional approaches by specifically improving the accuracy of voicing detection in speech codes. The novel pitch tracking algorithm using a specific type of predictive filter, which considers both current and past speech data, is also presented. This algorithm uses a predictive filter to calculate the fundamental frequency, which is followed by applying a specific type of smoothing to filter out transient disruptions. When tested on speech codes, this algorithm demonstrated a significant improvement in accuracy over traditional methods. For instance, when evaluating voicing detection on speech codes, our research found that this algorithm reduced errors by up to 64% compared to a prominent baseline method. These results suggest that the proposed voicing detection and pitch tracking methods are reliable and efficient, which in turn may facilitate the development of new algorithms utilizing speech codes to alter speech patterns. The study of this modification, which we refer to as speech alteration, could have significant implications given the widespread use of speech codes. To fully explore this potential, we plan to investigate automatic speech recognition algorithms using speech alteration as a fundamental feature. This could ultimately lead to novel applications, such as altering speech for better recognition, which in turn could lead to new research directions in speech processing. To determine whether a speech signal is voiced or unvoiced, we employed a method that calculates a specific feature from each frame, which is combined with data from previous frames using a forward-backward predictive filtering approach. This approach relies on a predetermined threshold, which is optimized to match a ground-truth voicing label. In this research, we explore various combinations of spatial, frequency, and polarization encoding for multi-group multicasting in millimeter-wave systems. By leveraging the characteristics of mmWave propagation to form distinct, group-specific beams, we can efficiently encode data and reduce the transmission data rate per subcarrier. However, the number of available beam directions may not suffice to support the number of active groups, limiting our design possibilities. To address this constraint, we propose the use of polarization diversity, enabling more flexible encoding options. This ultimately enables us to develop the HEMLCM scheme, a hybrid encoding method that maximizes the mmWave multicasting capacity to group and frequency divisions, while maintaining minimal transmission rate per group and subcarrier. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our proposed HEMLCM approach outperforms existing research and yields substantial performance gains. Specifically, under a 3D mmWave outdoor environment, HEMLCM achieves a 93% greater capacity than existing research over a 0.4 km distance, while also exhibiting faster data transfer rates than alternative methods. This superior performance is a direct result of our hybrid encoding approach, which enables more efficient data transmission while mitigating the effects of interference. As such, HEMLCM provides a reliable and efficient solution for mmWave multicasting systems. Exact optimization of HEMLCM may be computationally infeasible due to the scheme's complex nature. To address this limitation, we also develop a suboptimal heuristic, low MLCM, which simplifies the hybrid encoding process to achieve improved practical performance. Numerical simulations demonstrate that low MLCM reduces the data transmission latency by up to 71%. This low latency is a direct result of the simplified hybrid encoding process in low MLCM, which prioritizes beam selection and polarization modulation to achieve improved practical performance. To further investigate the effects of environmental factors, we also conduct a simulation in a 2D indoor environment, exhibiting results consistent with our previous findings. Expansion of our research to include various practical considerations, such as guard bands and beam switching delays, also reveals that low MLCM prioritizes these factors over optimal hybrid encoding in order to achieve a balanced trade-off between performance and latency. This prioritization is a key characteristic of low MLCM, making it a suitable solution for real-world mmWave multicasting systems. To confirm the scalability of our research beyond numerical simulations, we also analyze the performance of HEMLCM under real-world outdoor environments, exhibiting results that validate our previous findings and demonstrate the scheme's efficiency in mmWave multicasting systems. A significant issue with federated learning is communication cost. Several compression techniques have been proposed to address this problem, but they often necessitate additional iterations to achieve the same level of accuracy. This is because they either discard some gradient information or send an approximate gradient different from the actual one. In this paper, we introduce a new type of communication-efficient federated learning that addresses this challenge by optimizing local training periods. By formulating a mathematical representation of communication cost, we conduct rigorous analysis on its convergence under specific conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach converges faster while maintaining comparable test accuracy compared to existing methods. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jaefle/Cefla. To address this issue, we develop a dynamic management strategy that coordinates NDN-based computing nodes in real-time. This proposed strategy, which maximizes the network's overall performance, can be implemented via a control-theoretic approach. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of our management strategy in a specific scenario, where the goal is to manage a distributed queue in a NDN-based cluster scheduling system. Importantly, these outcomes are obtained without any prior knowledge of the network's parameters or traffic patterns. In this study, we explore the existence of inhomogeneous phases within the quark-meson model, particularly in the presence of a linear source of chiral symmetry breaking. By concentrating on a specific type of inhomogeneous configuration - where the quark density varies along one space dimension but remains constant in others - we demonstrate through linear stability analysis that this specific arrangement can indeed serve as a valid and stable phase of matter. Notably, our analysis reveals that as pion mass increases, the condition for the stability of this inhomogeneous phase undergoes alteration. When the pion mass exceeds a certain threshold - approximately 140 MeV in our model - the inhomogeneous phase becomes Chiral Condensation Driven Instability stable. Furthermore, for a specific range of the chiral symmetry breaking parameter - approximately between 320 and 470 MeV - this inhomogeneous phase can emerge at lower quark chemical potential than its relativistic saturation point. By comparing with prior research on the relativistic saturation point, we demonstrate that the inhomogeneous phase can claim a higher quark chemical potential within a specific parameter range. Additionally, we show graphically at low pion mass that the inhomogeneous phase can assert dominance over the quark-meson model's ground state within a relatively narrow quark chemical potential window - approximately 90 MeV. Finally, at high chiral symmetry breaking parameter - exceeding approximately 470 MeV - our model predicts that the inhomogeneous phase can assert dominance over the quark-meson model's ground state within a relatively wide quark chemical potential window - approximately 300 MeV in length. Throughout this study, we have relied on both analytical and numerical methods for our calculations. Notably, our results also validate the existence of another inhomogeneous configuration - where the quark density varies along two space dimensions - within a specific range of the chiral symmetry breaking parameter and reveal unique relationships between this configuration and a related arrangement where the quark density varies along three space dimensions in various quark chemical potential scenarios. These additional findings are not the focus of this present study but rather will be explored in a companion research paper. With respect to our current analysis, our results also hold under both weak and intermediate sources of chiral symmetry breaking. Consequently, our predictions for the inhomogeneous phase can extend into domains - such as dense nuclear matter and the early universe - where these sources play a crucial role. Ultimately, our study presents a new perspective on the inhomogeneous phase within the quark-meson model

Theoretical investigations have been conducted to identify potential topological insulators within the $p$-block series. Specifically, we examined the electronic structures, mechanical stabilities, and spin-orbit coupling effects of tetragonal $P4/mmm$ cadmium ($M$CdTe$_3$) and mercury ($M$HgTe$_3$) compounds, where $M$ denotes a elements from group 12. Using density functional theory with the HSE06 method, our results revealed that these mercury telluride compounds exhibit characteristics typical of a weak topological insulator with a band gap of approximately 0.16 eV, whereas the cadmium counterparts show properties of a semimetal with a large band gap of around 1.30 eV. Notably, both $M$HgTe$_3$ and $M$CdTe$_3$ (with $M$ = In, Tl) display stable hexagonal close-packed structures with high mechanical stabilities, positive formation energies, and relatively large direct band gaps. Ultimately, further research into these new wide band gap topological insulators may enable the efficient conversion of solar radiation into electrical energy due to their combination of large band gaps and unique topological properties. Additionally, exploring the dynamical stability under shear stress in $M$HgTe$_3$ and $M$CdTe$_3$ (with $M$ = In, Tl) could facilitate the creation of topological insulator films. Critical analysis of our findings suggests that these compounds can be synthesized through the reaction between $M$ (in the form of $M$X$_2$, with $X$ = Se, S) and In$_2$Te$_3$ or Tl$_2$Te$_3$ under high-pressure conditions, thereby presenting an exciting opportunity for experimental validation. Lastly, our proposed research aims to contribute to the existing literature on pressure-induced phase transitions in topological insulators. Although this study focuses on a specific class of compounds, its findings possess broader general applicability due to the prevalence of weak topological insulators among $p$-block series. Conversely, the absence of strong topological insulators within this series can be attributed to the relatively large band gaps of these materials. Consequently, our results may encourage the exploration of new weak topological insulators with vast applications in photovoltaic research. We developed a novel approach for learning utility functions in multi-objective optimization by incorporating prior knowledge derived from past experiments or expert input. This prior knowledge is represented as a set of pre-optimized parameter values, enabling us to define a collective utility function that favors these established options while discouraging untested ones. By incorporating utility-based and penalty components, our framework can adapt to various prior knowledge forms, including Pareto optimal sets, individually optimal sets, or a combination of both. As demonstrated through applications in multi-objective optimization of chemical reactions and a classic knapsupply problem, our framework is a versatile tool for tackling multi-objective optimization challenges in diverse domains. Its source code is openly accessible on GitHub for public review. Additionally, we have released a publicly accessible version of our framework called UFLearn, which allows users to easily import their own prior knowledge and optimize utility functions according to their specific needs. This framework leverages the performance of scipy and pandas libraries and features a user-friendly interface inspired by ipython notebook. UFLearn is openly accessible at https://github.com/aleksandrhayden/UFLearn. Further details on implementing utility function learning are available in the document provided. Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in various forms of adversarial attacks. Past attacks on policy-based agents typically required a detailed understanding of the model, limiting their practicality. This research aims to close the gap in finding effective black-box attacks on policy-based agents. 1. **Dynamic regret**: We introduce a concept called dynamic regret, which assesses the quality of an adaptive policy in changing environments over time. We show that in risk-sensitive bandit problems with changes in reward distributions, a single strategy can achieve a dynamic regret of O(√(T/ log T)) after T time steps, regardless of when and how the environment transitions occur.

2. **Adaptive identification**: To find the optimal policy dynamically, we develop an adaptive method for estimating the optimal action-value function, which works without pre-specifying the function class or its properties (e.g., convexity). We use uniform exploration to identify the function class adaptively and control the estimation error by adjusting the degree of exploration based on past findings.

3. **Separation design**: We use two approaches to control the uniform exploration. Initially, we establish a separator theorem for convex functions, which allows us to find a separating hyperplane between two function classes with a specific query complexity. Secondly, we implement a sampling algorithm to approximate the separator efficiently.

We use to model various astrophysical environments to explore how nitrogen is generated through different nucleosynthetic processes. By comparing our model results to the observed nitrogen abundance in the sun, we identify limitations in the nucleosynthesis of nitrogen. Specifically, we discover that low-energy cosmological supernovae explosions and stellar mergers are unable to produce sufficient amounts of nitrogen to align with solar abundance measurements. On the other hand, we find that nitrogen generated in rocketing stars and stellar AGB stars can align with solar abundance measurements, but poses problems when considering the time it takes for these stars to evolve before the nitrogen is dispersed into space. In contrast, we find that nitrogen generated in core-collapse supernovae can also align with solar abundance measurements, particularly when considering the contribution of massive stars. However, we determine that the low ratios of nitrogen to oxygen in the solar system cannot be accounted for using our model solely through core-collapse supernovae explosions. Ultimately, we conclude that nitrogen generated in both rocketing stars and stellar AGB stars is responsible for the low ratios of nitrogen to oxygen in the solar system, taking into account the time it takes for these stars to evolve before the nitrogen is dispersed into space. In addition, we find that nitrogen generated in stellar winds from stellar AGB stars can explain the observed abundance of nitrogen on the sun's surface. In the planetary nebula phase, we find that the ratio of nitrogen to oxygen can vary depending on both the mass of the initial star and the time it takes for the nebula to form, leading to complex patterns in the abundance ratios of nitrogen to oxygen in planetary nebulae. Finally, we determine that nitrogen generated in both rocketing stars and stellar AGB stars can explain the low ratios of nitrogen to oxygen in the solar system, but find that core-collapse supernovae are responsible for the high abundance of argon in the solar nebula. In the future, we plan to expand upon our model by incorporating more complex nucleosynthetic processes. Additionally, we aim to determine whether nitrogen generated in stellar winds from stellar AGB stars can account for the abundance of nitrogen in the solar nebula. Finally, we hope to resolve the discrepancy between our model results and the low ratios of nitrogen to oxygen in the solar system by incorporating more precise estimates of the time it takes for stellar material to be dispersed into space. Multilingual individuals commonly speak more than one language within the same conversation, known as code-mixing. This phenomenon is prevalent in numerous societies, particularly in urban areas where individuals speak multiple languages, such as Hindi-English, Spanish-English, Arabic-English, and many more. Code-mixing enables individuals to seamlessly navigate between languages, enabling social connections, commerce, and communication across different languages. Although widely practiced, efficient handling of code-mixing remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. This study compiles a comprehensive list of code-mixing characteristics and their related challenges, along with essential factors to consider when working with multilingual data. It identifies relevant topics under three primary headings: language aspects, required capabilities, and relevant applications. This catalog can serve as a valuable resource for researchers tackling code-mixing-related tasks, providing insights into relevant issues, necessary considerations, and useful references. Additionally, it organizes its content by topic, enabling researchers to submit their own research and compare it with existing studies. This catalog may also facilitate collaborative work among researchers, promoting cross-domain collaborations and knowledge-sharing. It presents data annotations for key tasks, along with relevant evaluation metrics and models to inspire future research. This collection of information aims to contribute to the community's collective knowledge, addressing the noted limitations, and highlighting potential research areas. Ultimately, this catalog aims to enhance our understanding of code-mixing, enabling significant breakthroughs in natural language processing. It positions itself as a community resource, inviting contributions to expand its content and make it more comprehensive. This includes but is not limited to code-mixing data enrichment, the development of innovative models and techniques, and the exploration of new applications and services. Social media users share extensive personal content with various service providers, 
including online advertisers. Advertisers then utilize shared content to target 
individuals, effectively bypassing intended privacy settings. To address this issue, 
a content-aware advisor is proposed that aids users in overriding sensitive content 
classification and advertising purposes. The advisor employs machine learning algorithms 
such as logistic regression, decision trees, and random forest to predict user intentions, 
and is evaluated using Facebook's open graph API and public datasets. Performance is 
assessed based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score for different user groups, 
and is influenced by factors like content type, group size, and training dataset availability. 
The advisor's effectiveness is further validated through user studies that demonstrate a 
significant increase in user control over shared content, and a notable reduction in 
unintended targeted advertising. Code and data are publicly accessible via the associated GitHub repository. 
This research highlights the significance of balancing content-based advertising and user 
privacy, and offers a viable solution through machine learning. Future work can build upon 
this research by refining the advisor's performance using more advanced machine learning 
models, and exploring other mechanisms to complement content-based advertising 
regulation. Additionally, this project raises important ethical considerations for social media 
advertising, and raises questions about user consent and data protection. The associated 
advisors offer a means for users to regain control over their shared data, and may serve as a 
prototype for broader data protection initiatives. Ultimately, this research may contribute 
to improved best practices among social media companies for handling user data, and could 
potentially lead to regulatory changes at a national level. At the very least, this research offers a 
means for individual users to regain control over their shared data, and provides a model for 
other users to follow in managing their social media data. The research has been presented 
at prestigious conferences including ACM CCS and PAM, and has garnered significant 
media attention through featured stories in leading publications, including The New York

Graph neural networks have achieved significant success in various social media
applications, yet their reliance on labeled data has become a major limitation.
The task of predicting social media posts' impact becomes even more complicated
due to difficulties in sourcing high-quality labels. In this research, a new
approach is introduced to enhance the social media post impact prediction task
using labeled and unlabeled data. To address the labeled data shortage, a
multi-scale graph neural network design is presented, featuring interchangeable
attention mechanisms that facilitate flexible feature combination. In order to
make the most of unlabeled information, a supervised learning method is
developed to dynamically generate new graph nodes and edges from unlabeled
data while considering the labeled data's distribution. This unsupervised
graph transformation is integrated into the training and testing processes of the
model. To evaluate the proposed method's effectiveness, comprehensive
experiments were conducted using three publicly accessible datasets for social
media post impact prediction, revealing its ability to improve prediction
performance by up to 5.0% over traditional graph neural network designs. Further
analysis demonstrates that test-time unlabeled data utilization has a positive
impact on prediction performance in social media applications. Specifically, it
enhances prediction accuracy by as much as 4.0%, showcasing the model's
ability to effectively process and incorporate unlabeled information at the test
stage. Consequently, models trained with this method can achieve better
performance, even when unlabeled data is absent, as its benefits persist in
graph neural network designs that do not utilize unlabeled data. Consequently, a
new state-of-the-art benchmark result of 73.6% accuracy was achieved on the
Twitter sentiment classification dataset without employing unlabeled data. On the
Facebook93 dataset, a maximum accuracy of 84.2% was achieved through the
integration of unlabeled information, surpassing the current best-performed
model by 1.0%. Additionally, a new benchmark result of 66.9% accuracy was
achieved on the Amazon review sentiment classification dataset, outperforming
existing models by 1.0% or 0.5% depending on the unlabeled data utilization. 
This research presents a novel method to efficiently utilize both unlabeled and
labeled data for social media post impact prediction, resulting in consistent
performance enhancements of up to 5.0% or 4.0% with or without unlabeled data.

The concept of the universe's thermal history is a fundamental idea in cosmology, but its current state represents just a single temperature segment, leaving numerous "concealed" sectors of temperatures unexplored. We propose a theoretical framework in our universe for these concealed sectors, suggesting the existence of an infinite number of them. Specifically, we can envision a universe with an infinite number of thermal components by utilizing the principles of superstring theory, which predicts the existence of various "string sectors" based on different vacuum states. We can adapt this theory to our understanding of the universe's black hole distribution, yielding the possibility of these concealed sectors containing the underlying mechanics of our universe's thermal evolution. In particular, our analysis suggests that the interaction between our primary "visible" sector and other conceivable sectors could be dimly visible, potentially observable only at extremely small distances or extremely small timescales. We hypothesize that measuring the universe's thermal evolution at early stages using primordial gravitational waves could offer a way to directly detect these concealed sectors. If these strategies fail to yield results, our theory suggests that the dimly visible sectors could be mistakenly attributed to "systematic errors" or "noise," thereby hiding their presence. We also explore the possibility of these concealed sectors possessing different numbers of dimensions, leading to novel interpretations of our understanding of the universe's thermal evolution, particularly in scenarios with additional dimensions in the dark radiation component. In this context, our universe's thermal evolution could be the result of interactions between our primary sector and a limited number of these dimly visible sectors, with the existence of a finite number of thermal components providing natural constraints on dark parameter estimates, thereby helping to resolve long-standing dark matter and dark energy parameter estimation disputes. Finally, our analysis offers a general framework for constraining the properties of these concealed sectors using black hole information, with our universe's thermal evolution serving as a visible manifestation of their presence. We can envision various applications of this theoretical framework in our understanding of the universe's thermal evolution and its potential for uncovering the underlying mechanics of our universe's thermal evolution. We provide a detailed exploration of a specific type of domain called strong small loop transfer domains, with a focus on those related to subgroups of the fundamental group. Initially, we establish the relationship between horizontal surface embeddings and these domains. Subsequently, we demonstrate that every strong small loop transfer domain associated with a finitely generated fundamental group can be represented as a horizontal surface embedding. Notably, we show that the associated transfer structure is invariant under group automorphisms, and we give an example illustrating that group-generated transfer structures may not be so invariant. Additionally, we examine horizontal surface embeddings in the context of the real plane and 3-space, and we offer an open question regarding whether every strong small loop transfer domain in this setting can be topologically embedded. Finally, we establish a connection between horizontal surface embeddings and crossed modules, specifically showing that certain group invariants can be expressed in terms of loop transfer data. This research is an extension of our previous work on small loop transfer domains, and it is anticipated that our findings will shed new light on the topological properties of 3-manifolds. Ultimately, this may facilitate the computation of volume functions for these manifolds. Specifically, we investigate how the volume function of a principal bundle is related to the loopy volume function of its associated loop space, and we explore examples of these volume functions in simplified contexts. Interestingly, we find that certain strong small loop transfer domains associated with abelian groups can be expressed as horizontal surface embeddings with particularly straightforward properties. In the course of this research, we developed a method for constructing volume functions on 3-manifolds by leveraging data from simple loops, and we believe that our methods will provide a useful lens through which to view the topological properties of 3-manifolds. Furthermore, we see potential applications of our findings in combinatorial topology, particularly in relation to combinatorial volume functions on 3-manifolds. It is anticipated that further investigation will reveal a more profound interplay between the topological properties of 3-manifolds and the properties of strong small loop transfer domains. As such, we consider the research presented herein to be primarily inductive. Conversely, we also see the potential for insights from our research to illuminate various questions and problems in topology, and we expect that a more extensive study of strong small loop transfer domains will yield novel and insightful results. To achieve this goal, it is our hope that others will construct horizontal surface embeddings in novel 3-manifolds and explore the properties of their associated transfer domains

We introduce TDRL, a two-stage deep reinforcement learning approach for control problems. The underlying principle of TDRL is to divide complex problems into two manageable sections by simplifying the action space in the initial stage, which significantly reduces complexity. Our method mimics a dual-stage strategy commonly found in industrial processes where the first stage is often the production planning phase and the second stage is real-time execution of the planned strategy. We demonstrate the efficacy of TDRL by comparing it to state-of-the-art models, including DDPG and SARDGP, on a set of controlled chaotic systems, specifically the hyperplane learning problem, and a real-world industrial case study involving optimal cutting of sheet metal, which showcases a notable improvement in performance and computational efficiency. By decomposing this problem into two manageable stages - the planning of routes and the execution of those plans - TDRL can significantly improve the performance of self-driving cars and reduce computing costs. This same dual-stage strategy is a standard practice in industrial production management, where planning often precedes and guides the execution of production orders. In a related context, TDRL is anticipated to yield notable gains in processing efficiency. Over the past thirty years, preprint systems have undergone significant growth and change. Originally designed for individual researchers and small groups, preprints are now an integral part of the entire scientific community. Preprint systems, such as arXiv, have successfully captured a substantial portion of the scientific literature in specific fields. However, the preprint model still faces significant obstacles before it can be widely adopted within the scientific community. To this day, authors are still compelled to wait for official journal publications to gain recognition, highlighting the persistent gap between preprints and published articles. This shift may signal a profound transformation in the dissemination of scientific knowledge. To better comprehend this development, we have conducted a comprehensive review of the history and progress of preprint systems over the past thirty years. Our analysis focuses on the key factors contributing to the success and failures of preprint systems, utilizing advanced network techniques to evaluate the influence of preprints on scientific collaboration and literature development. Our findings reveal that preprint systems can accelerate research dissemination, enhance international collaboration, and compress the time between preprint submission and publication. These outcomes suggest that preprints can significantly alter the landscape of scientific communication. To further bridge the gap between preprints and published articles, we have devised a collaborative model that integrates preprint servers and scientific journals, aiming to streamline the preprint evaluation and publication process. Our ultimate goal is to accelerate research advancement through a faster dissemination of novel information and to facilitate international collaboration through equal opportunities for early preprint submissions. Ultimately, a seamless transition between preprints and published articles will pave the way for the open and rapid dissemination of scientific knowledge among researchers. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research. Researchers often examine these data using summary statistics such as the matrix mean, variances, or principal components. We show that the distribution of their entries converges to a mixture of two continuous distributions, a result that can be utilized to create simulated matrix data. We build on the work of Kluck-Miller-Tao by defining a new type of random subgroup and demonstrate its existence within any acylindrically hyperbolic group. This subgroup is both invariant and loyal, meaning its conjugates never intersect properly. Additionally, we prove that virtually abelian loyal invariant random subgroups do not exist. Building on Kluck-Miller-Tao's techniques, we modify them to handle the acylindrically hyperbolic groups, and as a result, we derive a simplified version of their original theorem. Notably, we avoid using most of their deep theorems, instead relying on core properties of acylindrically hyperbolic groups. This simplification allows us to answer a question posed by Kluck-Miller-Tao by showing that the stabilizers of points in their constructed subgroups behave similarly to their own stabilizers. This, in turn, enables us to define a new, probabilistic geometric structure on these subgroups, which we term "random geometric". Finally, we conjecture that the central element of our constructed subgroup has a stable length within the group's word metric and that this stable length is greater than the conjugation invariant, geodesic length of the subgroup itself. If this holds, it would resolve a long-standing question posed by Kapovich. This work also derives a number of other independent theorems and conjectures, as well as simplifies and skews existing results, also uncovering a previously unknown connection between our constructed subgroup and the "mixed" arithmetic triads previously identified by the second author. However, the potential for errors in quantum calculations is even higher than in classical computing, necessitating verification to ensure results accuracy. The current verification methods for quantum calculations are mainly based on either classical homomorphic evaluation or checking the results of running the calculation multiple times. Yet, these approaches are often impractical due to their high computational overhead. In this work, we present a pioneering traditional verification method that runs in linear time with respect to the number of qubits in the calculation. Our approach leverages the principles of unitary and additivity to break down the verification process into straightforward comparisons. We also propose a novel concept, the epsilon-net, that allows us to achieve this breakthrough result. The efficiency of our verification method is unaffected by the complexity of the calculation and can therefore be employed even for highly complex quantum algorithms even if they cannot be fully understood due to their complex nature. We thoroughly tested our verification method by evaluating it on real-world circuits comprising up to 40 qubits and specific calculations that were difficult to solve efficiently. Signal processing research involving the localization and classification of audio events has gained significant interest due to the capabilities offered by recent advances in deep learning. Through the application of Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks, the performance of audio classification has been notably improved. This study proposes a CRNN architecture that utilizes rectangular filters and integrates data augmentation via channel shifting for optimal results. By evaluating the system on the Sound Event Localization and Classification (SELT) dataset, remarkable overall accuracy and localization accuracy was achieved, surpassing existing best-recorded values. Additionally, the system's performance under various conditions, including the number of classes and data channels, was thoroughly examined. Although channel rotation augmentation exhibited some benefit, it wasn't necessary for achieving high performance, indicating that the proposed method can produce outstanding results through a straightforward design. Furthermore, the method demonstrated resilience and generalizability when handling challenging scenarios, including the classification of multiple sound events. With a total of 19 classes, an overall accuracy of 67.43% was achieved, showcasing promising prospects for this system in real-world applications. Detailed data augmentation and system examination is provided in Supplemental Material. Supplemental figure and code are available at https://github.com/ArjunDeshpande123/SELT_CRNNaug and https://github.com/ArjunDeshpande123/SLOC.git. Additionally, the submitted model parameters can be accessed via huggingface.co/ArjunDeshpande123. Note: The provided GitHub links contain: 1) a Python script for data augmentation, 2) a Python script for training the model, 3) a published paper in ICASSP2022, and 4) a published paper in EURASIP. The survey also delves into several low-complexity superposition techniques and examines connection models that facilitate coordinate transmission. Finally, this survey concludes by highlighting promising applications of superposition techniques in emerging technologies, such as IoT, SDR, and millimeter wave communications. The potential for superposition techniques to contribute to these technologies is a promising area of exploration. This potential contributes to various exciting developments in the field of wireless communications. Relevant publications from the past five years that discuss superposition techniques in various wireless settings are extensively reviewed in this survey. Key concepts related to superposition techniques, including multi-way AM, AM-compression, multi-carrier transmission, and multi-antenna techniques, are also reviewed. The relevant applications of superposition techniques in IoT, SDR, millimeter wave communications, and other areas are also discussed. Finally, this survey also discusses the common challenges associated with these techniques. These challenges include the need to carefully evaluate the trade-offs between energy efficiency and complexity, as well as the potential for superposition techniques to be highly dependent on channel state information. These challenges mean that further research is needed to fully realize the potential of superposition techniques. Specifically, it will be important to develop new algorithms and techniques that can effectively handle a range of complex scenarios. These scenarios may involve complex interference, difficult channel conditions, and other challenges. The development of these future techniques will likely require a range of different approaches, from traditional information-theoretic analyses to more practical engineering-focused studies. By exploring these various avenues of research, it may be possible to design a range of efficient wireless systems that take full advantage of the power of superposition. These systems could potentially include applications like multi-antenna-based wireless distributions, 5G-based wireless distributions, and reconfigurable wireless distributions. These applications could offer significant improvements in terms of energy efficiency and other key metrics. For example, it may be possible to design a system that allows a single node to efficiently transmit data to multiple nodes at the same time, while also maximizing energy efficiency and minimizing complexity. A new theoretical framework, based on the correlation energy density functional approach, is developed and applied to study these correlated systems. Focus is given to analyzing information entropies related to Coulomb correlation, and preliminary results indicate that this correlation leads to an increase in electronic entropy and a reduction in mutual information between electrons and their distance from the confining potential wall. These outcomes suggest that Coulomb correlation results in a more dispersed electronic charge distribution within confined atoms. The confinement potential wall parameters considered in this work range from very soft to very hard, with some cases approaching those of finite nuclei. The derived formulae for information entropies are general and applicable to any confined atom under these confined conditions. Time series analysis often employs cross-correlation and predictive modeling techniques.
However, these methods' effectiveness can be compromised by non-linear relationships in time series data.
The cross-recurrence plot (CRP) analysis provides a powerful tool for detecting non-linearity in time series data and has been effectively applied to diverse scientific studies.
In this research, we explore the possibility of utilizing CRP-based indicators to forecast the stability of synchronized states in complex financial time series.
Our findings reveal that an (infrastructure) network time series can be regarded as a synchronized state, and the cross-recurrence plot analysis is capable of detecting non-linear relationships.
Additionally, we establish that CRP-based statistical features can serve as reliable predictors of future synchronization instability.
Our proposed methodology is evaluated using real-world financial daily index data from Europe and the US from 2004 to 2019. 
The results show that NRPL-based forecasts can predict periods of anticipated instability with notable precision, outperforming the accuracy of predictions using the persistent homology approach. 
The cross-validation evaluations indicate an average accuracy of 0.81 for predicting impending synchronization instability and 0.79 for predicting periods of stability. 
The accuracy of our cross-validation predictions using the persistent homology approach was significantly lower at 0.62. 
Further studies are needed to investigate the applicability of our research in other fields. 
The code and data used in this research are publicly accessible via GitHub repositories: https://github.com/Agostinho-Silveira/cross_recurrence_plots and https://github.com/Agostinho-Silveira/PRP_forecasts.

The problem of predicting click-through rates (CTRs) for online advertisements is being addressed by a novel model called ViDA. By integrating the concepts of pre-trained language models and the characteristics of visual content, ViDA surpasses traditional CTR prediction models that solely rely on text input. Two key limitations of current CTR models are addressed: 1) the inherent subjectivity of human judgments in evaluating AdRank, and 2) the inability to effectively utilize the visual elements present in advertisements. To overcome these challenges, ViDA consists of three primary components. First, the preprocessed visual features of advertisements are incorporated into a self-attention network. Second, the text and visual inputs are combined through a multi-head attention mechanism. Third, a global attention layer is used to aggregate multiple local representations into a unified global representation. By incorporating these mechanisms, ViDA is capable of learning a more comprehensive and robust representation that can accurately predict CTRs. Experimental results demonstrate the exceptional performance of ViDA in CTR prediction. For example, when testing on a dataset containing one million ads, ViDA achieves an accuracy of 85.4% in ranking unsold ads for a specific query. Notably, ViDA also exhibits improved results when compared to other state-of-the-art CTR prediction models. The 3D visualization of ViDA's embedding space further highlights its ability to effectively capture the visual content of advertisements. Using a combination of density functional theory and the Boltzmann transport equation, a numerical model has been developed to investigate the electron-phonon interaction in the H$_3$S hydride superconductor under varying pressure. The models employed, including two different tight-binding models, each using different numbers of Brillouin zones, and a full first-principles model, were all used to determine how the density of states affects the critical temperature and isotope effect as a function of pressure. While the two TB models produced similar results in terms of critical temperature, the differences between these models and the first-principles model increased as pressure increased, with the largest discrepancy occurring along the mitochondrial axis. Furthermore, all three models showed that the critical temperature and isotope effect are highly sensitive to the density of states along this axis. Ultimately, the results of this simulation predict that further increases in critical temperature in H$_3$S compounds could be achieved by identifying a structure that allows for more efficient electron phonon coupling in this region. Based on initial calculations, such a structure may exist in the Cmcc$_{126}$ space group, with a under pressure of 225 GPa. This paper proposes an approach to optimize bipedal robot walking by leveraging its thrusters in a swimming-like motion. Our model, based on the Central Pattern Generator concept, uses a simplified state-space methodology to evaluate the walking pattern generated by the interconnection of oscillators. To demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy, we performed a series of simulations, showcasing improved efficiency when the robot utilizes its thrusters in conjunction with its legs, as evidenced by our simulation results presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation in 2021. Additionally, we successfully tested our approach on a prototype, integrating a swimming pattern onto a actual bipedal robot, thereby validating our model's capabilities in a practical setting. With ongoing refinement, we are confident that thruster-supported locomotion will offer enhanced robustness and efficiency for bipedal robots. Our research aims to pave the way for a novel class of robots that can effectively operate in both terrestrial and aquatic environments. Visual relocalization, which estimates a robot's location and orientation within a previously mapped environment, is crucial for resetting the pose in situations where the standard Surfel Map framework fails. This failure occurs when no sufficient geometric information is available for localization. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a method that combines key features from both geometric and semantic approaches. By generating a 3D map of visual entities called surfelets, we enable the robot to localize itself within a previously constructed environment by analyzing the characteristics of both spatially linked and distinct surfelets. This self-localization technique relies on the computation of a surfelet correlation score, which indicates the likelihood of corresponding surfelets sharing a common origin. To optimize the correlation computation, we employed a robust set of low-level features, which were trained using a self-supervised learning approach inspired by SSDL's learning of semantic entities. This process leverages the 2.5D Gaussian descriptors previously introduced and combines them with spatial context information to maximize descriptor discrimination. Experimental results indicate that our method successfully localizes the robot's pose in scenarios where the standard Surfel Map approach fails. Additionally, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art geometric and semantic localization methods without utilizing additional information. It is noteworthy that our approach does not rely on any RGB-D data; instead, it can be derived from standard color and depth images. To validate the robustness of our approach in various environments, we tested it on three distinct datasets, which can be accessed at: https://github.com/LSPI-AI/3DSF_dataset. Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning technique that processes data across multiple devices without compromising data privacy. Despite its benefits, the model it creates can suffer from performance inconsistencies and uncertainty, which is particularly problematic in scenarios where limited labeled data is available. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods to enhance the model's reliability under data label ambiguity. In this study, a novel decentralized algorithm is presented to optimize a customized semi-supervised model, which simultaneously minimizes both ambiguity and random noise in the learning process. The algorithm's efficacy is evaluated in real-world wireless network scenarios, and the results demonstrate significant improvements in performance, particularly in terms of reliability, when compared with existing decentralized learning methods. Furthermore, the results show that our approach outperforms centralized models in terms of computational overhead while achieving better accuracy. Specifically, the results indicate that our approach can achieve up to 103% improvement in test accuracy over decentralized models under label ambiguity, and as much as 35% improvement in test accuracy over centralized models under perfect label clarity conditions.
