This paper introduces a novel low-dimensional representation, known as compressive singular component analysis (CSCA), which is an extension of the singular value decomposition (SVD) for high-dimensional data expressed through the lens of compressive sensing. We will illustrate the equivalency between CSCA and CS through two equivalent optimization problems, subsequently presenting relaxations and design constraints for obtaining a feasible solution. Two algorithms, namely a bisection method and a subgradient method, have been proposed to solve this problem, which is subsequently validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data. Furthermore, we will discuss the theoretical convergence of these algorithms to optimal solutions. Lastly, we will showcase the efficacy of CSCA through not one but two substantial applications: (i) low-rank matrix completion and (ii) low-dimensional embedding of images. The former demonstrates the ability of CSCA to excel in matrix completion tasks by extracting more compact representations while achieving competitive reconstruction performance. Conversely, the latter highlights the capability of CSCA to yield state-of-the-art performance in dimensionality reduction tasks with the resultant compressed images exhibiting minimal perceptual degradation while retaining nearly equivalent INNS scores with full SVD. This study demonstrates the feasibility of acquiring two-dimensional airflow patterns using a single-point LDV system with an overhead light source. By taking advantage of the light source's presence in the measurement volume, the method employs the system in a distant operation setup, enabling the acquisition of two-dimensional velocity distributions without adjusting the probe's position. A comprehensive investigation is conducted to validate this approach through comparisons with: 1) a closely monitored, high-resolution measurement of a specific airflow pattern, 2) a three-dimensional numerical simulation of turbulent airflow behind a square cylinder, and 3) corresponding, physically replicated wind tunnel experiments. The results show that the method yields accurate measurements on an ongoing basis in all referenced scenarios. Additionally, the experiments' measurements are compared with the corresponding numerical simulation outcomes to document their level of agreement. The findings indicate that the two-dimensional airflow patterns obtained through this approach match 90% of the corresponding simulation values within a tolerance range of 5% or less. Overall, the research presents an economical and portable solution for measuring two-dimensional airflow patterns using an existing single-point LDV system without requiring expensive modifications to the setup. This approach is expected to contribute positively to LDV system operation and experimentation worldwide. Based on the findings, the method's potential applications include airborne vehicle design, atmospheric research, and cooling fan design, among others. Future research will aim to expand the method's capabilities to acquire three-dimensional measurements, extending the system's operational range even further. Additionally, we've identified a counterexample contradicting Mascarenhas' initial theorem, which posed an open question regarding the feasibility of an infinite descending sequence of first-order patterns. Our contribution answers this question affirmatively. We've also introduce the concept of 'overlapping patterns,' providing a novel characterization of the decision problem for first-order logic with unary and binary symbols. Specifically, we've shown that the decision problem reduces to a finite set of distinct 'overlapping patterns,' and that an infinite descending sequence of first-order patterns exists. The introduction of programmable phase plates in transmission electron microscopy has significantly improved the resolution capabilities of microscopes. However, the concept of utilizing these phase plates as a remedy for correcting aberrations in the microscope's optics has gained consideration. This study aims to examine the potential of a programmable phase plate acting as an aberration corrector in a transmission electron microscope. To this end, we employed a wave-optical simulator that models a defocus and spherical aberration using coherent waves, followed by the introduction of a phase plate model derived from an electrostatic biprism. By analyzing the simulated images of a 2D crystalline structure at varying resolutions, we determined the effectiveness of the phase plate in providing residual correction of spherical aberration. Furthermore, we found that high levels of spherical aberrage can be compensated for through the implementation of a phase plate with an optimal phase function. Consequently, this leads to the image formation of a specimen with optimal resolution in the coherent differential phase-contrast imaging mode, even in the absence of coherence. Additionally, our research indicates that the utilization of in-line hybrid imaging, which incorporates both coherent and direct imaging, enables the extraction of unique information equivalent to 1/nth of a pixel: this effect arises not only from the specimen but also coherently from the microscope's propagation plane, thereby facilitating the extraction of interplane structure details. A by-product of our study is the recognition that the imaging mode we term in-line hybrid can be realized through various combinations of coherence and propagation phases in the microscope. Consequently, this can be achieved not only by means of a programmable phase plate but also through the merging of Coherent and Direct Imaging, which may be available in future TEM models without phase plates. This study defines a C-step C-walk on the lattice as a sequence of points in Zn that adheres to a specific distance constraint, where each step lies within a CJ sphere. A simple counting formula is derived to calculate the number of C-walk positions that fall within a KJ ball in Zd, where it's demonstrated that the count is proportional to (2K)^ndC. This count is further shown to be accurate for a wide range of walk configurations, including undirected walks with unequal step sizes, where a generalized formula is developed. Additionally, the findings' generality is illustrated through an examination of the specific case of random walks in Zn. A surprising connection is observed between our generalized count and Euler's phi-function in number theory. Lastly, the count's applicability is exemplified in a random walk scenario in Zn. Building upon Daniele's work in 2002, I propose a new model that accommodates a variety of applications where the direction of an instrument's effect is not clearly defined. From a theoretical standpoint, I establish the conditions necessary for this model to yield unique and consistent results. In practice, I apply this approach to an analysis of the return on investment in higher education by field of study in the UK using data from the National Student Survey. By utilizing a novel application of Daniele's treatment parameters, I identify key characteristics of fields of study that influence their respective returns on investment, taking into account the uncertainty associated with the order in which these interventions occur. My findings reveal that certain fields of study derive greater value from investment in students with higher A-level grades. This research demonstrates the utility of approachable instrumental variables in a diverse range of contexts. Crucially, I find that the common practice of ranking policy interventions based on their expected impact may not always be justified, and this oversight can lead to inaccurate inferences. Ultimately, I highlight the importance of carefully interpreting an instrument's effect and supporting its direction, and I suggest an alternative method called the "union IV bound" that provides a threshold for when this interpretation is justified. The union IV bound is comprised of the sum of the standard Daniele IV bound and the standard naive IV bound. Through simulation testing on various applications, I validate the union IV bound as a reliable measure of an instrument's effectiveness, even in cases where an instrument has negative effects. Specifically, I observe that the union IV bound consistently narrows down the range of an instrument's true effect, and it does so with increasing precision as the number of applications increases. Ultimately, I determine that the return on investment in higher education by field of study in the UK yields an instrumented effect that is positive, significant, and substantially larger than its uncorrected counterpart. Moreover, I identify key characteristics of fields of study that influence their respective returns on investment, and these findings hold true even in fields of study that are commonly associated with negative returns on investment when the direction of an instrument's effect is assumed. Specifically, I find that fields of study in science and engineering tend to have higher returns on investment than fields of social science and the humanities, and this difference is particularly pronounced among students with higher A-level grades. Lastly, I determine that the return on investment in higher education by field of study in the UK is highly variable and subject to within-field changes over time, even after an instrument is used to correct for differences in an instrument

The spherical accretion of a collisionless gas onto a black hole is investigated, considering a gas expanding from a finite radius and encompassing a wide range of initial angular momentum. Calculations show that when the accretion radius' rotational velocity exceeds that of the black hole, the accretion rate differs significantly depending on whether angular momentum is conserved or a Vlasov-Poisson solution is used. In non-rotating scenarios, the bound mass typically represents less than 10 per cent of the total angular momentum. However, when rotational velocity is involved, the bound mass can reach 100 per cent of the total angular momentum. Consequently, estimates of gas density and net accretion rates may be inaccurately high if angular momentum is assumed to be conserved. Furthermore, these findings suggest that when a gas with low angular momentum falls into a black hole, the resulting estimate of gas density and net accretion rates may be inaccurately high due to the influence of rotational velocity. In such cases, the Eddington-limited accretion rate could be reduced by a factor of ten or more. Additionally, estimates of black hole mass based on gas density may be inaccurately high due to rotational velocity effects. In particular, this may be a concern for intermediate-mass and extreme-mass black hole applications. Finally, the role of radial angular momentum transfer in the formation of a cosmological structure is discussed. Due to opposing forces, gas particles near the accretion radius experience a radial transfer of angular momentum, which can lead to a gas-free sphere surrounding the black hole. In this scenario, radial transfer mitigates the accumulation of angular momentum and potentially forms a gas-free sphere. As a result, the formation of a cosmological structure may be less efficient than previously thought. In particular, this may be a concern for predictions of cosmological structure formation based on angular momentum conservation. Additional work is needed to clarify these findings and explore their applications to astrophysical phenomena. The function $g(x,u)$ meets specific requirements and exhibits subcritical growth. We leverage the constrained minimization method and variational techniques to demonstrate the existence of a normalized ground state solution for this equation. Notably, our research achieves a nonlocal ground state solution for the biharmonic Choquard equation with exponential essential growth in four-dimensional space. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic formula for the solutions under certain condition limitations. Our study expands the existing literature on single-phase solutions for the biharmonic Choquard equation, which typically applies to one- and two-dimensional spaces. The key drivers behind these findings involve the localized nature of the Riesz potentials and the exponential decay of the solutions near their origins. The maximum principle fails in this four-dimensional scenario, which prevents obtaining two-phase solutions for the given equation. However, we conjecture that the solutions obtained will remain symmetric under certain condition limitations. The normalized ground state solutions for this equation represent a new development in mathematical research. This work is closely related to our recently published papers on the normalized ground state solutions for the fractional Choquard equation in various dimensions and the exponential growth scenario in one-dimensional space. The key technical hurdle in this research involves constructing suitable trial functions that combine the effects of the Riesz potentials and the exponential growth conditions on both the solution and its conjugate. The key technical innovations in this research involve Lebowitz-Thirring bounds and constructing suitable trial functions that meet these criteria under exponential growth conditions in four-dimensional space. Despite this, vehicle-driven changes in channel can cause data transmission disruptions. To resolve this issue, researchers have introduced an innovative 802.11p baseline scheme that utilizes multiple channels for transmission, allowing the vehicle to switch between these channels without disrupting data transmission. When analyzing a median absolute deviation, using a quantile regression model for data where the data is drawn from a Laplace distribution produces biased results, especially when estimating the parameters, because the traditional estimation method does not account for the censoring caused by this distribution. To overcome this issue, existing solutions involve applying the expectation operator twice or using an alternative objective function, such as the integral of a squared quantity, to eliminate the effect of censorship in the Laplace distribution. However, these methods introduce additional complexity. A simpler approach, proposed in this paper, Involves applying a data transformation before estimating the parameters of the model, and then reversing the transformation to obtain the final estimate of the median absolute deviation. In order to control the complexity of this approach, the estimation process is restricted to a local area centered on the median, and the transformation is applied only within this area. The proposed method exhibits improvements over the existing approaches, and these improvements can be quantified in terms of mean squared errors. The performance of this method is evaluated using simulated data drawn from a Laplace distribution, as well as real data from various fields, and the results show that it outperforms the existing approaches in estimating the median absolute deviation. The necessary code to reproduce the results of this research, including both the mathematical derivations and the numerical simulations, is provided in an open source package called R. The developer of this package recognized the similarity between this research and existing works, and took inspiration from one such work, specifically the challenge of estimating the parameters of a bi-parameter model that combines a Laplace distribution with a location and scale parameter. The proposed method in this paper addresses this challenge by reducing the problem of bi-parameter estimation to a single-parameter estimation problem. Notably, this compound exhibits unique magnetic properties due to the presence of spin-1/2 and spin-3/2 ions in a unique crystal structure. The results show that the magnetic arrangements of Ru and Tb ions are dependent on the exchange interactions and external magnetic field strength. When the Ru spins are completely ordered (at 5K), they exhibit a magnetic structure similar to that of related compounds in the same family, with alternating bonds of Ru spin arrangements. However, this is observed only when the Ru spins are fully ordered and not affected by the external magnetic field. When the external magnetic field strength surpasses a critical threshold (7K), the Ru spins within the chains align antiparallel to the field, while those at the chain ends remain disordered. This unique magnetic arrangement is attributed to the competing effects of exchange interactions and external magnetic field on the Ru spins, as well as the uneven magnetic field strength across the chains. The latter phenomenon, specifically the varying magnetic field strength at the chain ends and within the chains, is a unique consequence of the terbium ions contributing to the uneven magnetic field strength experienced by the Ru spins. In a partially disordered state, the magnetic arrangements of Ru and Tb ions exhibit unique time-dependent magnetic properties, with magnetic arrangements that can be analyzed through dynamic magnetic property analyses. The time-dependent analysis shows that the internal magnetic arrangements of the Ru spins are not uniform, with those at the chain ends experiencing a magnetic field that is different from those in the chain, leading to distinct magnetic arrangements. The time-dependent analysis also shows that the magnetic arrangements of Ru and Tb spins are distinct, with those of Ru being time-dependent and ordered, and those of Tb being time-dependent and disordered. are confined to local regions of the brain. This is due to the fact that current
methods train separate modules for visualization and prediction, resulting in
predictions that are highly dependent on specific training data. As a consequence,
these approaches are unsuitable for a wide range of applications, including the
visualization of complex functional brain connectivity and the generation of
brain-age-matched control groups for clinical studies. In an effort to overcome
this limitation, we introduce MODPA, an innovative method that trains a single
network to both generate visualizations and make predictions about the data,
while also controlling for data overfitting through the use of modulated periodic
activations. MODPA is an end-to-end deep learning framework that can be used on
various types of CBV tasks and is highly adaptable to a wide range of applications
and datasets. When evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets, MODPA
demonstrated significant performance improvements over industry-standard periodic
activation-based methods. For instance, our technique showed an average 8.1% error
reduction over the industry-standard in the classification of functional
illustrations, while also exhibiting enhanced robustness and efficiency. MODPA's
source code is freely available online. mod-pa.github.io/

In the second phase, our model leverages these correlations to develop a universal representation for the input data, minimizing displacement. A ring is called $\sigma$-elementary if it can be divided into $\sigma$ ideal components where each component has only two ideal subgroups. We create a formula to produce new rings from existing ones that maintain this $\sigma$-elementary property. Using this formula, we demonstrate the existence of an endless family of $\sigma$-elementary rings. These rings are also shown to be non-isomorphic to the ring of integers in a specific type of extension. Additionally, we find a relationship between these rings and another established class of $\sigma$-elementary rings. Using these results, we demonstrate that the $\sigma$-elementary property is not universal among commutative rings with a specific additional property. We then examine similar concepts in the context of commutative $\sigma$-elementary rings. Firstly, we define a ring as weakly $\sigma$-elementary if it can be divided into $\sigma$ ideal components where each component has at most two ideal subgroups. We then demonstrate the existence of an endless family of weakly $\sigma$-elementary rings. Secondly, we define a ring as properly $\sigma$-elementary if it can be divided into $\sigma$ ideal components where each component has an infinite number of ideal subgroups. We then show that the class of properly $\sigma$-elementary rings is extensive but does not include the ring of integers in a specific type of extension. Lastly, we examine the relationship between the $\sigma$-elementary and properly $\sigma$-elementary classes. Using these results, we demonstrate that the $\sigma$-elementary property is not universal among certain rings with a specific nilpotency property. Finally, we present a question regarding the $\sigma$-elementary property in division rings. Using these results, we confirm a partially modified version of an established conjecture. We then provide a characterization of the integers in terms of $\sigma$-elementary rings. We demonstrate that a ring is isomorphic to the integers if and only if it is $\sigma$-elementary and has a specific valuated property. We then present a characterization of locally ringed spaces with a specific separated property. Using these results, we demonstrate that the classification of $\sigma$-elementary rings is equivalent to the classification of locally ringed spaces with a specific valuated property. We then examine similar concepts but with a different valuation system. We discuss the properties and present a characterization of locally ringed spaces with a specific valuated property

The proliferation of unfalsifiable claims across social media platforms poses complex problems for fact-checking efforts. The conventional fact-checking approach, which relies on verifying the accuracy of specific statements, falls short in addressing this challenge due to the statements' often abstract nature and the lack of clear evidence supporting them. In contrast, we propose a novel framework for evaluating unfalsifiable claims by breaking them down into their underlying components, which we refer to as the unfalsifiable claim framework (UCF). By leveraging this framework, we can break down unfalsifiable claims into manageable sections, such as the identity of the claimant, the claimed achievement, the proposed solution, and the expected outcome, all of which can be cross-referenced with existing information sources. In a pilot study, we tested the UCF on a dataset of 288 unfalsifiable claims made by politicians and celebrities, demonstrating its efficacy in identifying relevant information and failing to verify the claims' accuracy. Notably, the UCF's development was accomplished without any domain-specific knowledge regarding the characteristics of unfalsifiable claims. Our findings indicate that this approach has significant potential for being scaled up and applied in a fully automated manner. We intend to share the detailed methodology underlying the UCF framework through a public repository, enabling its further development and refinement by the AI research community. We hope that this framework will serve as a starting point for exploring innovative solutions to the complex problem of fact-checking unfalsifiable claims. We explore how Bayesian estimation handles uncertainty in parameters of a model, when its training data has been manipulated by an adversary for maximum disruption. We identify conditions under which an adversary's attack can be effectively countered, even when the victimizer has access to sensitive information. To frame this problem, we enhance traditional statistical estimation with an adversary's possible actions, forming a robust version of Bayesian estimation. This robust method, based on an attack-resistant likelihood, measures a estimator's performance using the maximum possible loss an adversary could inflict. It is shown that under mild conditions, this Bayesian estimation remains solvable, and we illustrate its benefits through simple examples. We further extend this concept to the case where multiple adversaries are involved. We investigate fast and approximate methods for implementing this robust Bayesian estimation, focusing on situations where an adversary's possible attacks are uniformly distributed. These algorithms are evaluated through comprehensive numerical experiments. We demonstrate the practical value of our approach by applying it to real-world problems, such as estimating a linear model under attack and Bayesian inference in a Gaussian graphical model. The latter application is particularly notable as it is the first to tackle an adversary in a graphical model setting, and our inference method maintains design similarities to its non-robust counterpart. The performance of our robust estimators can be tracked via their robust mean squared error. We show that compared to traditional Bayesian estimators, our robust methods exhibit substantial improvement, particularly in scenarios where an adversary's attack can be anticipated. For instance, in the linear model setting, robust Bayesian estimators perform at least as well as their non-robust counterparts but with a maximum possible loss reduced by as much as 2600%. Similarly, in the Gaussian graphical model setting, robust Bayesian estimators perform at least as well as their non-robust counterparts but with a maximum possible loss reduced by as much as 120%. The source code for our methods is available through public links. Additionally, we have completed a comprehensive document that includes further details on theoretical justifications for our approaches and their design variations, along with an alternative fast method, plus further numerical examples and their accompanying data. This information can be accessed via a publicly shared URL. Lastly, we have prepared a separate manuscript that delves into the theoretical underpinnings of our robust Bayesian estimation, along with key lemmas and our robust mean squared error framework. This study examines the effects of dimensionality reduction in hyperspectral image classification, specifically using five different spectral dimensionality reduction techniques: principal component analysis, independent component analysis, minimum noise autoencoders, K-means clustering, and random forest. We utilize a self-built dataset comprising approximately 350,000 pixels from various natural scene categories, spanning 240 wavelengths. Notably, this dataset is significantly larger and more diverse than standard hyperspectral benchmarks, such as the Pavia University scene, with each pixel describing a spectrum of 240 dimensions. We found through our experiments that the two latter methods, K-means and random forest, tend to compress relevant features into fewer dimensions than the former three methods, with PCA and ICA being particularly susceptible to compressing noise alongside relevant features. Furthermore, we observed that using these two methods for dimensionality reduction leads to more stable classification results across various numbers of compressed dimensions. Nonetheless, all the evaluated methods struggled to extract meaningful features from our extensive dataset, with their performance being surpassed by a simple baseline that achieved 5-10% higher accuracy. Based on these findings, we conclude that hyperspectral image classification currently benefits little from dimensionality reduction techniques, likely due to the vast complexity of our dataset. Therefore, future research using more advanced machine learning methods, such as generative adversarial networks, is recommended to tackle datasets of this nature. Additionally, a comprehensive hyperspectral image classification repository, including our dataset, implementations, and results, is made available for public use through GitHub at <https://github.com/conorgriffin/hyperspectral-repo>. This repository aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on benchmarking in hyperspectral image classification and reduce the existing gap in publicly accessible hyperspectral datasets. Specifically, it includes a dataset of natural scene categories, spanning 240 spectral dimensions, with approximately 350,000 pixels, and a corresponding t-SNE visualization, along with the repository's contents and download links, are shown in Fig. 1. From left to right, the visualization showcases three natural scene categories, namely vegetation, buildings, and vehicles, with increasing numbers of compressed dimensions, respectively 120, 60, 30, 15, 7, 4, 2, and 1. It is evident through visual inspection that the two latter methods, K-means and random forest, yield more meaningful and semantically relevant compressed features than the former three methods, with their performance being exemplified by the distinct separation of vegetation, buildings, and vehicles across various numbers of compressed dimensions.

Compressing large language models with new algorithms has become an essential area of study, as it allows these models to be run on devices with limited resources that weren't previously capable of supporting them. Recent findings indicate that current model compression techniques, which primarily rely on shared representations in transformer layers, are largely ineffective, particularly when it comes to capturing the unique characteristics of encoder and decoder layers. To address this issue, we're exploring a novel model compression method that focuses on optimizing the weights of individual model weights during the quantization process. This method leverages statistical properties of the weights and can be applied to various types of neural networks, including RNNs, CNNs, and LMs. When tested on GPT-2 and GPT-3, our algorithm achieved impressive compression ratios of 10x to 30x without experiencing a noticeable drop in accuracy or inference speed. Additionally, our models demonstrated comparable or superior conversational performance when evaluated on multi-step conversations in the CoVoL benchmark. These results suggest that future model compression efforts should prioritize capturing distinct encoder and decoder features through fine-tuned weight configurations rather than relying on shared representations. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, but a critical aspect of this selection process - how different loss functions affect the network's behavior - remains poorly understood. In this research, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the influence of loss functions in deep, convolutional networks used for binary classification tasks. Our investigation reveals that commonly selected loss functions often fail to minimize the network's misclassification errors, specifically targeting misclassified samples accurately. In contrast, we demonstrate the benefits of utilizing the Crammer and Singer loss function, which outperforms traditional alternatives after the network has converged. Furthermore, our findings suggest that incorporating regularization techniques can enhance the discriminative capabilities of deep learning models when paired with the CS loss function. A thorough exploration of loss function variation through theoretical analysis, empirical evidence, and intuitive explanations is also presented, highlighting key areas for future research and development. Ultimately, our work underlines the importance of selecting an appropriate loss function for a neural network, and sheds light on potential avenues for improving deep learning classifiers. A Python package used to implement the CS loss function, along with training and evaluation scripts, is available for public access at https://github.com/shivamtuli/CS-Loss. This research was inspired by a seminar presented at Stanford University in 2009, initially sparking our interest in loss function investigation. In the course of our analysis, we discovered that the CS loss function - though innovative - has not been widely adopted in deep learning practice. In contrast, we found that optimizing loss functions - such as mean squared error and cross-entropy - for a network can still yield improved classification accuracy, even after the network has converged. In contrast, our experiments surprisingly revealed that optimizing the MSE loss function can lead to degraded performance on certain datasets, and resulted in a significant 11.2% drop in accuracy on CIFAR-10. These experiments underscore the influence of dataset characteristics and feature distributions on the optimal loss function selection process. In addition, we conducted a comprehensive survey of loss function variation through empirical evaluation, testing a range of candidate loss functions - including their permutations and combinations. Interestingly, our experiments surprisingly revealed that incorporating regularization techniques can enhance the discriminative capabilities of deep learning classifiers when paired with the CS loss function. Furthermore, we demonstrated the benefits of utilizing a deep learning model equipped with the CS loss function and regularization techniques - yielding a 3.6% improvement in accuracy over state-of-the-art deep learning classifiers on CIFAR-10. In the US, various communities rely on text-based systems for safety to report incidents to dispatchers. These interactions often involve users' personal details, incident facts, and locations, which are usually transmitted without ensuring confidentiality. Unfortunately, these systems lack comprehensive safeguards, exposing users to potential risks and violations of privacy. To investigate the extent of this issue, we developed and released a dataset containing 1,520 incident records from a real-world safety hotline service. Our analysis of this data reveals the prevalence of sensitive information, such as home addresses, and demonstrates the ease with which location information can be compromised. Our analysis also shows the effectiveness of basic data protection methods in securing users' data. Our findings and data can guide system developers, users, and policymakers in addressing this vulnerability and protecting users' privacy. To measure musical complexity, we employed the functional connectivity density index from neuroscience, applying it to representative albums from six decades of popular music. From the 1950s to the 2000s, musical complexity gradually increased, with each decade's complexity surpassing the previous. This trend correlated with the growing popularity of electronic elements. However, musical complexity remained stable from the 1980s to the 2000s, suggesting that digital technology did not significantly alter the musical landscape. Notably, our model revealed patterns of musical complexity that resembled power-law distributions, with the severity of these patterns evolving over time. While the patterns became less severe over time, the underlying network properties of these patterns remained unchanged, indicating that changes in musical complexity were likely driven by technological innovations rather than shifts in how people create music. Our findings illustrate how musical complexity is intertwined with technological advancements and suggest that similar approaches could uncover hidden laws governing other forms of cultural evolution. Additionally, these findings demonstrate how musical complexity, particularly in popular music, is distinct from other types of music and may even serve as a benchmark for measuring cultural complexity. By applying this method to musical networks, we can reevaluate the conventional view of cultural evolution and refine our understanding of how musical complexity evolved over time. Furthermore, our model may aid in predicting how musical complexity could be impacted by emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and virtual reality. Finally, our study provides a new, quantitative approach for describing and comparing the informational complexity of musical cultures, which could be extended to other domains beyond music. Ultimately, our model contributes to a broader understanding of cultural evolution and may have far-reaching applications in various fields. Supplemental material is available online. A new type of random process, called the multiple-entry reinforcement process, is investigated where an individual can engage in various activities, each potentially yielding a reward. The probability distribution of rewards is assumed to be similar, sharing a common scale parameter, but differing in location and shape. The multiple-entry reinforcement process is essentially a discrete-time version of a stochastic process studied in "Stochastic Environments and Survival Evolutionary Games," published in 2018. As the number of activities an individual can engage in grows larger, the long-term average rate of return approaches its maximum, revealing a long-term "price" of participation, regardless of the number of activities involved. The mathematical formula derived in this study can be applied to determine the long-term rate of return in scenarios involving numerous choices. The findings also hold true for their continuous-time counterparts. The long-term rate of return in the multiple-entry reinforcement process depends on the shared scale parameter and can be used to estimate the "effort" required in evolutionary games over diverse environmental conditions. The mathematical approach employed in this study relies heavily on large-deviation principles and asymptotic evaluations. Consequently, this study may contribute to the development of new techniques to analyze random processes under specific conditions. The findings presented here are a extension of a broader theoretical framework aimed at understanding random processes under various scales, as seen in a study by Herdean and Ispas in 2020. The primary objective of this theoretical framework is to establish a paradigm where the rate of return in random processes can be measured by the effort an individual exerts. The multiple-entry reinforcement process is a key component in this theoretical framework, as it facilitates the analysis of an individual's rate of return under two distinct scales: the short-term and the long-term. The short-term scale refers to the rate of return under a single choice, while the long-term scale refers to the rate of return under various options. In both scenarios, the rate of return is directly proportional to the effort an individual exerts. The findings presented here are a fundamental aspect of this theoretical framework, as they ensure the consistency of the model on arbitrary effort scales. Ludics is a mathematical framework for concurrent interaction developed by Girard, focusing on the core aspects of interaction and leaving aside the specifics of the representation. This originates from Girard's intention to incorporate the concepts of hyperintegers into the system. This paper explores the extension of the Ludics framework through employing a semantics-based methodology. This methodality is grounded in the examination of a derivate operator, $\Downarrow$, which is initially defined within a structural framework. By analyzing the properties of this operator, a suitable axiomatic structure can be determined. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that the derived axioms align with Girard's original intentions. Furthermore, this paper delves into a novel proof of cut-elimination for Ludics. This is achieved by rewriting the Ludics calculus to resemble a matrix-based calculus, which is analogous to the Girard's translation of Linear Logic to Hyperconvex Logic. This translation enables a direct application of Muroya's cut-elimination proof for Hyperconvex Logic. Additionally, this paper examines a notion of 'harmony' in Ludics, which is originally presented by Muroya for Hyperconvex Logic. Harmony serves as a decoherence effect, facilitating the extraction of a judgemental interpretation from the Ludics calculus. This interpretation is analogous to Birkhoff's kernel homology for groups. This paper presents a geometric interpretation of the Ludics calculus through kernel homology, analogous to Girard's hyperreal geometry. Finally, this paper samples a range of proof-theoretic flavours by demonstrating that the extended Ludics calculus retains the key features of Girard's original hyperintegers, as well as the core aspects of Girard's Ludics framework. Additionally, this paper shows that the derived concepts and geometries are resilient to the introduction of additional structural features. Rather than exploring further extensions, this paper suggests an alternative approach of translating hyperintegers to Ludics, and examining the derived calculus through the lens of hyperreal geometry. By doing so, this paper offers a novel understanding of the hyperreal concept of convergence, and exposes a connection to an independent philosophical idea known as the 'harmony' principle. Ultimately, this paper presents a harmonious structure, integrating the concepts of hyperreal geometry, Ludics, and hyperconvex logic. As a result, this paper reveals a range of interesting relationships and embeddings between these various mathematical structures. Since harmony in the image of the world is reflected in its logical foundations, this paper hopes to contribute to the quest for a life-friendly logic

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a state space map, marking areas where agreed upon preferences are shared among agents. Through our experimental comparisons on mobile robots and video game controllers, we demonstrate that our approach can significantly reduce the requirement for shared preferences (up to 6 times less) while achieving nearly identical learning performance. This efficiency is due to processing multiple comparisons at once and leveraging spatial constraints to infer preferences from human labels. As a result, time-consuming inspections become obsolete, and preference acquisition speeds up, ultimately facilitating more efficient reward learning. Probability weighting methods, particularly neural network-based predictions, have shown potential in addressing balance issues in treatment assignment. However, the techniques have several limitations: they often overlook the standard deviation of the prediction error, resulting in biased estimates; difficulties arise when dealing with large samples or specific assumptions are not met; and the reasoning behind the model is compromised due to the black-box nature of the neural network. To address these concerns, we introduce a new approach, Standardized Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting with Neural Network predictions, aiming to improve the accuracy and reliability of treatment effect estimations. Through theoretical analysis and real-world data applications, we evaluate the effectiveness of our method. Moreover, a comprehensive simulation study reveals that our approach excels over the current state-of-the-art AIPNN method in both large and small sample tests. Lastly, a case study utilizing the Medicare claims data showcases the advantages of our method when dealing with at-risk populations and treatment assignments based on medical procedure usage. Ultimately, our method provides a reliable solution for estimating treatment effects under various empirical research scenarios. The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current pursuit of discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model. With the LHC's ability to produce large volumes of data, a thorough investigation into the properties of the $\tau$ lepton can be performed. As the most massive known lepton, its behavior serves as a highly sensitive indicator of potential deviations from the Standard Model, particularly when examining its interactions with hadrons and hadron decays. Recent analyses from the LHCb experiment have revealed new areas of investigation, such as the formation of $\tau$-lepton pairs and $\tau$ decays within jet activity, which may be signs of extra dimensions and hidden sectors that affect $\tau$ production and decay patterns. This article aims to summarize the latest research findings from the LHCb experiment concerning the $\tau$ lepton and hadrons involved in the particle's life cycle, as well as the theoretical implications these findings hold for extra dimensions and the Higgs boson role in these processes. Examined are the influences of new physics on the $\tau$ lepton mass and decay rate, as well as the particle's interactions with hadrons and hadron decays. This article also serves as a comprehensive guide to the various methods used by the LHCb experiment to study $\tau$ lepton decays and hadron activity surrounding the particle. These methods include multi-body decays, radiative decays, semileptonic decays, hadronic decays, and di-tau events, providing a thorough examination of the $\tau$ lepton from all angles. This article further delves into specific research topics such as extra dimensions, hidden sectors, and the influence of new physics on $\tau$ lepton production and decay processes in the CMSSM, NMSSM, and $U(1)_X$ models. It also discusses methodological advancements, offering suggestions for further investigation into the properties of the $\tau$ lepton and associated hadron activity. This article also explores future research opportunities, such as examining quasi-exclusive decays of hadrons and the prospective discoveries at the high-luminosity LHC. With the LHC's ongoing data collection, the LHCb experiment is poised to reveal critical new insights into the properties of the $\tau$ lepton and its interactions with hadrons. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the cutting-edge research being performed and the promising future developments that may uncover new physics beyond the Standard Model. This new information could significantly impact our current understanding of extra dimensions

Our research reveals that even a small level of corruption in the data can lead to a substantial decline in the learned model's performance. To mitigate this issue, we develop a framework to estimate the corruption level in data and identify a robust offline RL approach that can thrive under corrupted conditions. Notably, our framework does not necessitate knowledge of the corruption mechanism or the environment dynamics. Our method is also adaptable to various RL contexts, including both value function estimation and policy optimization. Moreover, our results demonstrate that under the presence of corrupted data, a focus on policy optimization often yields superior outcomes compared to value function estimation. To further enhance robustness, we propose a novel RL objective, known as the Robust Q-function, which we solve using an iterative two-step process. Our theoretical analysis confirms that our approach can yield a model that performs within a constant factor of the true Q-function under corrupted conditions. Our experimental evaluations, conducted using multiple simulated environments and a public dataset, showcase the efficacy of our method, revealing robust performance in the presence of corrupted data. Crucially, our method surpasses existing RL baselines by delivering superior performance even under the highest level of corruption. Moreover, our results indicate that in several cases, our approach can yield performance comparable to that achieved using high-quality, corruption-free data. To facilitate low-data training, our findings also suggest that offline RL can be combined with few-shot online learning, yielding state-of-the-art results in various scenarios. Ultimately, our research substantiates the idea that in the presence of corrupted data, policy optimization offers a reliable and robust approach to RL model estimation. Moreover, our work introduces novel techniques for dealing with corrupted data, including an innovative method for detecting corruption level and an iterative solution to the Robust Q-function. Furthermore, our results reveal that a focus on policy optimization can yield robust and effective performance even under high levels of corruption. It introduces a control-theoretic framework for problems with abrupt changes within small time intervals at the edge of a semi-infinite bar. The paper examines basic characteristics of controls with rapid changes, and it identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for the controllability of such controls in the one-dimensional heat equation with dynamic boundaries. When a model is given data not from its original source, it's considered out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior. Currently, there's no straightforward way to tell if new data falls under OOD categories, which can cause serious issues in real-world applications. There's a common assumption that one key sign of OOD data is a significant drop in performance. Yet, this isn't always the case when we look at data that's fundamentally different in structure, or what we call semantic OOD data. Unlike other types of OOD data, which mainly differ in statistics, semantic OOD data varies greatly in its content. This includes a more detailed exploration of the concept of'resynchroneability', a means of determining under specific conditions whether two distinct transitions can be synchronized. This new framework has significant implications in areas such as software verification and model checking. Furthermore, while Synchronizability is a decidable property, Resynchroneability proves to be more complex and ultimately undecidible. However, under certain restricted conditions, one-directional Resynchroneability does become decidable. This research presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding resynchroneability, as well as the effectiveness of the Alur-D'Amorino method in practical, real-world applications. Ultimately, the paper provides evidence that the resynchroneability property is not only undecidible but also that it has an essential undecidibility link to the halting problem. To determine the CP-violating parameters $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ in the Standard Model, the LHCb experiment is generating precise data through the study of $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$. The experiment's results are usually presented in terms of two observables, $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$, which are extracted from the time-dependent decay rate equations using the mesons' time evolution. The $\phi_s$ value represents the CP-violating phase, while $\Delta\Gamma_s$ is a measure of CP violation in the mixing rate of $B_s^0$ mesons. The determination of these parameters is crucial for verifying the Standard Model's predictions and constraining alternative theories. This work outlines the current status of $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ research, focusing on the method used to extract these parameters from $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$ decay rates. The study incorporates data from early LHC running (run I), corresponding to a 1 fb^-1 integrated luminosity, as well as a subset of run II data, with 3 fb^-1 integrated luminosity. The incorporated information also includes a detailed discussion of experimental uncertainties, including those associated with the $B_s^0$ and $J/\psi$ decay modes, and systematic uncertainties. A specific systematic uncertainty relevant to this study is the uncertainty of the $\phi$ meson polarisation, which affects the time-dependent decay rate analysis. Ultimately, this research presents the currently accepted values of $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$, along with their corresponding uncertainties, for the $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$ process. The study also discusses future LHCb plans to refine these measurements further. The experiment aims to achieve a precision of 0.6 × 10^-3 for $\phi_s$ and 0.8 × 10^-3 for $\Delta\Gamma_s$ in a forthcoming update. These new measurements will likely incorporate data amounting to roughly 3 fb^-3, with a corresponding increase in integrated luminosity expected during LHC run II. The updated research will also explore various data manipulation strategies to understand the impact of potential biases in the measurement, leading to more precise predictions in the future. The updated predictions will be in line with the Standard Model's expectations, with these predictions ranging from -0.7 × 10^-3 to 1.7 × 10^-3

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is complex and influenced by various factors, such as the airflow patterns generated by passengers' movements, seat arrangements, and the viruses' ability to float in the air. Predicting disease transmission in these settings requires accurate modeling of virus transport and deposition. We investigated the effectiveness of numerical models in predicting transmission risk by simulating a virus cloud's evolution within a bus compartment. Our results revealed considerable variations in predicted risk levels among different models, highlighting the importance of accurately capturing turbulence and air circulation patterns. Notably, a 10% discrepancy in the prediction of a specific risk metric corresponded to a 40% difference in the predicted risk level, emphasizing the need for detailed modeling in this context. While complex models can offer valuable insights into disease transmission in urban buses, we also examined the reliability of simpler, "well-mixed" models that assume uniform virus distribution within a bus compartment. For the model used in our study, this approach resulted in a relatively low error margin of less than 5% when compared to more comprehensive models. Furthermore, our results did not show any situation where this error margin increased to over 5%. Consequently, we conclude that the well-mixed model can serve as a reliable and efficient tool for predicting disease transmission in urban buses, reducing the computational demands associated with more complex models while yielding error margins significantly lower than those seen with other predictive methods. If a more accurate estimation of risk is essential, the developers suggest employing more intricate models, such as the Lagrangian particle model, to account for the unpredictable movements of passengers and the resulting complex airflow patterns. Ultimately, our study's findings contribute to an understanding of the most effective modeling approaches that can be utilized to inform public health policies and mitigate the spread of infectious diseases within urban communities. Additionally, our results with respect to virus transport may be applicable to other airborne pathogens, and we observed that the general principles governing the spread of viruses could also be relevant to other airborne pathogens. To facilitate further research and development, we publicly disseminated the code used in our study, and we believe that the anisotropic turbulence model employed in our simulation holds potential for addressing various research questions across multiple domains. In particular, we observed that this model may also be useful in simulating scenarios involving fire safety and climate modeling, and we observed that the complex airflow patterns generated by passengers' movements, as well as the resulting airflow patterns, could be influenced by certain tunable parameters whose impact on disease transmission risk has not been extensively explored in the existing body of research

This study investigates the beta decay characteristics of $^{135,137}$Te, focusing on theoretical interpretations through the shell-model. Employing specific effective interactions, the shell-model calculations determined the level structures of these Te isotopes. By integrating experimental data into the shell-model framework via the matrix elements of the unified theory of beta decay, a comprehensive theoretical model was established. The results of this model, including the half-life and the feeding pattern of the beta decay of $^{135,137}$Te, are presented. The aim is to enhance the accuracy of beta decay measurements at the Hans-Knözinger-Laboratory by performing these theoretical calculations. Furthermore, the study's findings on the 1$v$1$p and 1$v$2$p gate intensities are significant for understanding electronic structure. In particular, the study reveals the influence of the Pauli principle on the electronic structure of Te isotopes and the relative significance of radial integrals in determining beta-decay feeding patterns. By comparing theoretical and experimental results, the proton and neutron coupling schemes governing the electronic structures of $^{135,137}$Te were evaluated. The study demonstrates that the shell-model is an effective tool for interpreting and refining experimental data related to beta decay. Based on these results and related considerations, the shell-model is an ideal framework for modeling complex nuclear systems, particularly those characterized by complex electronic structures. The related theoretical applications will be extended to other isotopes of the I-VI group. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate trades between multiple buyers and sellers. Our research aims to investigate and assess the fairness of these auctions when participants have access to varying levels of market information. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that in the presence of unfair trades, the prices offered by the auction house to buyers and sellers differ. Building on this finding, we develop a validated double-sided auction model that ensures a level playing field for all participants. Our model relies on a refined price calculation formula, taking into account the auction house's revenue functions. Furthermore, we extend the validated auction model to accommodate market participants' individual assessments of the auction's rules. We illustrate the application of our double-sided auction model to a European power exchange market. Experimental results show that when all market participants view the auction as a fair process, our modified model yields revenue for the auction house that increases over time. Additionally, we compare the performance of our double-sided auction model to existing alternatives in a simulated market scenario. Experimental findings indicate that when market participants have differing opinions on the auction's fairness, our model achieves higher revenue for the auction house. Moreover, we demonstrate that in a fair auction environment, our double-sided auction model is comparable to established methods while outperforming them when participants' views on the auction's fairness differ. The theoretical analysis underpinning our double-sided auction model provides insights into designing and evaluating auction systems. Furthermore, this work contributes to ongoing research in dynamic existence of equilibria in auction theory. Lastly, our double-sided auction model offers a versatile solution that can be applied to a wide range of online systems, exemplified by its application to the European power exchange market. In modern research on data-driven systems, the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) method holds significant influence. Although the original DMD relies heavily on the assumption of a fully informative snapshot space, which can be critically flawed in practical applications, it has been shown that optimizing a sparse overcomplete basis through sparse pursuit leads to improved snapshot compression and accurate results even with underinformative snapshot spaces. However, this approach still assumes an optimal match between the original and compressed spaces, which can be unrealistic in highly noisy environments. In order to address this limitation, we introduce the linear and nonlinear clarification optimization (LANDO) algorithm, which seeks an optimal low-dimensional representation by minimizing both compression and transformation errors while fitting to the original data. Building upon previous sparse DMD work, we incorporate kernel learning into LANDO to accommodate nonlinearity and improve its scalability, particularly when handling low-dimensional data. Through comprehensive numerical and experimental validation, we demonstrate the ability of the proposed LANDO method to achieve superior accuracy and robustness across a range of challenging conditions, outperforming existing sparse DMD techniques. Additionally, we showcase its practical applicability to the study of turbulent flows using data obtained from planetary boundary layer simulations. This research explores the possibility that the acquisition of spin by paleo-dwarf white dwarfs results from the merger of a neutron star, analyzing the implications of this process for the masses of both the neutron star and the dwarf. By examining the initial spin properties of neutron stars, this study establishes a correlation between spin period and mass, which in turn enables the calculation of mass-to-radius ratios for compact stars. Utilizing this correlation, the study re-evaluates the properties of millisecond pulsar companions to paleo-dwarf white dwarfs, selecting targets with relevant light curves and radial velocities data available. As a consequence of this research, the sample of millisecond pulsars with known masses increases from one to four, including PSR J0337+1635, PSR J14157-6048, PSR J1719-4241, and PSR J1744-3925. Data from the observed systems indicate that these pulsars likely reside in binary systems with fundamental parameters within expected ranges for nuclear-powered mass transfer systems. Their spin-down ages align with the age of the Galactic disk, suggesting an approximate upper age limit for these pulsars. Their estimated masses show a positive correlation with orbital period, with implications for the initial rotation properties of neutron stars, with a trend consistent with the magnetic field-dictated spin evolution hypothesis. Three-dimensional objects can be identified by their visual characteristics in three-dimensional drawings.  This study introduces the first task of three-dimensional (3D) shape retrieval via virtual reality (VR) drawings.  To accomplish this goal, a novel technique called VR drawing to 3D shape retrieval has been developed.  Initially, an experiment was conducted to establish a standard set of standard three-dimensional models by assessing the complexity of human-generated 3D sketches in three-dimensional drawings.  Additionally, another set of novel models called POSS  was also created for further evaluation.  By comparing classical sketch-based 3D shape retrieval approaches with depth and RGB video inputs, a significant performance gap was found.  The proposed technique outperformed existing methods by achieving a 9 percentage point improvement in mean average precision (MAP) when using depth and RGB video inputs.  The retrieved models were found to match the drawn 3D shapes more effectively, demonstrating the potential of 3D sketch-based retrieval through VR drawings.  The developed method and associated datasets have been made available for further research.  Future studies can investigate how to further integrate human insights into 3D shape retrieval by combining the proposed technique with additional human feedback.  Additionally, exploring low-resolution and real-time 3D shape retrieval applications using VR technology could lead to more practical outcomes.  Evaluating the created dataset, POSS, using Amazon Mechanical Turk to determine its practical value and extend the current research to image-based 3D shape retrieval by incorporating VR drawings as additional input. A crucial condition for proper fluid collapse is that the EoS parameter $\Gamma$ should not exceed two-thirds, a standard restriction for proper fluid collapse. Additionally, this study provides guidelines for selecting suitable sequence parameters, thus facilitating further research into collapse models with linear EoS models. A major issue in current deep reinforcement learning for robotics is the lack of efficient policy search within robotic tasks. The main challenge here involves discovering a connection between action parameters and the desired goals. The key to overcoming this hurdle lies in end-effect manipulation, which refers to the direct comparison of actual outcomes with desired outcomes in task-related space. However, current end-effect manipulation methods typically rely on the forward simulation of robot movements to map joint angles to task coordinates. Despite being conceptually simple, these methods can be impractical due to high computational requirements. This study proposes the idea of end-effect investigation, which involves analyzing task-related outcomes through actual robot movement instead of forward simulation. The end-effect investigation drive, a novel task-independent algorithm, allows robots to establish a correlation between joint angles and task coordinates using real-world data. The end-effect investigation drive has been found to significantly accelerate robotic task learning in comparison to traditional end-effect manipulation methods. Moreover, it has been shown that end-effect investigation does not introduce additional bias and can be effectively combined with pre-training using random exploration. The efficacy of the end-effect investigation drive has been validated through experiments using both a 2-DoF manipulator and a PR2 robot. The end-effect investigation drive has the potential to significantly enhance the efficient search of robotic policies. The proposed method could also be applied to other areas such as robot development and robot training in simulated environments. The code used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/RoboEduc/end-effect-investigation-drive. The end-effect investigation drive has been successfully tested in various real-world scenarios, and the associated videos can be found at https://youtu.be/Watch_the_video_here. Image-based goal-oriented navigation is a complex problem in vision and robotics.
Previously, recurrent models were widely used for this task, but they were largely
successful due to memory augmentation, which added capacity to process entire images.
In this research, we present a novel recurrent model, MemoNav, designed to effectively
utilize image and memory-based features for visual navigation. By incorporating a
memory selection mechanism, MemoNav determines which images to associate with
each memory unit during training, thereby optimizing feature extraction and representation.
As a result, MemoNav outperforms existing navigation models in multiple benchmark
datasets and achieves higher accuracy with reduced memory and parameter count. Moreover,
MemoNav's memory selection strategy can be generalized to other vision and robotics tasks. 
Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of MemoNav. The code for this project
is available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharath/MemoNav.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three tightly bound $\alpha$ particles or a dense liquid-like cluster state is still being investigated. In order to better understand the Hoyle state's internal structure, the direct decay of the Hoyle state into two $\alpha$ particles was studied through the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$($^{7}\mathrm{Be}$,$^{7}\mathrm{Li}\alpha$)$^8}$B angular distribution at an energy range of 15-25 MeV using the LST. The analysis of the data collected from the TSOLI beam facility targeting near-laboratory angles revealed the presence of a Hoyle state direct-decay component, which had not been measured before. The newly determined branching ratio for this process is 2.0(3)% ± 0.3%, which matches calculations based on the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ inelastic scattering data. The observation of this process using a 4$\pi$ TPC detector without medium interference provides strong evidence that the Hoyle state has a high-density liquid-like core. The ratio of electromagnetic to nuclear cross-sections for the Hoyle state decay process was also determined to be 0.095(2) ± 0.003, which closely matches theoretical predictions based on the cluster model. The outcome of this research supports the idea that the Hoyle state consists of densely bound $\alpha$ particles. The findings of this study will help refine theoretical calculations of the Hoyle state's internal structure. Furthermore, the observation of the Hoyle state direct-decay component using a 4$\pi$ TPC detector without medium interference will aid the understanding of other exotic nuclear cluster state decays in lighter nuclei. Lastly, the outcome of this research will lead to breakthroughs in the understanding of phase transitions in the matter of atomic nuclei. By taking advantage of this state information, it's possible to establish a characterization of capacity for these systems, which surpasses the known lower bound under the name "state-known-at-encoder" or SKA capacity. When there is no need for feedback, encoding using a deterministic method that utilizes state information does not add complexity. However, with feedback involved, using state information in encoding does introduce complexity. These findings provide insight into how system state can influence communication efficiency when feedback is factored in. Furthermore, these results are reinforced through relevant examples. 

In particular, it's demonstrated that there exists a class of highly structured, state-dependent systems where feedback leads to higher communication efficiency compared to systems without feedback. These systems are known as "skew-reversible." These skew-reversible systems offer valuable insights into how feedback affects efficient data transmission in systems with varying states. It's established that system parameters, including unique path structures and state dependencies, are sufficient to ensure optimal communication efficiency is reached when state information is utilized. These findings are applicable to a wide range of systems, where system parameters are easily measurable or controllable, such as wireless channels subject to tap distribution uncertainty. 

Finally, these research findings are further illustrated through analysis of a specific example, where a system state depends on a random variable, leading to highly stochastic encoding processes. These research outcomes contribute to existing knowledge on communication systems with feedback, offering novel perspectives on state-dependent system performance. By exploring system state influences on communication efficiency, these papers lay the groundwork for future research into dynamic system interactions. 

In another direction, these research findings can be seen as extending existing research in two key areas. Firstly, it's established that state information can be utilized to enhance communication efficiency in systems with feedback, confirming a long-held hypothesis. Secondly, it's recognized that system state dependencies can be fully leveraged in achieving optimal communication efficiency, where system parameters are prioritized over other factors. 

In contrast to existing research into state-known-at-encoder capacity, these research outcomes focus on highly structured, skew-reversible systems. It's established that system parameters can be used to achieve optimal communication efficiency in these systems, where feedback leads to higher communication efficiency compared to systems without feedback. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face significant challenges when designing and simulating these complex systems. Current simulation tools are unable to efficiently test the full potential of neuromorphic architectures, due to limitations in simulation speed and concurrency. To address this, we present a reliable and portable SystemC-based virtual platform that enables concurrent simulation of large-scale neuromorphic systems. Our platform is specifically designed for the Petram toolset and can be easily integrated into existing designs. For demonstration purposes, we developed a full-system model utilizing a 64-bit ARM Cortex-A9 processor, 2 GB of DDR2 memory, and a synapse-dendrite unit (SDU) inspired by biological neuron characteristics. The results show that our SDU-based model can significantly enhance simulation performance by up to 2.4 times compared to a sequential approach. Furthermore, this platform offers flexibility, allowing the substitution of various processor models for a comprehensive evaluation. Our findings suggest that with the incorporation of advanced extensions, such as the VFPv3-32 floating-point unit, neuromorphic computing systems can achieve substantial gains in simulation efficiency. Specifically, by up to 6.2 times when compared to a base model, particularly when tasks involve floating-point operations like matrix multiplication. These outcomes have profound implications, suggesting that by leveraging concurrency, neuromorphic computing systems can attain simulation speeds closer to their theoretical peak performance. In the future, this research will pave the way for efficient hardware evaluations, potentially increasing simulation throughput by an estimated 100 times. Ultimately, this will enable more precise and realistic emulations of complex biological brains. Keywords: Neuromorphic Computing, Concurrent Simulation, SystemC, Virtual Platform, Architectures. Decision theory and argumentation have distinct methods of handling uncertainty, although they are not often combined in the same framework. This research proposes the concept of indeterminacy forests, a machine learning method that incorporates argumentation and decision theory to model complex, semantically rich domains with inherent uncertainty. By leveraging existing structures within these domains, as identified through techniques such as Dung's framework, this framework builds upon existing knowledge and extends it through novel extensions of Bayesian networks to accommodate various forms of quantified uncertainty, including probabilistic, modal, and fuzzy uncertainties. Experimental case studies are also demonstrated to illustrate the potential applications and benefits of this approach. Fury's domain, a well-established benchmark in the study of learning under uncertainty, is utilized as the primary subject for these experiments. The results show that indeterminacy forests can learn to draw precise conclusions in Fury's domain, even when the structure and relationships between its components are unknown. Fury's domain offers a valuable set of challenges to test the robustness of this approach, as it encompasses various forms of semantically rich relationships, including inheritance, which are often expressed through arguments and uncertainty-related properties. Therefore, this framework is versatile and can be applied in diverse domains, such as knowledge graph embedding, semi-supervised learning, and decision-making under uncertainty. Current educational tools in software testing deliver comprehensive feedback after each question has been answered, highlighting both correct and wrong aspects of the student's response. In contrast, our goal is to investigate whether inquiry-based testing, which provides feedback only on specific areas of each answer, can be an effective teaching tool. By mimicking human instructor behavior, our system was designed to first identify areas of each student response that require further clarification, and then provide conceptual feedback only on those particular sections. An empirical study was conducted at the University of Texas at Dallas with 150 software testing students who received either standard thorough feedback or the inquiry-based type, and the results showed that the latter led to equivalent, if not superior, test coverage levels and significantly reduced the time students spent answering questions. These findings suggest that the inquiry-based method not only saves students' time but also facilitates more efficient use of instructors' time, as it mimics human-like questioning behavior. The study's effects lasted for at least six months, and further analysis revealed that the primary advantage of the inquiry-based method was its ability to prompt more active cognitive processes in students. Based on these outcomes, our system is now being used in various testing education scenarios, and we believe it has the potential to improve the overall learning experience. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming a crucial factor in whether or not a certain machine learning method can be used. However, the majority of existing explainable methods are only applicable to certain models or have limitations in other areas. This paper proposes a novel and flexible approach called CAE, which combines concept formation and ILP to explain complex DNNs in a comprehensive manner. By creating interdependent logical statements representing key neural network properties and incorporating relevant mathematical expressions into these statements, CAE generates accurate ILPs for DNNs with any structure. This system is then solved using an ATP to generate human-readable explanations, which are also validated as logically provable theorems. When compared to other state-of-the-art methods, CAE demonstrates superior performance on multiple tasks, including surrogate model generation, rule extraction, and concept formation. Interestingly, CAE shows promising results in generating accurate surrogate models for DNNs learned from real-world data. This breakthrough approach paves the way for the widespread application of explainable methods across various machine learning models.
