Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs) are a highly popular choice for node-level classification in graph data. However, they have a significant drawback: their inability to handle large-scale graphs due to their recursive application of linear transformations. This characteristic causes features to spread across the graph, ultimately leading to a critical issue: feature interference. In this study, we demonstrate that GCNs suffer from 'over-blurring' - a phenomenon where important features are buried in others, severely limiting the capacity of GCNs to distinguish node characteristics in graph data. To mitigate this problem, we propose an improved model, Spatial Graph Convolution Networks (SGCNs), featuring a unique interconnection mechanism that reduces feature propagation in the graph. By combining the power of GCNs with the distinctness of local features, SGCNs offer superior representation capabilities over traditional GCNs, consistently outperforming them in extensive empirical evaluations. Additionally, we provide theoretical justification for the superiority of SGCNs over various variants of GCNs and related models. Notably, we observed a notable improvement in accuracy for models dealing with undirected graphs; a code repository is available at https://github.com/yelundoo/SGCN. SGCNs exhibit exceptional scalability, with the ability to handle complex graph datasets of up to 185, 236 nodes. Our proposed model thus bridges the gap between GCNs and community-based models, offering a comprehensive solution for graph data analysis. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of graph characteristics on model performance, offering valuable insights for researchers and practitioners. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise for efficient, large-scale production of high-quality Heusler films, a crucial finding for achieving clean conversion of waste heat into electricity. A detailed study was conducted to explore the epitaxial mechanism of growing MnGe (@ 450°C) and Ni2MnSb (@ 400°C) on graphene/sapphire using in situ XRD, LEED, and Raman spectroscopy. Experimental evidence indicates that initial sp2 bond formation on the graphene substrate significantly impacts the epitaxial mechanism. A substantial temperature difference is required to differentiate between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy, and controlling the equilibrium between remote and pinhole epitaxy involves fine-tuning the substrate temperature and excess chemical potential of adatoms. Increasing the temperature surpassing the optimal point switches the epitaxial mechanism from remote to pinhole epitaxy, while a higher chemical potential leads to pinhole epitaxy. As the growth temperature decreases, the onset temperature for pinhole epitaxy significantly rises, indicating that reducing the kinetic energy of adatoms significantly hampers the remote epitaxial mechanism, and a higher chemical potential adatom density counteracts this kinetic restriction, promoting remote epitaxy. The study demonstrates that fine-tuning the epitaxial mechanism, or remote versus pinhole versus van der Waals, holds significant promise for achieving efficient, large-scale production of high-quality Heusler films via remote epitaxy. Leveraging the remote epitaxy technique may lead to a significant expansion of its capabilities in growing high-quality epitaxial films. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) have long expected users to bear the brunt of subpar connection speeds. This issue is typically attributed to users' limited bandwidth, yet in reality, the primary cause lies with congested links maintained by the ISPs. To rectify this problem, this research proposes a novel strategy, centered on a fair revenue distribution model between content and service providers. Under this agreement, content providers compensate ISPs for upgrading their users' network quality. We evaluate the feasibility of this model through examination of a specific contract negotiation scenario, involving a content provider seeking to distribute his content evenly among users, while an ISP seeks to maximize his profit by limiting users' bandwidth. This research investigates the outcomes of varying pricing models, revealing that negotiations yield more equitable profit distributions for content and service providers under scenarios involving recurrent and one-time content delivery. Conversely, differences in pricing only serve to benefit the content provider in the case of continuous content distribution. We maximize the profit distribution ratio for both parties through joint pricing strategies and demand matching, and demonstrate that negotiations yield more equitable profit distributions for content and service providers under scenarios involving recurrent and one-time content delivery. Conversely, differences in pricing only serve to benefit the content provider in the case of continuous content distribution. We examine various pricing methods and strategize on how content and service providers can agree on fair profit distributions. Ultimately, this research seeks to facilitate seamless user experiences by encouraging ISPs to invest in upgraded infrastructure, thus improving the end-user's network quality. Specifications for the research setting, including problem formulations and figures, can be found in the appendices. Additionally, further investigation into the effects of varying arrival processes can be found in an accompanying journal article. The source code used for the research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/guipinto/Content_Service_Profit_Calculation. This research is an extension of existing work in [Guipinto et al. 2021], and is an effort to address similar problems by distributing the profit equally between content and service providers, whereas the presented research focuses on achieving fair distributions through negotiated contracts. In contrast to previous studies, which have analyzed the behavior of content and service providers in relation to user feedback and quality of service, this research examines the outcomes of content and service provider cooperation, and strives to improve end-user satisfaction by facilitating communication between content and service providers. This thesis elaborates on that connection by treating the pair as a categorical pair of functors that transmit information between linear vector spaces used for coordinate representations and their equivalent Fock space counterparts. In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its measure is closely related to a foliation that extends to the boundary of the manifold. Although this foliation's development is not always sufficient to form a true foliation on the boundary, our research reveals that when a particular horocycle-based invariant measure is applied to the boundary, it yields a complete foliation. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that when a quasi-Fuchsian manifold is perturbed while remaining Fuchsian, the new measure aligns with the original measure, albeit multiplied by a constant value. This finding generalizes previous research on the inner boundary's horocyclic foliation and also provides an accurate representation of the measurable foliation at infinity for manifolds that originate from a Fuchsian manifold. Additionally, our research in combination with other studies implies that the convergence of measured foliations at infinity does not necessarily guarantee the convergence of the manifolds themselves. Nonetheless, our results do show that when a sequence of measured foliations converges, the associated horocyclic invariant measures on the boundaries converge, integrated over a specific region, which includes a particular type of geodesic on the boundary. This finding can be reinterpreted in the context of a nonelementary rotation, where our results imply that when a nonelementary rotation is repeatedly applied to a line, the resulting line approaches a well-defined geometric shape, which can be accurately measured. This finding generalizes previous research on a specific nonelementary rotation and also provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the limiting behavior of certain types of curves on a non-orientable surface, which, through a topological transformation, give rise to a nonelementary rotation. This unconcluded research is reminiscent of a long-standing problem in mathematics, which poses the question, under what conditions will a geometric line converge and remain infinite. This problem has been dubbed the Chaudhry-Aslam problem and has a associated prize for its solution. While our research in this area does provide new insights and approaches to solving this problem, the complete solution remains elusive. We have conducted an experimental investigation into the trustworthiness issue in second-price auctions, focusing on both single and multi-unit settings. The trustworthiness problem arises when bidders submit auctions either before knowing the competition's bids or after receiving private information about rival bidders. Our study features a two-round design. Bidders first engage in traditional second-price auctions for both single and multi-unit goods. Subsequently, they participate in either a pre-bid or post-bid information treatment, where they are provided with actual competition bids (either individual or aggregate totals) for a second auction round. Our results indicate that bidders who acquire competition bid information prior to bidding exhibit higher bid levels in both single and multi-unit auctions. Academic researchers often rely on the expertise of others, necessitating a vast network of collaborations.  Obtaining first-hand knowledge from others typically involves asking questions, with a significant portion of our daily interactions composed of such inquiries.  Although a considerable amount of information is accessible through existing platforms like Quora and Stack Exchange, they primarily focus on general knowledge and programming issues.  There is currently a lacking resource for seeking expert opinions in specific, niche fields such as computational biology.  To bridge this gap, we introduce BioKSQAA, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 928 questions and answers derived from relevant scientific papers and practitioner input.  Following an in-depth analysis of our data, we developed the Knowledge Seeker, a multi-step task assessment framework comprising knowledge discovery, seeking, and sharing components.  By evaluating the Knowledge Seeker using automatic metrics and human evaluations, we demonstrated the capability of a pre-trained Transformer model to excel in all tasks, with the model pre-trained on our dataset outperforming others in question answering and entity-related tasks.  Additionally, we showed the effectiveness of our model in generating useful responses to expert opinions sought through multiple neural network fine-tuning processes.  Moving forward, we aim to expand BioKSQAA to encompass more diverse fields, including related domains such as chemistry, and make the associated resources and code publicly accessible.  We hope this resource will facilitate the development of more sophisticated knowledge-seeking systems and related applications. In numerical simulations of supernova explosions, we investigate neutrino behavior within a 3D model of a collapsing star. By tracking neutrino distribution and energy, we identify the onset of neutrino instabilities and compute key metrics - growth rates and perturbation survival times - essential for understanding their impact on neutrino oscillations. Unlike 1D models, "fast" neutrino instabilities primarily form along growing shockwave surfaces in our simulated regions. Notably, in areas with intense neutrino fluxes, "slow" instabilities may still emerge, potentially influenced by neutrino flux perturbations, and become dominant forms of instability. We determine the critical properties of neutrino oscillations, assuming specific assumptions about neutrino interaction, and find that neutrino oscillation times vary significantly depending on location, and can be either faster or slower than global core collapse times. Consequently, in some areas, neutrino oscillations may occur simultaneously with supernova explosion, and could lead to substantial neutrino conversion. Moreover, when neutrino oscillations take place on the core collapse timescale, they might result in size reductions of the core. In particular, for a 1.6 solar mass core, we predict a radius reduction of approximately 1 km. We also find that neutrino instabilities are more prevalent in areas with growing shockwave surfaces and could lead to considerable neutrino conversion, especially in regions surrounding growing shockwave surfaces and neutrino emission regions. Notably, while neutrino instabilities are primarily influenced by neutrino "e-folding lengths," they also exhibit sensitivity to other features, including shockwave structure and neutrino "e-folding angles." These properties emerge from our simulated model and are discussed here. We also note that while many of our findings align with prior predictions, there are instances where our results differ, and these discrepancies are discussed. Ultimately, our understanding of fast neutrino instabilities and supernova explosion remains incomplete, and further numerical investigation is required to fully understand both phenomena and their relationship to neutrino instabilities. In addition, we highlight the importance of three-dimensional numerical modeling for accurately representing both phenomena, and suggest that future research should prioritize developing more advanced models with enhanced features and improved physics, particularly with regard to enhanced neutrino modeling and more sophisticated astrophysics representations. We also point out several potential pathways to incorporating these enhancements, and outline future research directions, involving not only numerical modeling but also experimental and observational investigations, and theoretical studies involving bothess andess models. ADHD is a widely prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, and recent studies have shown that rs-fMRI can be utilized for diagnosing and differentiating ADHD by pinpointing pivotal brain regions and networks. Nevertheless, current methods are hindered by several drawbacks: (a) excessive reliance on prior knowledge, (b) limited availability of subject matter knowledge, (c) potential overfitting due to small datasets, (d) insufficient generalizability to new, unseen data, and (e) absence of a clear diagnostic metric. To develop a novel, data-driven, unsupervised, and generalizable method for identifying crucial brain regions and diagnosing ADHD, we introduce EssentialRfMRI. In a comparative assessment with existing rFMI-AKD and DeepComplexMultiTaskNet, we employ the Meta-SAT toolbox to investigate rs-fMRI datasets from the ADHD-200 global competition. Data analysis indicates that EssentialRfMRI surpasses the competing models in accuracy, AUC, F1-score, and processing speed while using minimal subject matter knowledge. Moreover, we demonstrate the importance of employing a data-driven, unsupervised approach over a supervised one and highlight the efficacy of our method for diagnosing ADHD and identifying pivotal brain regions in a data-driven manner. Crucially, our work shows that enhancing model robustness and generalizability is crucial for evaluating machine learning models in neuroscience applications. Ultimately, we advocate for further research in multiple domains: ADHD diagnosis, rs-fMRI analysis, and Meta-SAT. The code for our project is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Asinovhq/Meta-SAT.essential-rfMRI.git. Additionally, the processed data can be accessed on MINDA: https://minda.cmap.isc-karachi.org/index.php/2022/06/22/rfmi-essential/. With the integration of EssentialRfMRI and MINDA, researchers can replicate our approach and leverage rs-fMRI data to develop innovative, data-driven solutions for diagnosing ADHD and identifying pivotal brain regions in a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders. Our proposed DNA storage system addresses two significant issues of current DNA storage systems, which typically rely on interleaving data and indexing information. Firstly, we develop a compact hierarchy of folders and files, allowing for an arbitrary level of folder nesting. This is achieved through a binary refinement of folder and subfolder names. Secondly, we design a data update mechanism, enabling the revision of individual files within a large DNA storage without having to extract and re-encode the entire previous file. Instead, we only update the revised file's DNA strands, as the revised folding is implemented using a set of pre-crafted indexing vectors. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficiency of our proposed methods, showing they can maintain data integrity with reduced error rate, and provide faster indexing and file retrieval at a comparable error rate compared to current best approaches. Furthermore, our results indicate that, at a 10% error rate, our system allows for 2.8 times faster file retrieval and 3.3 times faster indexing operations compared to current benchmarks. This performance is maintained up to a 20% error rate. Additionally, our system allows for the use of shorter indexing vectors, resulting in a reduction of indexing vector length, thereby facilitating easier indexing, especially at higher error rates. This phenomenon is observed in every test, confirming the efficacy of our system design. Ultimately, our system validates the feasibility of maintaining hierarchical file organization and supporting data updates within large-scale DNA storage facilities. For clinical data labeling, a leading method, supervised learning, requires a substantial amount of annotated data which can be very expensive to obtain. In response, researchers turned to self-supervised learning techniques, a type of semi-supervised learning method that uses existing unlabeled data for model training. This paper explores self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled clinical text data for Improved Categorical Document (ICD) classification tasks. It demonstrates that pretraining a BERT model on unlabeled data results in significant performance enhancements when applied to classification tasks, particularly those with limited labeled data. Additionally, we found that using medical domain-specific unlabeled data alone is sufficient to achieve notable improvements in classification accuracy. This approach prevents potential biases from labeled data distribution shifts to unlabeled data and ensures that the model does not make unfounded assumptions about the data distribution. This semi-supervised method delivers state-of-the-art results on multiple clinical datasets, matching or exceeding the performance of fully supervised models. New types of quantum processors are being developed which use quantum circuits to learn patterns in data, potentially leading to new insights and applications, especially with unsupervised learning which can analyze complex data to find hidden patterns, unlike traditional machine learning which often requires extensive labeling. The current problem is the lack of understanding how quantum processors implement unsupervised learning and how to use them effectively to extract insights from data, especially with noisy quantum data that can cause incorrect results. Our research presents a new way of understanding how quantum processors learn patterns using clustering algorithms and experiments, and shows that incorporating prior knowledge into the learning process using constraints can improve the results by limiting the search space. This can be done effectively by adding penalties to the cost function for each constraint. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in extracting meaningful data from quantum measurements, and aligns with previous theoretical studies on the capabilities of quantum processors for unsupervised learning tasks. Additionally, our study showcases the first practical application of quantum processor's capability to learn patterns without prior knowledge of what the results should look like, specifically identifying overlapping communities in a graph of connections. Furthermore, our study also presents the first practical use of prior knowledge to improve the results by incorporating knowledge of data labels, specifically identifying countries sharing a common border. Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 KMTNet dataset, spanning a range of $0.15\,M_{\earth}$ to $10.2\,M_{\earth}$. Out of 112 prime-field planets, 81 were discovered by our analysis, a significant increase from the 56 previously reported by the KMTNet Anomaly Flagging Algorithm. Furthermore, 31 of these planets were identified in Gaia-EDR3 stars, demonstrating an enhanced level of completeness compared to the previous findings. A detailed examination of several key factors, including planet distribution, mass-to-projected separation ratios, and planetary mass range, reveals that our analysis is significantly more comprehensive than the previous findings. A substantial gain in completeness was observed for the planets with mass less than $3\,M_{\earth}$, particularly in the $0.15\,-\,0.5\,M_{\earth}$ mass range, where the new detection rate exceeded four times that of the previous findings. In contrast, the completeness of the massive planets ($>3\,M_{\earth}$) did not significantly improve, indicating that our algorithm performed optimally at higher mass ranges. A direct comparison between our analysis and the previous findings revealed that the main factor hindering the discovery of the massive planets was the excessive time invested in the follow-up observations. In an effort to facilitate smooth discovery processes, several suggested solutions, including the implementation of an automatic decision-making process and the use of Bayesian sampling method, are presented. Ultimately, our analysis led to the publication of eight new planetary anomalies, in addition to updating six previously reported values to a more reliable range. A total number of forty new prime-field planet masses were used, thereby expanding our existing knowledge and understanding of the microlensing method for planet detection. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based systems that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared content with standardised or ad-hoc terminology. While such collaborative knowledge graphs offer valuable insights to various domains, several aspects of these systems remain unexplored, including (1) content reuse across different platforms, (2) the evolution of tagging practices over time, (3) the reciprocal exchange of knowledge among users, and (4) the emergence of user collaboration. This study addresses these unanswered questions by conducting a comprehensive analysis of two large tag datasets extracted from Del.icio.us and Pinterest, providing valuable practical implications for system designers and developers in designing more efficient and effective annotation systems. Our analysis reveals several key findings, highlighted below. Firstly, content reuse occurs more frequently between Del.icio.us and Pinterest than expected, under shared domains. Secondly, tagging practices exhibit dynamic development, influenced by content popularity and user interest. Thirdly, user expertise is reflected in their contributions to knowledge graph entities, and fourthly, user collaboration is essential to maintaining and expanding the coverage of shared annotations. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the substantial potential of these collaborative knowledge graphs in supporting various social tasks. Based on these results, we offer several practical recommendations for system designers and developers in designing more efficient and effective annotation systems. These guidelines involve implementing user role definitions, informing tagging practices, and providing knowledge feedback to users, with the aim of optimising these collaborative knowledge graphs in practical applications. Additionally, code and data used in this study are publicly available at the specified links. Furthermore, a live demonstration of this study is accessible online. Lastly, we have formulated a research question that these results contribute to answering. Specifically, the interaction between technology and user-generated content. This challenge can be addressed by designing subwavelength structures that modulate curvature at the expense of thickness, effectively introducing an anisotropic and curvatures-dependent acoustic impedance. Implementing interactive augmented reality (AR) on mobile devices through Internet of Things (IoT) devices via wireless connections such as Bluetooth LE is addressed in this work. By drawing on existing standards, a proposed scheme called mobile IoT-based augmented reality (M-IABR) is outlined. This involves mapping 3D content to device IDs and translating this into readable data, which is then broadcast over the chosen wireless channel. The received data is then decoded and presented in a format understandable by the mobile device, allowing for the creation of an immersive AR experience. This can be achieved by combining the advantages of channelized and non-channelized IoT technologies, such as LoRaWAN and Bluetooth LE, in conjunction with an external server for data interpretation. In this study, we employ three global sensitivity analysis methods - Sobol, Saltelli, and generalized method - to rank the importance of hyperparameters in evolutionary algorithms. By conducting a comprehensive survey, we select six hyperparameters for further investigation in relation to a high-level optimization task. Using a robust and efficient implementation, we generate 1000 sets of random hyperparameters through Monte Carlo sampling, and evaluate their effectiveness in optimizing a fitness function. Subsequent global sensitivity analysis reveals the ranking of hyperparameter importance varies significantly depending on the method employed. However, all three approaches agree on the top three hyperparameters - crossover probability, mutation probability, and population size - as being particularly important. A comparison of the methods' results shows the Sobol method produces the most accurate rankings, while the generalized method offers the most efficient computations with potential to reduce runtime by a factor of 13 for this type of analysis. Based on these findings, we outline best practices for future research on EA hyperparameters, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive studies involving greater numbers of hyperparameters. Additionally, we highlight the prospect of employing global sensitivity analysis in a multi-faceted approach to optimal evolutionary algorithm design. Such an approach could leverage this method's strengths, addressing the challenges inherent in optimizing many parameters at once. This research also raises implications for selecting hyperparameters in actual evolutionary algorithm implementations, suggesting a range of possible strategies from tuning a single parameter in isolation to a comprehensive global search. The first-principles derivation of the wave formula for two-body scattering problems, dating back to the 1930s, has been reexamined with a focus on its underlying mathematical structure. This investigation reveals that the conventional approaches, based on partial wave analysis or impact parameter representations, introduce unneeded complexities. A streamlined proof is presented, leveraging the rotational invariance of the scattering process and the structure of plane-wave states. Additionally, this analysis sheds light on the wave formula's generalizability to relativistic quantum mechanics, involving the substitution of relativistic covariance for rotational invariance. Further discussion explores the wave formula's significance in the context of modern experimental techniques. It is contended that, not only does the wave formula offer a clear, conceptually grounded understanding of the scattering process, but it also provides an opportune framework for the interpretation and analysis of measurement data. By expressing the wave formula in terms of the relative distance $t$ between the constancy centers of the initial and final plane-wave states, the scattering amplitude can be directly linked to the measured intensity distribution. This derivation, using the wave formula's singularities, also offers an innovative explanation for the origin of the diffracted wave and its connection to the non-relativistic Schrödinger scattering solution. Finally, the notion that the wave formula encapsulates the all-encompassing principles of quantum mechanics, as initially suggested by Heisenberg, is reconsidered and expanded upon, particularly with regard to the role of gauge transformations in relativistic quantum scattering. It is argued that the wave formula stands as a singular representation of quantum mechanics, encompassing the principles of rotational invariance and relativistic covariance, and that its Scattering amplitude, with the extraction of the non-relativistic Schrödinger potential, offers a comprehensive framework for the interpretation of quantum mechanical principles. Specifically, it is contended that the wave formula's singularities, encompassing both the Dirac and soft photon singularities, serve as a distinct manifestation of the quantum mechanical double-slits experiment, encapsulating the fundamental, irreducible nature of quantum mechanics. Additionally, it is suggested that the volume phase space, corresponding to the wave formula's extraction of the non-relativistic Schrödinger potential and their successive corrections, offers an essential understanding of the quantization of electromagnetic radiation. Ultimately, this analysis seeks to revive Heisenberg's views and introduce a fresh perspective on the wave formula's significance in relating the principles of quantum mechanics to the observable properties of scattering processes.

Despite the potential of lifelong reinforcement reinforcement learning to save time, effort, and resources, current methods often struggle to adapt and generalize across diverse sets of skills. One significant obstacle is the absence of comprehensive evaluation frameworks that can assess a variety of abilities and adapt to various scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present L2Explorer, an extensive benchmark environment designed to evaluate lifelong reinforcement learning strategies through a wide range of tasks. L2Explorer integrates multiple challenge types, including discrete and continuous action spaces, dynamics variations, and a mix of simple and complex target skills. We develop a methodology to categorize skills at different levels of difficulty and propose metrics to gauge the effectiveness of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. We evaluate our framework using four state-of-the-art algorithms and report its performance on various skill levels, demonstrating the potential for future improvement in lifelong reinforcement learning. The code and benchmark are openly accessible on https://github.com/ashwink/L2Explorer.

We explore a class of perturbations to the 2D Euler equation on a torus, examining non-linear disturbances that decay over time while maintaining a fixed energy level. The study reveals that these perturbations can induce a unique phenomenon - the emergence of traveling waves within the flow field - where the location of these waves exhibits a specific, irregular pattern as they move. This phenomenon is akin to the 'wavetrain' patterns observed in other types of flows, and similar to the behavior seen in the quasi-geostrophic equation. The results we obtain are contingent on a specific assumption regarding the structure of these perturbations. This assumption posits the existence of a specific type of oscillatory behavior ('geodesic orbit') within the flow, and asserts that these oscillations can be found everywhere within the flow field. This 'geodesic orbit' assumption is reminiscent of concepts seen in other research on quasi-geostrophic equations, and its validity can be confirmed through analytical reasoning for certain types of perturbations ('small-scale' perturbations with sufficiently high frequencies). The application of these geodesic orbits enables us to demonstrate the existence of unique 'interactions,' in which two geodesic orbits with distinct frequencies and directions merge to form a single, more complex wave pattern, retaining the characteristics of its constituent orbits. The merging of these geodesic orbits represents a unique instance of non-linear interaction within the flow dynamic. The study strongly suggests that these perturbations can induce an infinite number of interacting wave patterns within the flow, and implies the existence of an intricate, lattice-like structure underlying these wave patterns, as well as their energy distribution. The realization of this lattice-like structure is contingent on understanding how these wave patterns ('lattice sites')) compose the flow, and how their interaction produces more complex patterns ('lattice solvents')), a concept first proposed by Edwards in the context of quasi-geostrophic equations. The observed changes in polarization are the result of geometric resonance, caused by excitation transfer between modes, and can be modelled using a system of coupled McGhee-Singer equations. By adjusting the beam's polarization, we control the growth of a single condensate, and study its coupling and coherence for various modes. The observed effects are comparable to all-optical spin manipulation techniques. The ability to control linear polarization offers potential applications in the creation of polariton lasers with unique properties. Moreover, our research provides insight into the complex dynamics of anisotropic exciton-polariton systems, and paves the way for further exploration of optically trapped polariton condensates. The findings have implications for the development of new materials with unusual optical properties. The work also opens doors for future research on all-optical polarization control, and could lead to the design of novel optical devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solutions to these equations exhibit both a large-time growth rate and a form of 'weak comparison principle'. Additionally, we expand upon the existing parabolic equation theories by showing that the solutions to these KPZ-type equations are continuous and have a specific, quantifiable growth rate in space. Our work builds upon previous research by providing the first proof of the solutions' space-time regularity and H\"older continuity. Finally, we propose a set of related non-local'slope type' equations and demonstrate the existence of a single, "viscous nature" solution class for these equations. X-ray images contain valuable information about ICU admission criteria for COVID-19 patients, which can help clinicians make more informed decisions by providing a quick visual assessment of patients' lung conditions. Previous studies primarily focused on COVID-19 diagnosis, ignoring the images' potential for guiding ICU admissions. This study investigated lung conditions in severe COVID-19 cases through X-ray images to explore their connection with ARDS, oxygen therapy needs, and life-threatening respiratory complications, which are key factors for ICU admissions. By leveraging a diverse dataset of 11,566 paired images, the researchers evaluated six clinical indicators, including PaO2/FiO2 ratios, pneumonia severity indices, acute respiratory distress syndrome severity, the need for oxygen therapy, respiratory failure, and life-threatening respiratory complications. To quantify lung conditions, the researchers employed quantitative measurement analysis, which estimated the percentage of damaged lung tissue from chest X-ray images. By combining human judgment and computational methods, the researchers derived potential attributes of ICU admission in X-ray images, which are correlated with patients' underlying lung conditions. These findings suggest that computational models using paired image datasets can accurately measure the percentage of damaged lung tissue, which is a reliable indicator for clinicians to assess patients' underlying lung conditions. This study draws inspiration from Yang's work in 2001, where he introduced an H2 equation that has since been extensively studied by many mathematicians and physicists over the past 20 years. Our analysis includes an in-depth examination of various symmetry conditions and the generation of exact solution families to the H2 equation. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the H2 equation and other renowned integrable equations, such as the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) and the Yang-Baxter equation. Our discussion also delves into various approaches used to construct solutions to the H2 equation and related problems. Lastly, we make a formal statement regarding ongoing conjectures related to the H2 equation. The primary aim of this paper is to provide an approachable entry point for young mathematicians and physicists who are interested in exploring the recent advancements in this field. Yielding to the abundance of novel results and ideas in this field, we have inevitably encountered a challenge of condensing the content and presenting it coherently within the scope of this review. In an effort to make the content more readable, we have divided the paper into multiple sections, each focusing on distinct topics, while making sure the content is self-contained. It is hoped that this review will inspire further exploration into the latest developments in this field and foster collaborative efforts between mathematicians and physicists to tackle the remaining unsolved problems. This framework is based on weak measurement techniques and can detect quantum correlations that remain hidden in classical form. This price of quantum correlation is inversely proportional to the measurement strength and increases with the level of decoherence. To illustrate our approach, we apply it to two specific situations: first, to a single qubit in an arbitrary state, where we show that small but non-zero quantum correlation prices are possible even when all relevant probabilities are small; second, to multi-qubit systems specifically studying the correlation price in the GHZ state. This framework has potential for use in precision measurement and quantum sensing applications. The use of weak measurement-induced quantum correlation price allows us to extract and evaluate non-classical quantum effects in systems like quantum sensing and precision measurement. This involves monitoring the evolution of a quantum state and its non-classical correlations as it interacts with a noisy environment. To this end, we also derive a general formula for tracking the time-dependent correlation price of a quantum state over time. This approach provides a way to understand and quantify the impact of environmental influences on quantum correlations. This understanding can be applied to design protocols for protecting and maintaining quantum correlations in reality. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. This paper tackles a critical issue in MCM optimization, which is the selection of appropriate coefficients to reduce hardware costs. A novel method is proposed to find the optimal coefficients with the least number of hardware components. This approach, known as Opt-HW-Cost, uses a novel hardware cost model (HW-Cost) that accurately predicts hardware expenses during the coefficient optimization process. HW-Cost quantifies hardware usage by counting unique bits in multiplier and accumulator circuits, as well as essential control signals. HW-Cost is highly efficient, enabling its computation within 0.1 ms, even for large circuits. This paper also proposes an iterative optimization algorithm (Iter-Opt-HW-Cost) that further reduces hardware costs by iteratively fine-tuning HW-Cost-optimized coefficients. Both Opt-HW-Cost and Iter-Opt-HW-Cost algorithms demonstrate superior performance in extensive experiments, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods, such as GCOs, DPGCOs, and SGPMCs. These methods are suboptimal and can only be approxately computed in $O(N\log N)$ time, whereas HW-Cost optimization takes $O(N^3)$ and Iter-Opt-HW-Cost takes $O(N^2\log N)$. HW-Cost also offers a versatile hardware cost model that can be adapted for various hardware constraints, such as popular Xilinx and Microsemi FPGAs. Overall, this paper introduces a cutting-edge hardware optimization technique, HW-Cost, which is fast, efficient, and user-friendly. HW-Cost is now the best method in its class and is freely available for non-commercial use at www.hw-cost.com. Moreover, this paper introduces Iter-Opt-HW-Cost, a sophisticated algorithm that is the most efficient hardware optimizer in its class and is freely available for non-commercial use at www.hw-cost.com. HW-Cost is a hardware cost model that can be adapted to various hardware constraints and is one of the most versatile models of its type. Finally, this paper's experimental results are the first to demonstrate the relationship between HW-Cost and actual hardware usage. Consequently, HW-Cost is an accurate predictor of hardware expenses in embedded systems. For these reasons, HW-COST is an innovative approach

We derive generalized energy and momentum conservation equations for relativistic fluid dynamics with viscosity, incorporating external forces such as electric and magnetic fields. By applying the relativistic Stefan-Maxwell equation for diffusion, the entire set of hydrodynamic equations becomes self-consistent. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding Euler-Poincar\'e equations for an ideal fluid with external fields, excluding diffusion. In both cases, the energy-momentum tensor and diffusion flux are key components. The structure of our viscous hydrodynamic equations aligns with the second law of thermodynamics when the external fields vanish. By applying the linearized theory, we examine the characteristics of relativistic viscous viscoelastic shocks and the interaction between electromagnetic fields and relativistic viscous fluids. The theory we've developed can be applied to the study of heavy-ion collisions and cosmological perturbations. In particular, we evaluate the effects of relativistic viscosity on neutron star mergers. Finally, we have calculated the characteristic relaxation time of the transverse metric perturbation, yielding a time dependence governed by the equation $t_\sigma t_\rho = const.$, where $t_\sigma$ and $t_\rho$ represent the timescales associated with shear viscosity and charge diffusion, respectively. Furthermore, we explore how the phenomenon of ejection due to stellar disturbances affects the number of generating black holes, thereby influencing the intensity of the emitted signal. Ultimately, we relate our findings to existing observations of the universe's background radio radiation. Additionally, we speculate on the detection of electromagnetic signals from individual massive black hole mergers, which could result in a substantial expansion in the universe's magnetic field following a massive binary black hole merger that gives rise to a gamma-ray burst and gravitational waves. This process might also generate a significant amount of radio energy as the universe's matter falls into the newly formed black hole. A more substantial portion of this energy is concentrated at higher frequencies and powers a more energetic and shorter-lasting cosmic phenomenon compared to radio energy at lower frequencies and a longer-scale cosmic phenomenon. Consequently, heavy binary black hole mergers might not significantly alter the universe's background radio spectrum, which could be an essential indicator for identifying these events. High-definition video capture by conventional cameras typically yields just three color values, yet many important image details are lost in this process. To capture a wider range of information, systems that record four or more colors (e.g. 400-450) exist, a process known as multispectral or hyperspectral imaging. Capturing additional spectral data enables detection of hidden or hard-to-detect environmental factors like moisture, temperature, and atmospheric conditions. In this research, we explore how hyperspectral image analysis can improve urban street semantic segmentation, specifically using just four spectral bands. To achieve this, we designed and implemented a semantic segmentation framework that combines an existing model, a multispectral image conversion module, and a domain adaptation technique. While conventional RGB images are sufficient for many semantic segmentation tasks, our results demonstrate that accessing extra hyperspectral data can significantly improve related tasks. To test this, we created a new dataset by converting and extending the labels from the popular Cityscapes dataset to match the hyperspectral frequency. When applying our system to the newly created, expanded Cityscapes hyperspectral dataset, performance improved by nearly 5% over the standard version. These gains come at the cost of minimal computational complexity, roughly doubling runtime with minimal thread overhead. To validate our approach, corresponding 3D thermal and near-infrared images were captured and used in a separate experiment to convert and extend existing Cityscapes labels, revealing comparable performance to traditional RGB capture. The session-based recommender system leverages session information, while the user-id and item-id models utilize respective attributes. The key innovation here is the development of two self-supervised learning strategies, user-graph augmentation and item-graph augmentation, to create new, synthetic sessions for the user-id and item-id models. The resulting three models are then trained simultaneously to maximize the mutual information between the three models' outputs and the original data. Recent studies have introduced a novel concept, differential shapes, to further expand the meaning of forms from the Borel-Vargronce framework. This new framework has significant connections with various mathematical and physical concepts, such as homotopy classes, cohomology classes with coefficients, and integrals of Feynman paths. This article aims to develop a more general approach by applying the concept of differential shapes to the simplicial complexes representing graphs. This generalized framework is then demonstrated by computing the differential shapes of graph homology complexes, which are specifically derived from the Hodge theory. A graphical representation, known as shape graphs, is introduced to visually display the shapes, and their connections to Feynman integrals are explored through examples. Lastly, this article expresses suggestions and open questions related to generalizing this framework to higher-dimensional complexes.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the underlying rationale for the efficacy of RNNs in object categorization.  We've trained RNNs on an object-based image dataset to analyze the dependencies between object traits and categorization performance.  The findings indicate that RNNs exploit object trait relationships to overcome situations where low-level visual data is insufficient for categorization.  Additionally, it was observed that RNNs can efficiently handle categories with distinct subcategories, leveraging the inherent structure within these groups.  The study reveals that RNNs are capable of capturing object trait interactions, thus providing a solid justification for the use of RNNs in object categorization.  This work holds potential for expanding the scope of RNNs in object representation, potentially leading to broader applications in object-based tasks.  The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/pkulm11/object_categorization_rnn.  The dataset used in this study can be found at https://github.com/pkulm11/oorl_objects_dataset.  The dataset comprises images of everyday objects, along with their respective shapes, colors, and material properties.  This repository also includes a tutorial on training recurrent neural networks for object categorization.  This work is part of a larger research endeavor funded by the Fondation Blaer. Several techniques have been proposed to tackle optimization challenges using continuous values. Despite some methods outperforming others in specific scenarios, their heavy reliance on complex mathematical formulations often makes them difficult to implement. This can hinder the adoption of these techniques, particularly for those working outside the primary flow of cutting-edge research in optimization. To address this issue, we present a unified framework, called LibOPT, for encapsulating prominent soft optimization methods via straightforward, generic code. LibOPT aims to serve as an open-source resource, allowing users to effortlessly adapt existing approaches or combine elements from multiple sources. We evaluate the effectiveness of LibOPT by replicating recent research papers and comparing its performance to existing benchmark results, also providing an extensive collection of optimization problems to facilitate future replication. To cap off, we propose two novel improvements to the Kiwi optimizer, a previously dominant method, further demonstrating LibOPT's utility in developing custom optimization solutions. Kiwi's variants, along with other techniques, can be found within the LibOPT repository at https://github.com/CSSE-KBC/kiwi_optimizer. Source codes for our replication studies are available at https://github.com/CSSE-KBC/ LibOPT_tutorials. Additionally, the optimized solution hyperparameters for our replication experiments have been stored on AURORA at https://aurora.bj.bjd.com/#/project/home?id=62b5c0c1bea9f60001c6d0c9. Kiwi's performance hyperparameters can also be found on AURORA at https://aurora.bj.bjd.com/#/project/home?id=62bbaa1bea9f60001c6d0c9. Finally, the used programming language is Python 3.x, also featuring PyTorch 1.x for tensor-related operations, at https://pytorch.org/. The aim of this work is to examine the properties of quantum fields operating within a non-commutative space-time. Building on initial findings by Doublik et al. in 2018, we explore the behavior of the one-loop Casimir energy as the non-commutation length, $\Delta$, approaches its critical value, $\Delta_c$. We extend their work by investigating how the energy and its associated self-energy change as $\Delta$ tends towards $\Delta_c$ from both the above and below perspectives. These investigations lead to intriguing contrasts in the above/below behaviors for the energy and self-energy, especially when $\Delta \to \Delta_c$. Notably, while the energy exhibits regressive properties near $\Delta_c$, the self-energy showcases progressive properties. Additionally, a crucial identification emerges - the field normalization constant - which proves to be highly versatile in describing the above/below behaviors of quantum field operators as $\Delta \to \Delta_c$. Importantly, our work uncovers the impact of space-time non-commutativity on field identity, revealing that the $\Delta \to \delta$ limit may behave differently depending on whether $\Delta$ approaches $\delta$ from above or below. Lastly, we explore an interesting analogy with the Landau pole, where our analysis indicates that the field in question becomes an instanton field near $\Delta_c$, thereby losing its original identity, much like what happens near a Landau pole. Ultimately, our work provides fresh insights into space-time non-commutativity, thereby refuting a long-held conjecture that the effect is minimal. Instead, we find that the influence is substantial and identifiable, if the above/below distinction is taken into account. Ultimately, this distinction holds potential for resolving the identity crisis of quantum field theory in the non-commutative framework. Steps towards resolving this identity crisis have been outlined in a joint publication by the authors [arXiv:2306.19070]. Brief discussions on the broader implications are presented in [arXiv:2306.19071]. Further discussions on the spectral action are presented in [arXiv:2306.19072]. We introduce a novel technique called photo-capacitance transient-voltage technique, a two-photon absorption variation of the standard photoluminescence transient-voltage technique. This method utilizes 800 nm femtosecond laser pulses to generate electron-hole pairs near a p-type diamond/gap FET contact, and as these charges move towards the contact, they are detected by sensing a capacitance change. The technique allows for spatial resolution on the order of micrometers in three-dimensional charge transport mapping within the diamond material. We have successfully mapped the charge transport in single-crystalline diamond substrates, revealing a significant anisotropy in charge transport depending on the diamond's orientation. Our results show an average 30% increase in charge transport speed along the [110] axis compared to the [111] axis, and we attribute this phenomenon to the interaction between the charge carriers and the diamond's lattice structure. We have also demonstrated the ability to map charge transport at depths of up to 500 micrometers, and we believe this technique will enable further exploration into the physical properties of semiconductors. Additionally, we have discovered that the diamond's surface composition plays a crucial role in our measurements, and we have used this information to guide a successful method for removing surface impurities and enhancing the diamond's charge transport efficiency. A 30% improvement in charge transport speed through surface purification treatment was achieved, verifying the technique's potential for optimizing diamond-based device performance. We believe this novel approach will contribute significantly to the understanding and development of diamond semiconductor technology. The findings of this study confirm the reliability of the proposed controller and its compatibility with the underlying dynamics of the mobile base. The reliability of the controller can be further enhanced by adjusting certain parameters, as demonstrated in this research. The parameters in question control the rate at which control input is modified; thus, slower adjustment of control input is associated with increased robustness but also delays response time. Although its concept is straightforward, its practical application is often complicated by factors such as e-commerce platform constraints, limited performance, and complex mathematical calculations. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Importantly, our results indicate that a specific rate of convergence can be achieved even for functions with jump discontinuities. These findings validate the use of this new interpolation method in a range of real-world applications, including the approximation of piecewise linear functions. Due to its computationally expensive nature, we have devised an optimized implementation that reduces computational costs. Additionally, we discuss potential extensions of this method to support additional properties, such as symmetry. With further development, this interpolation function has the potential to significantly contribute to the field of scattered data interpolation. Although they offer several advantages in terms of flexibility and use cases, controlling them can be a difficult task. Controlling these grippers in a simulated online environment is particularly challenging, especially when dealing with the complexity of soft materials and their inherent variability. This paper presents an innovative approach using Koopman operator theory for modeling the dynamics of soft grippers and their control through a learning-based method, focusing on high-dimensional states and uncertain parameters. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, whether single-model or ensemble, typically rely solely on text data from various sources, including medical records. By neglecting valuable information in other modalities, these models may overlook crucial context, limiting their accuracy. To address this issue, we present a new approach, the Multimodal Survival Time to Treatment Duration ensemble model (MSTTDE), which integrates image and text data to facilitate more informed predictions. By combining a Deep Network with Meta Pooled Features, derived from images classified as lung cancer or not, our method enhances predictive performance, as demonstrated by experiments using two publicly available datasets. Notably, MSTTDE achieved a 0.30 multiple net reclassification improvement when evaluating model refinements with relevant clinical variables. To validate its utility in clinical settings, we applied our method to an actual patient case, resulting in more accurate survival time predictions compared to models relying solely on text data. The associated code is publicly accessible on the GitHub platform.

A natural language state description is a crucial component in Reinforcement Learning, enabling efficient representation of complex state spaces and promoting direct learning from real-world data. This overview showcases the effectiveness of state descriptions in various domains, highlights their advantages and challenges, and examines current evaluation methodologies. It also discusses the potential of state descriptions in general for Reinforcement Learning, and provides a comprehensive literature review on the topic. Additionally, the appendix includes a detailed discussion of relevant papers from the arXiv archive from 2020 to 2021. State descriptions have emerged as a viable solution for dealing with large state spaces in Reinforcement Learning. A key aspect of this is the use of natural language state descriptions in domain-knowledge-based policies and their potential for learning representations from real-world data. While state descriptions offer several benefits, working with them can be complex and challenging due to issues related to data privacy, comprehensibility, and the need for specialized data processing. As a result, the focus is often on the inherent properties of state descriptions rather than their processing. When evaluating state descriptions, the common metric is the immediate performance gain after representation. However, this is not the only aspect, and other factors such as data efficiency, generalization, and the impact of changes in the state description space should also be considered. Ultimately, the success of state descriptions depends on specific problem instances and domains, and their potential is reduced when the state space is small or well-structured. A key example of state descriptions in action can be seen in the autonomous driving domain, where descriptions are used to formulate actions and have shown significant performance gains in a variety of tasks. While there are many other domains where state descriptions have been applied, such as video games and text-based environments, their use in real-world tasks remains limited due to existing issues. A key example is the domain of navigation, where state descriptions have been used to guide agents in simulated environments. The detection of gravitational waves opened a new window into studying cosmic phenomena, allowing future observations of gravitational waves to comprise an evolving background noise that could significantly complicate detecting distant signals. We investigate this background noise, which is created by the gravitational wave memory generated by supernovae explosions in distant galaxies. Using an inelastic scattering model for the explosion process, we estimate the power density of this background noise and find that it varies according to the level of inelastic scattering, which ranges from a low value of $10^{-20}\mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$ to a high value of $10^{-16}\mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$, both of which are independent of frequency. We also observe that the amplitude of this background noise is directly proportional to the average gravitational wave signal power of supernovae, which can be used to estimate the order of magnitude of this background noise based on existing measurements. We conclude that this background noise may be a significant limitation for future gravitational wave detectors, such as LISA, unless the frequency at which it is measured is significantly elevated. If and when this background noise is observed, it could provide insight into the occurrence rates of core collapse supernovae in distant galaxies. Additionally, we note that the amplitude of this background noise is highly variable and can be altered by altering the explosion dynamics of supernovae. Thus, measuring the background noise could potentially offer new insights into the physical processes occurring during the explosion of these celestial events. We eventually outline an approach through which the background noise can be differentiated from stationary noise, which could provide more accurate estimates of explosion dynamics variability. We eventually estimate that this background noise could be in the range of $10^{-17} \mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$ to $10^{-13} \mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$. Due to our reliance on an external explosion model, we suspect that our estimates are only approximate and likely to be significantly altered by alternative explosion models. For example, models of magnetic explosion could generate a background noise with a frequency-dependent amplitude that might be within a more manageable range for future detectors. In any case, we believe that observing this background noise will offer a novel approach to studying the explosion dynamics of distant star explosions. We estimate that a signal frequency above $10^{-16} \mathrm{Hz}$ will mean that the background noise is within a range that could be managed by future detectors, while frequencies below this threshold may make it more challenging for these detectors to accurately measure gravitational wave signals. Lastly, a related universe scenario, where phases are swapped, results in the universe's large-scale scale and the presence of dark matter without needing any additional particles. A key aspect of intelligent brain function is causal reasoning, which enables individuals to integrate information about cause-and-effect relationships within complex environments. Although symbolic and connectionist approaches have been applied to reason causally, existing symbolic methods often rely on rigorous axiomatic frameworks that are difficult to extend symbolically. In contrast, connectionist methods are limited in their ability to generalize from one task to another due to overfitting and a lack of clear semantic meaning in their output representations. In this research, we combine the strengths of both symbolic and connectionist approaches by employing a signaling game framework to facilitate a dialogue between an agent using a connectionist network and a symbolic agent representing the causal structure of the environment. As a result, the connectionist network learns to signal the symbolic agent's underlying assumptions about cause-and-effect relationships, which in turn enables the symbolic agent to update its knowledge through new insights gained from the agent's new perspective. When applied to multiple tasks, our method allows the connectionist network to transfer knowledge across tasks and the symbolic agent to integrate knowledge from diverse tasks. Through experimentation, we show that both the connectionist and symbolic agents are able to generalize effectively to new tasks. The widespread adoption of Session-based recommendation systems has led to a surge in online shopping experiences, empowering users to make informed decisions during the purchasing process. Nonetheless, current advancements in Recurrent Neural Network-based session models have highlighted the importance of incorporating historical data in enhancing predictive capabilities. Nonetheless, the inherent limitations of session models in capturing long-term user preferences remain unaddressed. In an effort to fill this gap, we introduce an innovative method that integrates the established session model, NARM, in conjunction with a matrix factorization technique using Rank Embeddings. The newly proposed method, RE-NARM NDCG, exhibits exceptional performance when evaluated against current best practices, showcasing improved accuracy when provided with additional user knowledge. Specifically, the RE-NARM NDCG method achieves state-of-the-art results on two real-world datasets when evaluated under a 10-minute time constraint, with notable enhancements of 3.0% and 7.2% when supplemented with user item frequency and purchase history, respectively. Moreover, a comparative analysis of our method with data augmentation strategies confirms the efficacy of incorporating long-term user preferences in conjunction with session-based models for predicting long-term outcomes. Furthermore, an in-depth examination of our method's design choices, along with its theoretical underpinnings, is provided in the study. Lastly, the proposed method has been made available for public access through our implemented code repository. In particular, the RE-NARM NDCG method can be accessed via the link: https://github.com/asharathp/TwoStageSessionRank.git. By automating the process of incorporating long-term user preferences, our method offers an easily accessible means of integrating historical data for developers when designing and deploying modern SBRS systems. With continued advancements in the field of SBRS, the developed method can serve as an essential foundation for crafting data systems that cater to the diverse needs of online shoppers. Additionally, the underlying concepts of our study can be applied across a broader spectrum of recommendation systems, encompassing the crucial domains of user engagement and interactive advertising. In conclusion, our two-stage approach using NARM and Rank Embeddings embodies an innovative solution to enhancing the predictive capabilities of session-based recommendation systems, marked by its simplicity and effectiveness. The accompanying code can be found on the specified GitHub repository. Additionally, a demo of our method is available at the link provided at the end of the abstract. Recent research on active particles has expanded our knowledge of dynamic systems, generating significant interest due to their living-cell-inspired behavior and ability to simulate cellular interactions. To explore the behavior of active particles in activity gradients, we introduce a novel method using dynamic molecular clusters formed from colloidal particles. These clusters remain linked by short, flexible polymers whose ends are coated with complementary materials, facilitating bonding between adjacent particles. We have observed that these clusters can move through activity gradients at a speed influenced by the gradient's curvature, which in turn affects the rotation and oscillation of the clusters. Our findings reveal a notable similarity with the swimming behavior of individual active particles, and the dynamic characteristics of the clusters are influenced by their size and shape, as well as the presence of applied forces. In activity gradients, these colloidal molecules exhibit a range of motion from rotational oscillations to nearly linear motion, and we have observed that their movement is affected by activity-driven forces and the mechanical constraints imposed by the active bonds linking the particles. To understand the dynamic behavior of these clusters, we have developed a theoretical model, which when compared with our experimental results, demonstrates the importance of considering the persistent correlations present in active fluids. Furthermore, our research shows that the dynamic characteristics of the colloidal molecules can be harnessed to control their movement and that active materials can be designed to exhibit non-traditional forms of motion, such as geometric oscillations. In summary, our research on dynamic colloidal molecules provides a new perspective on the behavior of active materials and their numerous applications, which could soon impact various fields, including biotechnology, technology, and medicine. It is unlikely that these materials will be used in industry in the near future; however, further research on the dynamic behavior of active colloids is essential to exploring their full potential. Therefore, we recommend investigating more complex structures composed of multiple colloidal molecules, which could exhibit sophisticated forms of motion and provide a deeper understanding of the dynamic characteristics of active materials. These studies could be conducted using techniques such as light microscopy, imaging, and fluorescence, which allow for the observation of individual particles and structures in great detail. Ultimately, by advancing our knowledge of dynamic colloidal systems, we can develop novel designs for active materials that can outperform conventional designs. Similarly, by studying the behavior of smaller and larger dynamic particles, we may uncover universal principles that can be applied to a broader range of active materials and living systems. The discrete fracture model assumes fractures as 2D entities, while the proposed method generates and solves 3D meshes for fracture and rock domains. A generic fracture handling system allows for various fracture types, including non-planar and non-parallel cases. Numerical examples are provided to validate the model's performance. One such example examines flow in a fractured core from a real gas well in the Montney shale formation, highlighting the importance of resolving fracture boundaries correctly. This research explores the Seidel matrix associated with a linked graph, a type of graph that incorporates chain interactions, and provides a matrix representation of the graph's signed adjacency matrix. We investigate the maximum eigenvalue of the graph's Seidel matrix, determining its range and optimal values, in addition to examining the total Seidel energy for different types of chains, including chain graphs and cyclic graphs with distinct parameters. Our findings are further illustrated by examining examples of chain graphs. We also propose a possible generalization of our results to more complex graph structures.

We investigate optimal feedback controls for mean-field stochastic differential equations involving multidimensional systems with jumps, which are driven by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurwitz condition. The objective is to maximize expected discounts of future costs, subject to constraints on the system's state. To overcome the challenges posed by the fractional nature of the motion and the growth of the system's drift and cost functions, we establish the existence of a continuous solution to the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation under relaxed regularity assumptions. The solution represents the optimal feedback control strategy. Notably, our approach relies on distinct mathematical analyses, including an extension of the regularity theory for mean-field stochastic equations and a new estimate for the fractional White noise process. The latter estimates the probability of its self-intersecting paths. Furthermore, we develop a counterexample demonstrating the nonexistence of a continuous solution to the Hamilton-Jacii equation when the Hurwitz condition is not satisfied. The study also includes an in-depth numerical example illustrating the optimal control strategy using a combination of symbolic and numeric methods. The outcome shows that the optimal control strategy can be effectively implemented in a real-world application involving a queue with customers arriving and departing. The associated code is available at https://github.com/Matheur/Mean-field_optimal_control_fractional_BM. This research is part of a broader effort to develop essential mathematical tools for controlling complex multidimensional systems driven by fractional noise. The work is set to continue with an in-depth analysis of the fractional White noise process and its applications in optimal control problems. Specifically, it is intended to investigate the fractional White noise process as a controlling process in stochastic optimal control problems. The research is expected to contribute to existing literature on fractional Brownian motion and its applications in mathematical economics and finance, particularly in the areas of option pricing, risk management, and asset management. Additionally, it is poised to influence the field of control theory, enhancing our understanding of the optimal control of fractional SDE systems that are robust against controlling noises. Furthermore, the study may have practical implications for systems that are affected by fractional noise due to the presence of memory in their behavior. The outcome could potentially be utilized in the development of innovative algorithms capable of modeling the optimal control of systems that exhibit past-dependent behavior. To summarize, this research is a foundational study that is expected to expand into new areas in the future. The proposed work will include investigating the fractional White noise process and its applications in optimal control problems, particularly in multidimensional systems that are affected by the Hurwitz condition

This study focuses on transferring knowledge in a decision-based black-box setting, where little is known about the model's internal workings. In a zero-shot knowledge transfer context, limited information about the base model is required. We explore a novel 6-shot approach where we start with no initial knowledge and gather knowledge through six decisions made with the target model in mind. Our goal is to accurately predict unknown classes with little to no training data available. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on four different datasets by comparing it to a black-box knowledge distillation method and a white-box transfer method. The results show that our decision-based approach outperforms the black-box method and matches the performance of the white-box method. We also investigate the impact of varying shooting parameters, such as number of shots, shooting style, and shooting interval. Additionally, we analyze our model's robustness against potential threats, such as changes in shooting styles and the presence of shooting noise. A comprehensive evaluation of our proposed method can be found on our website. It has been observed that the proposed method performs well across different domains and can be an accessible option for developers who lack detailed information about the model they are working with. It is especially beneficial when compared to other methods that require more sophisticated representations, such as attention-based methods. We hypothesize that the method's success is due to its ability to focus on decision boundaries rather than detailed model structures. A potential area of improvement for this method would be its incorporation of more advanced learning techniques in machine learning. It is also interesting to explore its potential applications in areas such as computer vision and natural language processing. In the future, we plan to examine the following: The influence of different shooting types on the model and whether decision boundaries can effectively capture semantic representations. Whether knowledge transfer can be applied to areas such as image classification and sentimnt analysis. The use of more sophisticated shooting styles, such as multi-shot, to see if it could lead to better outcomes. By incorporating imitation learning into policy optimization, imitation learning can overcome challenges like limited data and slow training. Nevertheless, imitation learning typically necessitates an abundance of expert demonstrations, which is often impractical. Consequently, many existing methods rely on costly and time-consuming manual data collection. This paper proposes a novel imitation learning technique that omits the requirement for expert demonstrations. Our approach leverages peer agents' behavior to educate each other within the training process. We dub this method co-imitation training. By contrasting agent performance under this training method against traditional imitation learning, we demonstrate the co-imitation training technique surpasses expert imitation learning in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, by integrating co-imitation training with peer feedback, we show the approach yields comparable or superior results as compared to state-of-the-art imitation learning methods without expert demonstrations. Our research focuses on continuous control domains involving high-dimensional environments. For evaluation, we employ a range of challenging simulations, including robotic tasks and image-based navigation. Moreover, we achieve notable real-world robotic emulation results using the domain we define. Specifically, the robotic tasks we train replicate the warehouse-picker upper scenario exactly. Details regarding the implementation and video recordings are available upon access to our project website. With this success, we hope the concept of co-imitation training inspires innovative research in collaborative learning.  Key Code is hosted on https://github.com/yindong2009/Co-Imitation Training.
