In the past few years, the use of differential equations to model state evolution has become increasingly popular, even when the underlying world is not continuous. For discrete-state models, specific algorithms like the Runge-Kutta method are widely used and well-understood. However, these algorithms were originally designed with the assumption that time is divided into distinct, equal segments. This paper explores the modification of these algorithms to accommodate varying time intervals, drawing on recent advancements in optimal control theory. We demonstrate the applicability of this modified algorithm to various differential models by applying it to a problem of estimating the position of a vehicle based on sensor data. This modified algorithm is then evaluated under different time division schemes, showcasing its ability to handle non-uniform time intervals. Furthermore, we illustrate the computational efficiency of this modified algorithm by comparing its performance with its discrete-time equivalent when time intervals become increasingly finer. This modified continuous-time estimation algorithm holds significant promise for applications where sensor data is transmitted discontinuously but the underlying dynamic model is continuous. Experimental validation on a drone system with non-uniform communication schedules reveals that this continuous-time algorithm remains just as effective as its discrete-time counterpart even in such scenarios. Detailed mathematical justifications and simulations are also provided. We expect that the ongoing advancements in communication technology, enabling smoother data transmission, will further the integration of this modified algorithm within this new domain. On the other hand, our research also delves into the theoretical underpinnings of its application, which is primarily rooted in the relaxed-tensor representation approach and its connections to stochastic control problems. This approach, in turn, is linked to the fundamental concepts of relaxed control theory and its relationship with nonlinear stochastic differential equations. We provide a concise review of the key theorems underlying this approach, emphasizing its distinct strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, we present a step-by-step derivation of the explicit solution for a particular estimation problem, which we later generalize to cover a broader class of differential models. This research combines the theoretical underpinnings with practical illustrations of the algorithm's effectiveness, showcasing its applicability to a range of applications, including drone navigation and vehicle localization. We anticipate that the continuous-stage Runge-Kutta method will play a pivotal role in model estimation and control as the underlying dynamic model becomes increasingly continuous. In model-parallel distributed training of large neural networks, reducing the size of individual model segments is a pressing issue. We introduce a novel approach called regional critic training that utilizes feedback from a critic network to compact each model segment. Our method is built upon the idea of learning optimal layer outputs with minimal feedback loops. We implement regional critic training on a high-performance computing cluster and test its effectiveness on several large-scale neural network architectures, achieving significant reductions in model size and training complexity without compromising accuracy. Notably, regional critic training requires no model modifications and can be easily integrated into existing distributed training systems. We also provide detailed analysis of factors that affect regional critic training and propose a systematic strategy for model segmentation. Our code is openly available on the GitHub repository. Experimental results show that regional critic training can reduce model size by up to 30% and training complexity by up to 2 times without compromising accuracy. The 32-GPU training of ResNet-50 architecture illustrates these benefits, with regional critic training achieving model size reductions of 25.6% and speeding up the training process by 1.87 times compared to the baseline model. The effectiveness of regional critic training is also demonstrated on several real-world image classification tasks and a BERT language model, further highlighting its practical value for distributed neural network training. In particular, regional critic training was able to reduce model size by 21.5% and lower the memory usage per GPU by 46.3% in the BERT model. Moreover, regional critic training was able to reduce model size by 18.6% and lower the memory usage per GPU by 40.1% in the MobileNetV2 model. These substantial memory savings resulted in significant performance improvements, with an average speedup of 1.63 times in the 32-GPU training of the models. Therefore, regional critic training can be an invaluable tool for data scientists and machine learning engineers to reduce model size, lower memory usage, and accelerate the training process of large-scale neural networks. We expect this approach to continue to help researchers and engineers distribute model training efficiently across diverse hardware platforms in the future. To achieve this goal, regional critic training provides important insights on model design, informing how individual model segments should be designed to facilitate efficient distribution of the model. We anticipate that regional critic training will contribute significantly to advancing the state of the art in distributed neural network training. Human activity recognition, a significant area in field of computer vision, has far-reaching applications in social and human-made settings. This study focuses on recognizing activities spanning multiple frames, specifically involving human body parts that move over time. To achieve this, we introduce the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a model combining both hierarchical and attention-based mechanisms. HAN is comprised of two primary components: a) a hierarchical network that converts input frames to relevant body parts, and b) an attention module that assembles these parts into a coherent overall activity. We evaluate HAN using two popular video datasets, MuCo-1STARS and PASCAL-VOC-Virath, and compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, HAN achieved an 8% point improvement in average accuracy on the MuCo-1STARS dataset. This study reveals that activity recognition benefit substantially from incorporating both temporal and part-based attentional encodings. As a result, we propose using attentional encodings that are a weighted sum of temporal encodings and part-based attentional encodings. Moreover, we observed that HAN's performance on datasets lacking activity segments that involve the movement of a subject via attentional encoding of temporal and body parts. This study demonstrates the potential for body parts to serve as stable attentional encodings even in inactive scenes. To validate the efficacy of human body parts in activity recognition, we conduct an ablation study on the PASCAL-VOC-Virath dataset. The findings suggest that body parts act as strong generalizers, and body parts that are not visible in an activity can still contribute positively to its recognition. This study is the first to explore the use of invisible body parts in activity recognition. In summary, HAN is an innovative model that integrates hierarchical and attention-based mechanisms to recognize activities spanning multiple frames. In quantum gravity, the idea of cosmic censorship hypothesis (CCH) is a crucial concept that attempts to validate the view that naked singularities are uncommon in the universe. The minimum amount of matter or energy required to form a black hole from a spherically symmetric state can be mathematically deduced by analyzing the conditions necessary for the collapse of a scalar field. By examining the boundary of this minimum amount, researchers aim to test the feasibility of the feeble variant of the CCH (FCH). Utilizing this approach, the admissibility of the FCH can be evaluated in Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m anti-de Sitter black holes (RADANSBHs) under two distinct scenarios: one with a scalar field lacking backreaction, and another with backreaction. Interestingly, in the first scenario, FCH is upheld when the scalar field's energy-momentum tensor is energetically dominant, whereas in the second scenario, FCH's validity relies on the strength of the scalar field's energy-momentum tensor in relation to other components of the RADANSBHs. The possibility of forming naked singularities through the collapse of a scalar field in stationary black holes, such as RADANSBHs, offers new insights into this complex problem. Furthermore, in the absence of backreaction, the feasibility of the FCH can be explored through thermodynamic considerations, yielding a AdS soliton case in which the scalar field's energy-momentum tensor is energetically dominant, thereby rendering judgment on the FCH in this scenario. The potential connections and differences with AdS solitons are yet to be resolved and require further investigation. The admissibility of thermodynamic considerations in scenarios with backreaction remains uncertain and needs to be explored in greater detail. The relationship between cosmic censorship hypothesis (CCH) and thermodynamics can provide an alternative, feeble variant of CCH that is worthy of further examination in the ungravitating limit. The AdS soliton case presents an intriguing phenomenon in which the scalar field may collapse into a naked singularity, yet this scenario exhibits distinct differences from the black hole phase change, which is constrained by the feeble variant of CCH (FCH). Conversely, in scenarios with backreaction, the validity of CCH (FCH) can be evaluated by considering the minimum amount of matter or energy required to form a black hole from a spherically symmetric state, thereby yielding results that are constrained by this feeble variant. This article will be a part of a larger collection exploring the most recent significant breakthroughs in the field of astrophysics for the "Notices of Recent Research" section in the Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society. As the title suggests, the achievement in question revolves around the initial spark of star formation. As a mathematical representation, this process involves overcoming a challenging set of equations that describe how a gas cloud's properties change over time as it collapses under its own gravity. As a physical system, however, these equations can only be accurately solved with insights derived from high-resolution computer simulations and a deep understanding of the underlying physical phenomena. As a physical phenomenon, the initial star formation holds a dual significance - it marks both the beginning of a star's life and the eventual demise of our universe's primordial hydrogen. Utilizing recent advancements in computational hydrodynamic simulations, we will examine the intricate mechanisms involved in forming the first stars, which occur under a complex interplay of gas dynamics and radiative transfer, heavily influenced by the emerging starlight's impact on the surrounding gas cloud. As a result, this article will heavily draw from existing peer-reviewed literature and feature numerous references, primarily from the Bulletin's companion database, the arXiv. It will also leverage existing reviews and textbooks for introductory purposes, given the highly specialized and advanced nature of the topic at hand. Additionally, the article will include links to interactive 3D visualizations that can be accessed via web browsers, providing an innovative means to present and communicate complex 3D simulation data. These visualizations will complement our discussion and serve as a versatile means of exploration, enabling readers to delve into the core concepts and examine the resulting stars in greater detail. Lastly, the article will conclude by highlighting a range of open research issues and encouraging readers to join the ongoing quest to uncover the hidden secrets of star formation, either by leveraging simple analytical models to gain new insights or by conducting high-resolution simulations to shed more light on this enigmatic process. As a starting point, there are numerous unsolved problems listed throughout this article, marked with the abbreviation "RQ" (Request You). We hope that, through this article, our readers will be inspired to contribute their knowledge and help us better understand the initial star formation. As a final note, the article will be supplemented by an appendix containing essential information on key variables, units, and other relevant physical constants required for further exploration. It is also worth mentioning that the article would not have been possible without the support of the NSF grant award number 1820795

This review article discusses a method to estimate thermal states and their associated thermodynamic properties, specifically the entropy, using a technique called Nested Sampling. The NS approach provides an accurate and robust estimation of the entropy even in the presence of limited post-parameterization data. Formulations of the NS entropy are explored, particularly in relation to a model of sub-thermal neutrons, and comparisons are made with other methods such as the thermodynamic integration approach. One key advantage of NS is its ability to contribute meaningfully during the calculation of the entropy, an aspect it shares with thermodynamic integration. By integrating the contributions of all degrees of freedom, NS offers a comprehensive solution that can help bridge the inherent discrepancies existing between molecular dynamics simulations, lattice Monte Carlo calculations, and experimental measurements of entropy. Some critical considerations, like bias in the likelihood distribution, must however be taken into account when employing NS. A proposal is presented in the article to rectify this issue, thereby enabling the calculation of NS entropy based on Nested Sampling. The review concludes by highlighting future research directions, and suggesting that NS provides an ideal framework for the development of new, cutting-edge sampling techniques that could be used to investigate the thermodynamic properties of critical systems. These systems are characterized by strong interactions, and a deep understanding of their entropy is essential for advancing our knowledge in this field. In particular, the challenge of accurately calculating the entropy of a spin-3/2 particle, and thereby determining the g-factor, presents an unresolved issue, and one that NS is well-equipped to tackle. Some initial findings on this problem are presented in the article. It is hypothesized that NS, due to its ability to accurately estimate entropy, will play a pivotal role in the investigation of sub-thermal degrees of freedom in various fields such as nuclear and particle physics, and that this work will serve as a preview of future research directions in Nested Sampling applications. These future studies will focus on the thermodynamics of complex quantum systems. A significant amount of work remains to be done in this field, and it is only through the development of new, innovative techniques such as NS that it will be possible to obtain precise entropy measurements, a parameter that is crucial to the underlying structure of any thermodynamic system. Some key words that characterize the research in this article include Nested Sampling, bias correction, thermodynamic integration, bias distribution, the g-factor, spin-3/2 particle, quantum systems, nuclear physics, particle physics, and complex systems. These topics are interwoven throughout the review in order to facilitate clear and concise explanations

We re-examine solutions to a class of hyperbolic conservation laws, specifically those with nonlinear flux functions, in a particular type of measure called a feeble solution. Feeble solutions are a more general solution space that includes both classical and semisolutions. We derive conditions under which feeble solutions can be found and establish a key comparison principle. This comparison principle has significant implications, allowing for the existence of feeble solutions with arbitrarily large initial conditions and the construction of a unique, feeble solution for any given initial condition. Notably, this type of solution is robust to various perturbations of the initial data. We also consider a specific example - a traffic model with a particular type of nonlinear interaction - and demonstrate the existence of solutions with "chimney" solutions, a particular structure that can arise in situations where there are many lanes of traffic and an incident occurs. This type of solution is currently not well understood in the standard semisolution framework. Finally, we speculate on the possible equivalence or distinction between feeble solutions and another general type of solution called "discontinuous solutions" when certain conditions on the nonlinearity are met. This addresses a question from a previous study. In contrast to standard approaches, our approach uses elements of functional analysis to derive properties of feeble solutions. This includes the use of certain operator-theoretic tools. As a result, our work provides a new perspective on general solution theory for conservation laws. This perspective may also be applied to other systems of conservation laws. A companion paper will explore the analogous results in the case of systems of conservation laws. This research is part of a broader project, supported by ANR-3D-HPC, which aims to investigate feeble solutions in a mathematical framework. This requires a convergence theory that differs from classical semisolution convergence. As such, this research is focused on feeble solutions, although many of the underlying ideas are likely to be relevant to other types of general solutions as well. Cyberattacks on IoT devices are spreading rapidly, fueled by their widespread deployment in daily life. As a consequence, network security has become a pressing concern. To address this challenge, this research presents NBcoded, a novel, resource-efficient network assault detection system. NBcoded combines a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Maximal Objectives-based neural network with a Naive Bayes classifier to classify network behavior, leveraging the strength of deep learning models and the simplicity of supervised learning models. By utilizing a dataset of compressed IoT traffic, NBcoded demonstrates high accuracy in detecting various types of cyberattacks on resource-constrained devices, achieving an 87% true positive rate at a low false positive rate of 10%. Furthermore, NBcoded's performance exceeds that of existing commercial and open-source detection systems, showcasing its potential as a scalable and efficient solution for real-world deployment. Additionally, NBcoded's energy efficiency was evaluated using a Raspberry Pi, revealing that it can operate on low-power devices while maintaining high assault detection rates. With these capabilities, NBcoded can be used in various power-constrained applications, providing real-time protection against cyberattacks. Components of this project have been made available on GitHub for public access. Future developments of this research will focus on enhancing NBcoded's assault detection capabilities using an adaptive learning approach. Using a dataset of compressed IoT traffic, deep learning models can be fine-tuned to optimize assault detection performance. By comparing the radiation patterns of the emitters in our waveguide platform to those in a free space environment, we calculated the efficacy of our single-photon source, defined as the product of the power in the fundamental mode and the power in the two side modes, for different emitter configurations. For a dipole emitter in our ridge waveguide, the efficacy was approximately 0.98, primarily due to the emitter's interaction with the waveguide's fundamental mode and two side modes. Feynman integrals can be evaluated using physical principles, such as unitarity and causality, which enables us to bypass explicit integration techniques. This approach offers several advantages, including avoiding numerical integration, which may introduce additional errors, and providing a fundamental understanding of the parameters in question. This report serves as a submission for the 6th Workshop on Advanced Computational Methods for LHC Physics, where we share our findings on one-loop Feynermanude and two-loop Feynmanude processes involving the cone parameterization. Our method also allows for a built-in evolution of the Feynman rules, which facilitates the calculation of beyond-two-flavor PDFs. Nevertheless, our technique proves to be insufficient for certain scenarios, such as the calculation of Conformal Anomalous Magnetic Form Factors, where the Feynman rules experience discontinuities. Despite these limitations, our method exhibits several beneficial characteristics, including being loop-order independent, capable of handling scale and regularization uncertainties, and providing physical insights, such as the behavior of form factors in the forward direction. Nonetheless, we did not achieve the desired level of precision, likely due to the large value of certain coefficients in the DGLAP evolution equation. This large-coefficient issue also affects several other predictions, such as the Conformal Radius and the muon anomalous magnetic moment. This problem may potentially be addressed through a more accurate calculation of the relevant master integrals. Nonetheless, in specific scenarios, our method still allows for the calculation of form factors up to the two-loop order with precision comparable to all-order pole predictions. This includes the QCD corrections to the electromagnetic form factor of the muon and the g-2 muon. To achieve this level of precision, we employed a novel approach to the evolution of the Feynman rules, which may have further implications in the future. Although this report primarily focuses on form factors, our method can be applied to a broader range of processes, such as SSB Amplitude and Graviton Amplitude, which we plan to explore in the future. This will likely involve the extension of our code to also produce unpolarized Amplitude and Graviton Amplitude. Nonetheless, even in its current version, our method exhibits several beneficial characteristics, such as scale and regularization uncertainty robustness, which may be particularly important in future amplitude-on-demand calculations, particularly those involving gravity. In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation has been leveraged to deliver targeted energy deposits into a subset of spatial modes. To understand the probability distribution of energy deposition in a given area, we derive and substantiate two separate theorems. Firstly, an initial sum principle outlines the expected contribution of eigenchannels' cross-coupling in energy deposition. Secondly, a final sum principle assesses the impact of interference between different eigenchannels. Our analysis implies that in large volumes, the channel coupling pattern is the primary factor influencing deposition efficiency. By partitioning a complex domain into smaller sub-volumes, and analyzing the scattering matrices of individual components, our methodology enables detailed optimization of deposition efficiency in complex 3D geometries. By guiding channel selection based on volume-boundary interactions, our findings demonstrate over 90% efficient deposition is achievable in large volumes. Conversely, when designing deposits in channels, our analysis indicates that efficient deposition often comes at the cost of increased deposition risk in surrounding channels. Ultimately, our analysis suggests an inherent trade-off between deposition efficiency and the likelihood of energy spread in scattering systems. Specifically, in large volumes, efficient deposition in a target channel inevitably correlates with a higher likelihood of energy spread in that channel. Conversely, targeting fewer channels tends to yield higher deposition efficiency at the expense of increased energy spread. Our analysis confirms the universality of these findings across diverse scattering systems and offers a systematic approach to analyzing and optimizing energy deposition in complex 3D geometries. By empowering designers to balance deposition efficiency and spread, our research will contribute to the development of more sophisticated nanophotonic devices, from laser development to energy delivery applications. Additionally, our analysis suggests the possibility of achieving single-path, targeted delivery in complex 3D volumes, expanding the scope of eigenchannel research and delivering eigenchannel principles to new fields and applications. Recent studies of the Galaxy's radio emission have revealed a previously unknown feature, a faint spiral arm extending from $l \sim 310^{\circ}$ to $l \sim 320^{\circ}$. This new arm, which we call the Far 3-Kpc arm (FKA), exhibits characteristics similar to the well-documented Near 3-Kpc arm (NKA). The FKA's intensity patterns show a symmetric, sinusoidal variation with right ascension, and its position angle remains consistent with the northern Galactic spiral arm's overall structure. The FKA's location can be accurately modeled at $l \sim 315.5^{\circ}$, with a distance of $292$ pc, using the Taylor-Robson method. Observations indicate the FKA's expansion velocity is approximately $5.5$ km/s per year. Spectral analysis reveals that the FKA's intensity spectrum follows a $I \propto \nu^{-0.12}$ relationship, similar to the NKA. The FKA's brightness temperature distribution exhibits a distinctive, U-shaped variation with right ascencion, and its maximum and minimum values are $38$ and $18$ mK, respectively. The FKA's overall temperature pattern can be replicated using a cosine function with a $7.5^{\circ}$ phase difference. The FKA's radial distance and pattern retention time suggest a short (mean $6.4$ million year) existence period for spiral arm features in the Galaxy. The findings for the FKA are in good agreement with simulations by Wang et al. (2019) using a Galactic spiral arm model. The discovery of the FKA provides further evidence for dynamic and short-lived spiral arm structures in the Galaxy. The research also highlights the potential of sensitive radio surveys to reveal additional spiral arm features, ultimately improving models for the Galaxy's spiral arm structure. Future studies should focus on determining the birth period for the NKA and investigating variations in spiral arm density as a function of distance. Finally, the discovery of the FKA has significant implications for understanding spiral arm morphology and the dynamic behavior of barred galaxies. The findings encourage further exploration of sensitive emission surveys at $20-100$ m in frequency and angular resolutions of $10''$ to $1'$ in scale to reveal more features in the near and far 3-kpc arms. Increasingly, multi-objective optimization techniques are being employed not only to generate optimal solutions but also to foster the development of diverse phenotypes. This study, however, highlights a critical issue: phenotypic diversity might actually hinder evolutionary multi-objective optimization. We present a comprehensive evaluation of phenotypic diversity within the context of a core hypersphere optimization problem, using three distinct genetic algorithms. Our analysis reveals that phenotypic diversity tends to decline over the course of an evolutionary process. Although phenotypic diversity may positively correlate with solution diversity, our results also show that solution diversity is influenced by other factors, including genetic operations and the fitness landscape topology. Consequently, phenotypic diversity should not be the primary focus when aiming to enhance solution diversity in evolutionary multi-objective optimization. Instead, we propose additional research to elucidate the underlying relationship between phenotypic diversity and solution diversity. Furthermore, we recommend the investigation of new strategies to boost solution diversity without relying on phenotypic diversity. We provide concrete guidelines for practitioners based on our findings, and we outline possible future research avenues. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between phenotypic diversity and solution diversity, paving the way for the development of more effective genetic algorithms. The code used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Naikod/Phenotypic_Diversity. For technical details, please refer to Naik et al. in press. The Stable Roommates problem presents a scenario in which a group of agents need to form one-on-one relationships. Each agent values interactions based on specific preference metrics and will only participate in a match if it meets their preference threshold. A stable match will form when no agent would prefer a different partner. Under the requirement that agent preferences follow a specific symmetric format, we investigated whether it's possible to create a general VAP-efficient mechanism for one-shot mechanism design in scenarios with up to three dimensions of preferences. Mechanism design aims to find a mechanism that produces stable matches with minimal mechanism violation in one-shot settings. Our research reveals that designing a VAP-efficient mechanism for three-dimensional preferences is inherently complex, but we can achieve this efficiency for preferences with only two dimensions. Additionally, for one-dimensional preferences, existing literature has already established that a general VAP-efficient mechanism cannot exist. Diverging from traditional VAP analysis, we also explored the concept of infinite expectation, examining mechanisms under repeated interactions in large groups. Under this expectation, we designed a new mechanism that achieves a trade-off between efficiency and stability, the best of which maintains an expectation of $\frac{4}{5}$. This design introduces a random mechanism that in the long run produces matches which are $\frac{4}{5}$-stable, even in scenarios with up to three dimensions of preferences and any number of agents. Our research shows that while it may not be possible to achieve perfect $\frac{4}{5}$-stability of matches in the limit of infinitely large groups, our expectation of $\frac{4}{5}$ indeed holds for any number of agents. Furthermore, under the repeated interactions model, we can maintain the efficiency of our mechanism even when preferences are not symmetric in nature. A key finding from our research is that although we were unable to find a general VAP-efficient mechanism in the one-shot settings, our expectation of $\frac{4}{5}$ indeed holds for any number of agents, even when preferences only marginally favor one-over-one matches. To verify the efficacy of our mechanism in the repeated interactions model, we can maintain efficiency even when preferences only slightly favor one-over-one matches. Interestingly, under the repeated interactions model, the efficiency of our mechanism shows resilience to the complexity of preferences. In fact, we found that limiting the range of preferences does not compromise the efficiency of our mechanism. Additionally, we explored the concept of additive separability in preferences, demonstrating that it significantly complicates the design of VAP-efficient mechanisms when preferences have multiple dimensions.

In the case of a rotating hexagon model, our analysis suggests the presence of a pseudo-magnetic field, while a rotating dome model yields a significant magnetic field effect. A microstrip patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully constructed and tested. The designed antenna features a simplified structure with only three elements, achieving an impressive bandwidth of 14.2%, and a very large beamwidth of 88 degrees. The measurement results align closely with the simulated outcomes. Further analysis using the TEM wave resonator method revealed that minor adjustments to the microstrip line's length could achieve an even broader bandwidth. Ultimately, this design's simplicity, combined with its practical advantages, makes it an ideal solution for various wireless communication applications. Every step of the process needs to be encoded for error correction, which involves both data and operations. Researchers have developed various methods for encoding operations to prevent errors, but currently, these methods are primarily based on random unitary transformations which don't take into account the specific characteristics of the operations being performed. We've found that using reinforcement learning to create encoded transformations that are optimal for a specific operation can lead to more efficient conversions with fewer and more targeted qubit swaps, adjustments, and other corrections. By applying this approach to a range of two-qubit operations, including some simulated applications, we've discovered that the encoded transformations can often be implemented with fewer steps than those using random unitary transformations, which can result in cost savings when building quantum circuits from scratch. We've also tested the robustness of these encoded transformations under the influence of individual quantum gate failures within the process of reinforcement learning. The results show that the encoded transformations are resilient to such failures and remain effective even if several gates fail during the learning process. We're now planning to extend this technique to support the encoding of sequences of operations that are frequently used in quantum algorithms to expand its potential applications. By developing more efficient methods for encoding operations, we hope to create more robust and efficient fault-tolerant quantum gate implementations that can be used to build more reliable quantum circuits from scratch. By applying reinforcement learning to this problem, we hope to create more efficient encoded transformations that can help us better understand this trade-off and develop more efficient error suppression methods in the future. Deep sub-micron radiation hit-counting detectors based on CMOS technology are capable of achieving high collection efficiencies and resolving power. However, CMOS sensors have inherent drawbacks such as a high collection efficiency gap and a non-uniform electric field. The monolithic collection-electrode technology demonstrator CLICTD was designed to address these issues by integrating a high concentration n-type drift region directly into a CMOS sensor chip. The performance of CLICTD sensors with different substrate types and thin collector regions was evaluated using a 5.9 TeV proton beam at CERN's Proton Synchtron, and the experimental results were compared with corresponding 2-D sensor counterparts. The beam tests confirmed that thin collector devices offer improved spatial resolution and collection efficiency compared to their thicker counterparts, and the 500-micron p-type Czochralski substrate variant outperformed the 500-micron p-type Ge variant due to its reduced time resolution discrepancy with the thin collector devices. The 500-micron p-type CiS substrate variant exhibited the best overall performance, characterized by high collection efficiency, minimal time resolution gaps, and nearly uniform electric field distribution. The 120 mm wafer samples were analyzed using infrared thermography to investigate the technology's potential in large-area detectors. The study revealed that thin collector devices with a 500 micrometer substrate can accommodate a high concentration of 10^6 electrons per square millimeter without experiencing significant time resolution degradation. Lastly, the detector design and its components have proven to be capable of withstanding 1 MeV/cm radiation without significant performance degradation. Based on these findings, it appears that monolithic CLICTD sensors can serve as an adequate replacement for existing fully-depleted hybrid detectors. The proposed detectors exhibit the potential to handle large particle collisions with a high collection efficiency, minimal time resolution gaps, and uniform electric field distribution, making them particularly suitable for tracking systems at future particle accelerator facilities. The proposed detectors will be further tested and developed in collaboration with the Tracker Upgrade team at the CMS experiment. In particular, monolithic CLICTD sensors will be designed and manufactured in 200 mm wafers with a track-on-pitch of 50 microns or less with the express intention of being utilized in the CMS experiment. The proposed detectors will be evaluated in a real-world setting at the LHC's maximum luminosity to confirm their time resolution and collection efficiency capabilities. The CMS collaboration will also assess these detectors in a real-world environment to confirm their performance and determine their suitability for the tracker system

Advanced telescope design features a cutting-edge technology known as fast atmospheric self-coherent camera (FASTSCC), which utilizes the Coherent Diffraction Imaging method to eliminate atmospheric distortion during long-distance, ground-based astronomy observations.  This innovative technology employs a specialized camera to measure the coherent diffraction of light past the atmosphere, enabling the reconstruction of the speckle pattern and ultimately, the focus of a laser beam.  Recent laboratory tests utilizing the Besselian mean bright night sky at the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (XAO) testbed in California successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique.  By processing the reconstructed speckle field, the team was able to demonstrate the capability of FASTSCC to provide high-speed feedback for focal plane wavefront control, and possibly even beyond.  The test results revealed that FASTSCC can operate at speeds of up to 50 kHz while maintaining an accuracy of 0.8-0.9 in the Strehl ratio.  This accuracy is comparable to that of other advanced technologies, such as adaptive optics, and offers the potential for FASTSCC to significantly broaden the range of observational wavelengths available to astronomers.  Future implementations are expected to achieve even higher speeds and recoveries, potentially up to 300 kHz or higher, and could potentially extend the range of observable wavelengths to near-infrared frequencies of up to 2.2 micrometers.  The researchers are currently working on an algorithm designed to restore image quality from the speckle-affected images, and this new approach is expected to greatly enhance the capabilities of FASTSCC.  Additionally, the fast sensor capabilities of this technology are of significant interest due to their potential applications in other fields such as imaging through turbulent media and bio medical imaging.  This innovative research is offering a fresh perspective on ground-based astronomy observations, and could offer a cost-effective solution to overcoming atmospheric distortion until the development of a space-based telescope becomes a reality.  As such, this paper describes the results of laboratory tests and presents a new approach to fast atmospheric speckle measurement and focal plane wavefront control.  The reconstructed speckle images and test results are available for public download at https://casa.ucsd.edu/fast-scc/.  This research was funded by a grant from the Heising-Simons Foundation. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to ensure reliable operation. Recent trends in computing have led to the adoption of non-volatile memory (NVM), which can serve as a reliable storage alternative. Nevertheless, the high cost of NVM storage compared to traditional DRAM necessitates the use of page-level caching to minimize costs. Caches, however, introduce a significant obstacle to fault tolerance. This work proposes an innovative framework, CRASH, to maintain crash consistency in NVM-based caching systems. CRASH relies on runtime algorithms to identify failures, manage transactions, and restore system integrity after crashes. Our framework is versatile, allowing it to integrate various fault tolerance strategies and suitable algorithms, such as checkpointing, for running parallel applications on clusters. Notably, CRASH is capable of providing both crash consistency and fault tolerance during failures, without necessitating application modifications. Our experimental results with MPI applications on an NVM-based Linux cluster reveal that CRASH can efficiently handle failures, with a mean time-to-failure of under 200ms. Furthermore, CRASH's performance overhead is minimal, with a maximum mean slowdown of just 6%. Our research demonstrates that CRASH can effectively maintain reliable operation in HPC systems with NVM-based caching. After thorough evaluation and analysis, we recommend our framework as a reliable solution for HPC systems. Our future work will involve further research into whether CRASH's performance can be improved through hardware support. Additionally, we will continue to expand our evaluation by testing CRASH with a broader range of applications and realistic failure scenarios. Lastly, we will design and implement an autonomous runtime system to supplement CRASH, which will enable the dynamic detection and handling of page faults in real-time. Our ultimate goal is to design a general framework for fault tolerance in NVM-based caching, which can be applied across various programming models and languages. This research will ultimately contribute to the development of robust software for fault-tolerant HPC applications. In particular, we will focus on crafting a fault-tolerant version of the open-source MPI library. By achieving this goal, we will successfully address the research question of whether CRASH can effectively maintain reliable operation in practical scenarios. Our estimated timeline for this project is approximately 12-18 months. In the short term, we will focus on evaluating the performance of CRASH in real-world applications. Our paper presents the results of measuring X-ray polarization in the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using the IXPE mission. Between June and July 2022, the remnant was targeted in four observations totaling 234 ks. By analyzing X-rays emitted from the remnant's center and outer regions, we measured a horizontal polarization of 11% ± 3% and 20% ± 4%, respectively, with a significant polarization detected in all observations. The polarization measurements are consistent with the presence of a large-scale magnetic field of 2-10 milligauss and a smaller-scale magnetic field of 1-4 milligauss in the outer regions. The polarization's vertical and horizontal components indicate that the X-ray emission is primarily of electron-positron bubbles, with an age of 100-1000 years. By analyzing the polarization's angle distribution, we found that the large-scale magnetic field's orientation matches the remnant's tangent field. The measurements show that the X-ray emission is older than the 580-year gamma-ray ejection. Using the X-ray emission's brightness and polarization, we estimated the number of positrons ejected in Cassiopeia A to be (1-4)10^41 s^-1. Our study demonstrates how X-ray polarization measurement can quantify particle ejection in supernova remnant. The data and analysis code are accessible through DOI 10.5170/MASTO-000.002.

We examined over 8,000 non-edge-on spiral galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on understanding spiral galaxy deformation. Our analysis revealed that galaxies in groups or clusters exhibit a unique high-inclination U-type warp pattern, which is not seen in isolated galaxies. Additionally, we found that high-inclination U-type warp galaxies in groups or clusters are more likely to have blue colors and higher global stellar velocities. This high-velocity feature is typically associated with the phenomenon known as "fish-like" galaxies, which are thought to be the result of ram pressure stripping in group or cluster environments. This stripping can lead to the transformation of isolated spiral galaxies into the "jellyfish" type. Our findings indicate a significant correlation between high-velocity features and U-type warp patterns in group or cluster galaxies. We propose that ram pressure stripping may also contribute to the formation of U-type warp patterns, which can ultimately give rise to the "jellyfish" type. Our research provides insight into galaxy interaction and deformation in group or cluster environments. It also expands the known characteristics of jellyfish galaxies, including their high-velocity features, blue colors, and unique spiral arm configurations. Ultimately, our understanding of galaxy evolution may be redefined through the discovery of a potential new pathway from spiral to jellyfish galaxies. To further investigate this phenomenon, we plan to examine tidal interactions as an alternative mechanism for the formation of U-type warp patterns in group or cluster galaxies. In the near future, we aim to analyze data from Gaia DR3, which will enable us to make more precise measurements of galaxy velocities and further understand their evolution in group or cluster environments. To confirm our initial findings, we will also conduct follow-up analyses using the Hubble Space Telescope and the MMT TrueColor project. In particular, we will examine 12 high-inclination spiral galaxies using MMBF, which will allow us to make local velocity measurements and gain a deeper understanding of their structure. In addition, we will analyze data from the HST Cosmic Evolution Survey, which will provide high-resolution images of galaxy structures. Ultimately, we will explore the link between U-type warp patterns and the formation of high-velocity features in spiral galaxies through in-depth case studies. The study presents a new theoretical model for turbulent heat transfer in fluids. It's an adaptation of the Kolmogorov-1941 model, incorporating viscous dissipation and heat production from preceding research by the authors. The outcome reveals that the energy spectrum in the dissipation range is divided into two parts, an inert $k^3$ spectrum and a quasi-universal spectrum that intersects with the Kolmogorov spectrum. The quasi-universal spectrum's behavior varies significantly with the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers. Furthermore, the study's calculations demonstrate that the turbulent conductivity is determined by the average eddy viscosity and conductively interacts with large-scale energy transitions. An equation for the turbulent conductivity is developed and show excellent alignment with numerous experimental data points for water. Lastly, the study reveals that the average eddy temperature difference between the eddies can become very high, even reaching a thousandth of the actual temperature difference between the fluid's hot and cold surfaces. As a result, the study's findings contradict the assumption commonly held by many engineers that the average temperature difference between the eddies is equivalent to the actual temperature difference between the fluid's hot and cold surfaces. Instead, it's found that the average temperature difference between the eddies is closely tied to the fluid's Prandtl number. Additionally, the study's findings suggest that the highest oscillation frequencies in thermal fluids are significantly greater than the Kolmogorov frequency. In particular, when the Prandtl number is very low, the collective thermal properties of the eddies can cause extreme temperature fluctuations within an extremely short time frame. Due to such dynamic behavior, the study advises against using the Kolmogorov-1941 model without modifications for low-Prandtl-number fluids. Finally, the study's findings indicate that the energy spectrum in the energy-containing range is unaffected by thermal factors and can be modeled using the Kolmogorov-1941 theory with minimal adaptations. Conversely, when the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers are simultaneously very high, the energy spectrum in the energy-containing range exhibits a complex behavior driven by both inert and thermal factors. Consequently, a purely hydrodynamic approach is justified and effective in large-scale energy-containing scenarios, even when the Prandtl number is very high. In contrast, a more complex thermal consideration is necessary for accurate predictions in the dissipation range and turbulence parameters. Three-dimensional topological insulators can exhibit both intrinsic magnetoelectric and time-reversal-symmetric responses due to their unique surface properties. The nonlinear magnetoelectric response, for instance, is linked to a specific surface anomaly with origins dating back to Chern-Simons theory and the Witten effect related to anyon statistics. Focusing on time-reversal-symmetric responses, we thoroughly examine the Chern SIMONS and Witten contributions, as well as a previously unexplored geometric contribution arising from the insulator's bulk geometry. The sum of these three contributions results in a well-defined topological invariant capable of describing a half-integer quantum Hall effect on the surfaces of these insulators. By means of a simple Chern SIMONS realization, we are also able to provide a straightforward physical interpretation of the surface anomalous velocity observed in the Witten effect and the anomalous Hall drift observed in magnetic Witten states. Furthermore, we introduce a new concept known as the boundary Chern SIMON number, serving as a necessary and sufficient condition for realizing a nonvanishing surface drift observed in magnetoelectric responses, as well as an anomalous Hall effect under time-reversal-symmetric conditions. We base our discussion of surface drifts and anomalous Hall effects on a general framework applicable to both two- and three-dimensional systems. Lastly, we propose an experimental demonstration of the topological magnetoelectric property associated with a half-integer quantum Hall effect on the surfaces of three-dimensional topological insulators. This involves creating a sample consisting of a three-dimensional topological insulator and a superconductor in close proximity, with the application of an external magnetic field to induce chiral edge currents observable through detection using a scanning tunneling microscope or He plasma contact gap measurement test. Initially, the diffusion coefficient exhibits an irregular pattern as the time lag increases, but later it starts to display a more orderly decrease. Notably, certain time lag values can trigger an explosive growth in the diffusion coefficient, leading to simplified spatial patterns and reduced spatial complexity. This phenomenon is most pronounced in low-dimensional systems and those exhibiting strong nonlinear behavior. When the time lag is optimized for maximum diffusion, the system's temporal behavior transitions from a chaotic state to one characterized by periodic fluctuations. This unusual behavior is rooted in the interaction between the delay and nonlinearity. Moreover, we developed an analytical method to calculate the diffusion coefficient, revealing a connection between this coefficient and the system's nonlinear properties. Lastly, our experiments demonstrate that chaotic diffusion can be induced and controlled through time lag adjustment, opening up new avenues for the innovative application of delayed nonlinear systems in various fields. These systems can now display robust spatial patterns even at low dimensionalities, rendering them more versatile and efficient. Additionally, this knowledge may facilitate the development of delayed self-organizing systems capable of navigating the complex interplay between order and disorder. Discussions among software developers hold significant value in the design and development process, yet their implementation is frequently overlooked due to the labor-intensive process of adopting existing design methods tailored for text-based communication. A recent approach employs natural language processing to automatically extract relevant design discussions from developer comments on GitHub, but the obtained model requires validation in terms of conclusion stability - essentially, can varying inputs yield similar outcomes? In this study, multiple exhaustive human-labeled datasets were created to assess the consistency of the designed discussion extraction method. Results from three different testing approaches - duplicate detection, multi-instance learning, and k-fold cross-validation - showed the extracted discussions' conclusions were consistently determined, but their associated design discussions showed variations. Importantly, this study provides a novel benchmark for evaluating design discussion extraction methods. It suggests that our perception of gravity arises from the retro-causal emission of virtual states that are persistent and give rise to the coherence of the universe's quantum state. The potential for gravity to be detected through laser ranging and redshift measurements is considered, along with the possibility of an energy limit, approximately $10^{18}$ GeV, resulting from the absorption of virtual states by an observer. Proximal methods can efficiently solve a broad range of optimization problems, including those involving non-differentiable objectives and complex domain constraints. When the non-differentiable part of the objective can be efficiently optimized, proximal methods often struggle with slow convergence. In such cases, they reduce to a gradient method applied to a simplified problem on the original constraint set. We observe that this simplified problem is often a non-linear system of equations defining a manifold. We then focus on the convergence of the gradient method when applied to this simplified problem, considering both smooth and non-smooth objectives. Our results indicate that the gradient method converges to a solution on the manifold when applied to the simplified problem, and that the rate of convergence depends on the smoothness of the problem. We illustrate our results via an example from network optimization. We also propose a novel algorithm, ACCeL, which combines a non-linear solver with a proximal gradient method. ACCeL takes advantage of the efficiency of the non-linear solver to accelerate the gradient method. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experimental results showing that ACCeL converges faster than the standard proximal gradient method. Moreover, ACCeL's convergence to a solution on the manifold is confirmed by numerical experiments, even in the presence of non-smooth objectives. Our approach is grounded in the connection between proximal methods, manifolds, and the homotopy-like structure of the simplified problem. This framework allows us to generalize our results to various optimization problems, including those with additional constraints. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach via an example from a multi-product supply chain optimization problem. In this problem, we are given a set of products, each with a given demand, and a set of factories, each with a given supply, and we aim to assign each product to a factory in order to minimize costs. Our approach generalizes to a broad range of optimization problems, including those with complex domain constraints and non-differentiable objectives. Consequently, it provides a practical solution to a problem that has been studied theoretically. Moreover, it provides a flexible framework for algorithm design, as demonstrated via an example. This novel idea has yielded significant insights into the properties of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals. Notably, we have investigated the relationship between feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals and certain types of prime ideals, specifically those obtained from semiprime rings. This research aims to build upon previous studies and deepen our understanding of prime ideals within a commutative ring. In addition, we present numerous examples to illustrate the distinct differences and relationships between various types of prime ideals, including feebly 1-absorbing, weakly 1-absorbing, and strongly 1-absorbing prime ideals. This data may serve as a useful reference for future researchers. Finally, we present an extension of our findings to the set of feebly prime ideals within a commutative ring. This research is a continuation of our previous studies on prime ideals, and we hope to further contribute to the field in the future.

Interferometry plays a pivotal role in various spectroscopic methods due to its potential for high-resolution transformations, which can be achieved using traditional and photonic approaches. The latter leverages advanced materials and device manufacturing to enhance resolution, sensitivity, and scanning efficiency. This article serves as an introduction to interferometric spectroscopy and its applications, with a focus on photonics, as well as a guide to assessing the performance of photonics-based interferometers through fixed-pattern interference techniques. We will discuss the fundamental principles, advantages, and challenges associated with interferometric spectroscopy and photonics. Furthermore, we will outline the procedure to evaluate the resolution and sensitivity of these devices using fixed-pattern interference, as exemplified by our astrophotonic design. This methodology can be adapted for various applications, such as high-resolution spectral analysis in molecular and atomic molecules, as well as photonic devices. Current state-of-the-art approaches for identifying and categorizing road defects have achieved remarkable success in individual countries, but their multi-national applications are hindered by the limitations of models trained on a single country's data. To address this challenge, this research presents a pioneering approach for simultaneously training and fine-tuning a deep learning-based road damage detection system across multiple countries. By leveraging a diverse dataset of over 110,000 images from Australia and Australia-derived pre-trained models, this method enables widespread deployment of efficient and robust road condition assessment systems globally. The proposed framework comprises three primary components: a universal feature extractor, a shared classifier, and a customizable mapping function. To accommodate multi-label scenarios and varying road defect sets, this study also introduces an adaptive mapping technique and a technique for optimizing class distribution. The results of extensive experiments conducted on Australian and Canadian datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in outperforming traditional fine-tuning methods and achieving comparable performance to models trained from scratch on target-country data, all while retaining efficient computational costs. Additionally, this research showcases the remarkable generalization capabilities of the developed system on both Australian and Canadian roads. To facilitate its practical use in road condition assessment, the code and pre-trained models have been made publicly available for other researchers and practitioners to build upon. Furthermore, this research aims to contribute to the development of more resilient and efficient road condition assessment systems. We introduce an novel task called cross-domain mimicry, where from raw data in one domain, we mimic interventions in another domain without direct changes. This is demonstrated through a real-world application - cross-branch medical treatment recommendation. Given a patient's sensitive medical information in one branch of medicine, we observe how a therapist conducts an audit and achieves a desired outcome. Utilizing this information, we train a model that can generate effective treatments in a different branch of medicine. This trained model can then provide recommendations to unseen patient data in another branch, even without having seen the therapist's actions on this data. Our approach requires minimal supervision and successfully completes this complex task in an empirical setting. The code for this is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/plebani/cdm. Radio map estimation is crucial for optimizing wireless networks but is hindered by time-consuming and expensive surveying processes. Autonomous UAVs can collect spectrum data while simultaneously determining their positions, as specified by IEEE 802.11 standard guidelines. Utilizing real-world radio map estimation datasets, we analyzed the effectiveness of prior approaches under different assumptions. Our investigation into the properties of radio map estimation datasets revealed significant differences between these datasets, including varying spatial resolutions and resourcing requirements. These findings prompted us to introduce a novel optimization framework, referred to as AirViewU, which can estimate radio maps using UAV data collection routes that require minimal time and resources. Our proposed framework is validated through comparisons with existing baseline approaches in scenarios involving both single-band and multi-band operations. As a result, AirViewU demonstrates superior performance in terms of estimation quality, operational efficiency, and processing complexity. Moreover, AirViewU's design allows for its implementation on low-cost UAVs equipped with IEEE 802.11 radio frequency capabilities, thereby facilitating its integration into existing AirView systems. Successful evaluations of AirViewU on a real-world dataset in an indoor environment revealed a substantial reduction in system processing time of up to 87%. Furthermore, AirviewU offers a versatile design that can easily adapt to various radio access technologies. Leveraging a dataset derived from a TU-Darmstadt campus, we compared AirViewU's performance in outdoor settings against a frequency-hopping spread spectrum technique. Our results show that AirViewU surpasses the latter approach by as much as 93.57% in terms of processing time. Consequently, AirViewU is an optimal solution for radio map estimation, boasting enhanced performance, adaptability, and efficiency. Therefore, it is an ideal addition to existing UAV-enabled spectrum exploration mechanisms. Specifically, it can address the challenges posed by resource-constrained UAVs operating under strict real-time constraints while maintaining a balance between exploration depth and operational complexity. A person's unique voice, face, and speech patterns can be used to verify their identity, and by combining audio-visual information, the reliability of voice identification can be increased. However, since public speakers often wear masks, we are exploring the potential of using throat thermal images, in addition to audio-visual data, to create a more robust identification system. For this purpose, we created a publicly available dataset consisting of 540 video clips featuring 18 individuals, along with three different environments, including masked faces, varied lighting, and wind effects simulating outdoor acoustics. By applying individual verification metrics to this dataset, we observed that using audio-visual-thermal data yields a higher true acceptance rate (0.933) while maintaining a low false acceptance rate (0.001). Furthermore, when testing in masked face conditions, we noticed a slight decline (around 10%) in the distance metric's effectiveness. To validate our approach, we also compared our results with public deep learning models and found that our technique outperforms existing models by a significant margin. Based on these findings, we conclude that the incorporation of thermal images can increase the reliability of audio-visual individual verification. Achieving complete data protection under differential privacy can be prohibitively expensive, thus research has focused on introducing relaxation based on dependancy among data records. Based on this concept, a condition called one-sided differential privacy (OSDP) is introduced in this research, which takes into consideration the dependence among data records when evaluating and controlling the probability exposure. Under OSDP, a data set is considered safe if the exposure of an individual record does not exceed a predetermined threshold that is dependent on the record above it. This concept is further studied through the development of a data dependent Renyi one-sided differential privacy framework. Within this framework, the challenge of creating a safe summary from a data set, while minimizing excess risk under the R-OSDP metric, is defined as an optimization problem. This optimization problem is shown to be equivalent to a distribution estimation problem in which each record is assigned a weight that is directly related to its safety threshold. This research is further extended to develop a reusable safety mechanism for aggregated data. Specifically, a data dependent variance reducing mechanism under the F-OSDP framework is proposed and is shown to be superior to the existing state-of-the-art mechanism in terms of excess risk under the F-OSDP metric. This research is supported by analytical and numerical results which demonstrate its effectiveness. Numerical results also reveal the introduced mechanism to be more efficient while providing comparable privacy protection compared to existing mechanisms. In particular, it is shown that the introduced mechanism is resilient to interference and is more capable of reducing the variance under certain conditions compared to the existing state-of-the-art mechanism. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas substructures mirroring the structure of the solid material. Research has been conducted on the CO gas emission in the AS 209 disk, which exhibits a notable substructure reminiscent of the solid particles' structure as observed through scattering polarization observations. We investigated the origin of this gas substructure using CO line modeling at a high angular resolution of ~60 Maurits Korhonen. 

In the area of the disk far from its star, CO gas emission exhibits scatter due to the movement of grains, which is consistent with the observed structure. However, this is not the case for the inner region, which requires additional factors to explain. Two possibilities are presented: either the inner gas is composed of smaller CO molecules or the gas is processed through chemical reactions to alter its composition. 

We present model predictions for the 12 CO and 13 CO emission based on the 'puff' model, which suggests the presence of small CO molecules in the inner region. This 'puff' model can explain the observed structure with great accuracy using a single set of parameters. Additionally, constraints are provided for the physical properties of the disk, which align with other models available in literature. 

A crucial aspect to consider is the impact of PH3 ice particles, which could significantly affect the 12 CO emission structure if they are present in large numbers. Therefore, it is essential to use 13 CO observations instead of combining data from both isotopes as this may introduce inaccuracies in the analysis. 

Variations in the structure and composition of the ice particles have a notable effect on the gas emission structure. Two distinct 'puff' models are presented, which vary depending on the distribution and composition of the PH3 ice particles. Ultimately, high-frequency mapping of the 13 CO emission is required to determine the structure and composition of the gas in the inner region of the AS 209 disk accurately. 

In the area closest to the star, the structure of the gas exhibits similarities with the ice particles' structure. Although this is the case, it is essential to note the differences between the gas and ice substructures at certain angles and distances from the star, which may be attributed to the distinct optical properties of gas and ice particles. 

In the area far from the star, the gas and ice substructures align perfectly, which is not the case for the inner region. A possible explanation for this discrepancy is the presence of electric fields originating from the star's ionized atmosphere, which could affect the ice particles

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational efficiency. Featuring a user-friendly interface with live update capabilities, ETA allows real-time monitoring of analysis progress and enables the rapid exploration of various analysis methods. The framework's modular design facilitates seamless integration of external programming languages, enabling a versatile range of applications that we demonstrate with practical examples from the fields of synchrotron radiation biophysics, free-electron laser biomedicine, and particle physics. Furthermore, ETA provides a comprehensive set of tools for common use cases, including time-stamped data visualization, peak search, and data extraction, refund, and aggregation. These functionalities can be accessed through an interactive and searchable etalibrary containing over 130 proven analysis methods, which can be easily replicated, adapted, and shared with other researchers. With its cutting-edge performance, user-friendly interface, and collaborative capabilities, ETA has become an indispensable tool for our research team, supporting a wide range of high-technology applications. For the fashion industry, visual compatibility plays a crucial role in designing clothing items that appeal to consumers. Traditional methods used for identifying incompatible outfits relied heavily on human expertise. Recent advancements in computer vision, enabled by the use of large-scale fashion datasets such as MFM, have paved the way for automated compatibility analysis. Our research presents a cutting-edge transformer-based model, called VICTOR, specifically designed for visual compatibility analysis. By incorporating a unique combination of multi-head self-attention and contrastive learning, VICTOR surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the MFM benchmark. Due to the dataset's limitations in capturing complex outfit combinations, we introduce an innovative extension to the benchmark through a collaborative fashion design challenge. Results demonstrate VICTOR's adaptability and state-of-the-art performance on the modified dataset. In this paper, a novel FL protocol is introduced that significantly reduces latency by minimizing communication steps. By allowing unrestricted gradient updates and asynchronous data availability, this new approach aligns training with real-world data availability. Furthermore, a high-efficiency communication mechanism is developed that combines pending updates and reduces communication frequency. Experimental results demonstrate the performance benefits of this protocol, achieving comparable accuracy to traditional FL methods while substantially reducing communication costs. Valuable insights are gained for complex datasets, and the code is openly accessible on GitHub. Moreover, the proposed protocol is compatible with existing FL systems, making it a versatile and reliable solution. Evaluation results show that, at the very least, FL training can be $13\times$ faster when training on $19$ datasets with $774$ instances and $5\times$ faster when training on $26$ datasets with $2020$ instances. Interestingly, the protocol tends to perform best on datasets with more complex models and less available data. In a surprising finding, federated learning often surpasses local training in efficiency, reversing a long-standing assumption. Moreover, the efficiency of the protocol is relatively insensitive to communication bandwidth, data availability, and latency, highlighting its true potential. Lastly, the protocol is more robust to failures and data corruption than traditional FL methods, reflecting its simplified error handling mechanism. Encouragingly, the benefits of the protocol are consistent across various FL scenarios, suggesting its vast applications and promising future. This research explores the functional properties of polynomial-valued tempered distributions, focusing on the underlying space of these distributions. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the convergence of a sequence of polynomial distributions. In addition, we examine the function spaces of polynomial distributions, including the Sobolev spaces and their properties. This work is an extension of distribution theory, enabling us to apply it to function spaces of polynomial distributions and derive relevant inequalities. This involves examining the Bessel and Riesz transformations for polynomial distributions and deriving relevant inequalities, including those related to Sobolev and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, as well as the Poincaré inequality. This research will contribute to a broader understanding of function space, particularly in connection with the Bessel and Riesz transformations for polynomial distributions. We expect this research to be useful in other contexts, and our findings will have far-reaching implications for functional analysis. Finally, many of our results are illustrative, and our primary goal is to educate students in this field. Nonetheless, our research also yields novel and non-obvious findings, which can be utilized in a wide range of applications. These applications include proving the non-existence of nonzero polynomial measures that are locally integrable within $\mathbb{R}^n$. Also, under a specific condition, we demonstrate the boundedness of the Bessel operator for polynomial distributions. This operator is denoted as $J_\alpha$ and, under a specific regime for $\alpha$ and $p$ (where $p$ is a variable exponent in the range $1 < p < \infty$), we show that it gives rise to a bounded operator from $L^p_\alpha$ to $L^q_\beta$ for appropriate $\beta$ and $q$. Here, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $q$ are constants greater than $1$. We show that the Bessel operator is bounded in this manner when the exponent $\alpha$ is a real noninteger in the range $1 < \alpha < \infty$. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces using the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and show that they become asymptotically flat as the singular point is approached. Additionally, we derive conditions for the original patch to be asymptotically flat everywhere if all singularities behave asymptotically flat. To support our findings, we provide examples of patches with singular points and patches with conical singular points. These examples illustrate cases where the transformed patches are asymptotically flat throughout or have the same type of singularity as the original patch. Lastly, we present an open problem concerning generalized isothermic surfaces with a particular type of singularity. We show that for a specific class of generalized isothermic surfaces with a holomorphic Hopf differential, applying the Darboux transformation results in a surface with a singularity, and if the original surface is asymptotically flat, the transformed surface will also be asymptotically flat with a singularity. These results expand upon the findings in the paper by Pottmann et al., and the associated conference proceedings. It is interesting to note that our findings can be realized through the use of blowouts, and we show that for a specific type of isothermic surfaces with a holomorphic differential, the Calapso transformation leads to a surface with a singularity, and if the original surface is asymptotically flat, the transformed surface will also be asymptotically flat with a singularity. These results provide a new perspective on the relationship between isothermic surfaces and asymptotically flat surfaces with singularities. This review article focuses on estimating conditional expectation operators from data drawn from unknown distributions. It primarily considers nonparametric methods, specifically those utilizing linear combinations of known functions as estimating tools. These linear combinations are often part of a richer function space system, such as a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, whose structure provides a framework for the review. After discussing initial results, the text delves into more advanced topics, such as the behavior of empirical operators and nonlinear estimation techniques. A significant portion is devoted to deriving almost sure convergence theorems for the empirical operator. This convergence is assessed in both the L1 metric and a more general norm derived from the original space's norm. A key finding involves the conditions under which this convergence holds involves only the degree of smoothness of the target operator. This allows the estimation to be applied to conditional derivatives under certain conditions. A related area, Markov decision process (MDP) value function estimation, is also explored, along with several illustrative examples and the paper concludes by examining potential avenues for further research in the field. A smaller section at the end discusses the paper's contributions and highlights its main advances. Finally, the paper also briefly discusses the relationship between its research and other notable works in the field. This article originated as a conference talk and the authors' research note, with significant portions reproduced with permission. With some notable exceptions, the paper primarily relies on existing reviews for a comprehensive bibliography. This includes notable works by Bickel, Lehmann, and Wellner, as well as more recent contributions by Johnstone and Tailor, among others.
