The vastness of World Wide Web data makes conventional graph techniques unfeasible for processing temporal knowledge graphs (TGs), which are essential for numerous AI applications. To address this, a novel link prediction framework leveraging static models is proposed, enabling faster predictions on larger TGs. It integrates multiple models, including a straightforward method (SM), and two enhanced variations (EVM1 and EVM2), all of which capitalize on TGs having well-defined time intervals and incorporating time-based features. It is demonstrated that combining these models outperforms using individual models alone, and that the proposed framework excels over existing approaches in terms of accuracy and processing speed. Additionally, a methodology is outlined for quantitatively evaluating TG datasets, enabling fair model comparison. As a result, this framework becomes a practical solution for TGs, and its source code is made available. Experiments reveal that SM and EVM1/EVM2 surpass state-of-the-art models (including ComplEx, ConvE, and Model2) by 2.7% and 4.8% in terms of mean rank, respectively. Furthermore, a linearity boundary is established to guarantee sublinear query performance, and it is shown that the proposed framework attains a query time of 0.21 seconds per 10,000 queries, surpassing existing models and embedding models by a significant margin. Finally, it is shown through real-world scenarios that the predicted TGs obtained from the proposed framework are actionable and useful. Specifically, it is shown that 76% of predicted KGs are verified as correct, and by suggesting 1% of a TG's edges as new relations, a 25% increase in entity disambiguation accuracy is achieved. Overall, this research highlights the effectiveness of static models in link prediction for TGs, and it is proposed that a hybrid of TGs comprising static and temporal models will yield the best results. The source code has been made available for reproducibility. In the future, it is intended to enhance the proposed models by incorporating static aspects into temporal models. Considering the potential misuse of temporal knowledge graphs (TGs), a cautionary approach is taken in this research. Consequently, only general conclusions and theoretical underpinnings are provided, and specific numerical TG data remains undisclosed. Instead, processed TG data is made available for evaluation purposes. It is hypothesized that a similar research approach can be applied to other real-world datasets. As such, this research is only applicable to datasets having well-defined time intervals and excluding sensitive information.

In this research, we have examined the complex process of heavy quark disintegration in a complex, non-zero magnetic field environment. Building on previous work, we have expanded our analysis to include all virtual gluon modes and accounted for the unique properties of heavy quarks. We have developed a detailed mathematical framework, represented by a 4x4 matrix, to represent the interaction between heavy quarks and gluons at varying magnetic field strengths. Our findings reveal that, as heavy quark mass varies, its interaction patterns with gluons and magnetic fields exhibit distinct dependencies and differeences. We have also identified regional soft and hard components in these interactions, which are influenced by complex gluon dynamics and magnetic interactions, respectively. Notably, at high magnetic field strengths, heavy quark disintegration exhibits distinct anisotropic characteristics, influenced by complex gluon dynamics in one direction and magnetic interactions in another direction. We have further applied and verified our mathematical framework through the calculation of a complex process likelihood at varying magnetic field strengths. We have observed that, at high magnetic field strengths, process likelihood patterns can be described as either decreasing or increasing, depending on both heavy quark mass and magnetic field strength. These results are distinct from processes in zero-magnetic field environments, where process likelihood patterns are only affected by heavy quark mass. We have also noted similarities in process likelihood patterns at high magnetic field strengths and those in zero-magnetic field environments, where process likelihood patterns are only affected by heavy quark mass. Unfortunately, these models are often limited in their ability to understand the underlying structure of the world, which makes it hard for them to provide clear and confident answers to questions. To fix this, our approach involves giving these models a diagram of the relationships between entities in a specific domain and teaching them how to use it to answer questions, which can help provide clear and confident answers. We tested this approach by using a special diagram of the relationships between characters and places in the Harry Potter books and found that it significantly improved the performance of these models, whether they were trained using a small amount of data or a large amount of data. In fact, our approach helped these models match the performance of much stronger models that had been specially programmed to understand the context of the questions. To make sure that our approach would work in other situations, we also tested it using diagrams of the relationships between entities in two other domains and found that it helped improve performance there as well. We have developed new high-dimensional covering systems of points in lattices, utilizing covers of certain infinite regions within lattices. These covering systems enable us to create new forms of Brillouin regions, expanding upon previous work by Ginzburg and Sardakanian. We also establish a generalized version of Ginzburg's theorem regarding the density of orbits in these new systems. These results can be applied to generate new families of non-linear codes equipped with distance amplification properties. We have found explicit examples of these codes, with parameters supported by numerical density estimates. We expect the proposed code families to be valid, though the verification process might be hindered by complex parameter interdependencies. If the proposed codes exist, they would offer an alternative to the MCKS program and the LLL reduction for dense lattices, potentially providing code families with the Chowla conjecture implicit parameters and lattice reductions for low-density codes. We have also discovered that our work can be generalized to covering spaces of lattices containing subspaces with specific properties. The proof involves an inductive argument that could be useful in studying Orlik solids and other structures. We hope these results will contribute to further research in algebra, combinatorics, and number theory. We have provided an appendix containing an alternate proof of Ginzburg's theorem, along with a relevant arithmetic lemma, both of which rely on Ginzburg and Sardakanian's findings and offer complementary perspectives on the original proof. Additionally, the appendix contains a relevant lemma concerning exponents of lattices, along with some general remarks about the applied mathematics of lattices. Finally, the appendix contains an overview of the code families in question, along with numerical estimates of their parameters and a description of their expected properties. Please note that the overall structure and content of the manuscript could be revised and improved with further input from experts in the relevant fields. To evaluate how well various natural language prompts perform across different contexts, we developed the PromptEval benchmark, which was specifically designed for the zero-shot, multi-choice environment of the PMI (Prompt Meaning Inference) challenge. Our benchmark offers a comprehensive analysis by examining prompts' inherent meaning and exploring the boundaries of natural language through manipulation. Our study includes an in-depth examination of how different prompt types, as previously proposed in the literature, perform in the PMI setting. We discovered that modifying words within a prompt's statement or question can significantly impact its interpretation. Additionally, we found that using auxiliary phrases can enhance performance, while utilizing questions may not always yield better results. Our findings also show that a prompt's last token holds important semantic information. We will make our code, benchmark, and data available to the public. We hope that PromptEval will facilitate research in natural language understanding through prompt analysis and generation. We are also announcing the winners of the Promptroka challenge and PMI competition at NeurIPS 2021.

Achieving a balance between mitigating the spread of a highly contagious disease and allowing an economy to function is a delicate task. To address this issue, a fundamental mathematical problem is posed, where the goal is to minimize a measure of disease severity, represented by a quadratic function, subject to constraints related to the limited capacity of non-pharmaceutical interventions. The research presents a groundbreaking approach, providing a universally applicable solution that can be applied to any disease model characterized by similar nonlinear dynamics. The method is illustrated using the specific case of a pandemic affecting a population with social interactions, where individuals can choose to isolate themselves. The results show that a uniform policy of temporary lockdowns across the population yields the most effective outcomes, according to the defined measure of disease severity, when compared to targeted interventions tailored to individuals' behaviors. The research relies on fundamental concepts from mathematics, including convex optimization and the continuous principle of optimality, to establish a general solution that can be applied to a broad family of disease models. To further broaden its applicability, the solution is presented as a strategy for navigating a "landscape of optimality," a framework that can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of various intervention methods, such as lockdowns, and guide future research in optimal pandemic interventions. The research provides a mathematical demonstration of the efficacy of unified pandemic policies, supporting the arguments put forth by public health officials and advocating for temporary economic restrictions over targeted interventions that aim to balance health and economic risks. The development of complex end-to-end machine learning systems presents significant challenges in debugging, particularly due to the variety of inputs passed through the pipeline during training and testing. Many end-to-end systems consist of multiple modular components, such as automatic differentiation and annotation, which complicate the process of data analysis. In an effort to streamline data debugging, we have introduced a data debugging framework that utilizes the Shapley value formula to quantify the impact of individual data items. This innovative approach facilitates the efficient debugging of data-driven models by identifying the most critical data samples for each prediction outcome. We have applied our method to several machine learning pipelines, including a self-driving car system and a medical image diagnosis system, to illustrate its practical applications. The results show that a relatively small percentage of data samples (approximately 10%) yield a high percentage (greater than 70%) of the total prediction confidence. This lecture will demonstrate various statistical and combinatorial consequences that arise from applying theorems in enumerative geometry, specifically positive development theory. We will examine a statistical model used to measure social inequality, illustrating a practical instance where enumerative geometry yields quantifiable outcomes. Building on this, we will explore a general statistical model characterized by symmetric, non-symmetric and topological considerations. Combining principles from enumerative geometry, combinatorial methods and topology, we will derive a statistical model for random power series expansions. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the structural and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Sn, a unique material that exhibits an unusual Hall effect (AHE) due to time-reversal symmetry breaking. At ambient pressure, the material features a hexagonal structure with a layered arrangement, with two of the layers composed of ferromagnetically ordered triangles sharing a central atom. As pressure increases to 1.2 GPa, a significant structural transformation occurs, replacing the hexagonal pattern with a face-centered cubic structure, accompanied by a 14% reduction in lattice constant. Importantly, this structural change leads to a 20-fold enhancement of the AHE. Through the application of density functional theory and lattice dynamics analysis, the material's electronic and magnetic properties are thoroughly understood. At ambient pressure, the material's ferromagnetic $A$-type arrangement within the layers, combined with non-zero spin-polarized orbit contributions, gives rise to a robust AHE. Conversely, the application of high pressure induces a helical magnetic ground state with interlayer ordering, thereby eliminating the time-reversal symmetry breaking and resulting AHE. Instead, a strong spin-density wave (SDW) emerges, ultimately giving rise to the heightened AHE at high pressure. In summary, this research demonstrates that pressure can regulate the material's magnetic structure and, in turn, switch the AHE on or off through alterations to the time-reversal symmetry breaking and spin-polarized orbit contributions. Furthermore, this study is the first to illustrate pressure-induced switching of AHE in an antiferromagnet, opening up new avenues to controlling this phenomenon using external stimuli. These measurements are crucial for interpreting the solar wind's electric fields. The solar wind's electric fields were observed to be highly dynamic, with scale sizes of a few hundred meters up to several kilometers. This scale of the electric fields is similar to the solar wind's kinetic scale. We used the solar wind's electron density data in conjunction with the electric fields to determine the electric conductivity. This led to discovering that the solar wind's Hall conductivity is much larger than its longitudinal conductivity. This significant disparity is due to the vast differences in the solar wind's scale sizes and the electron heat flux. As a result, this property is unique to the solar wind and the ionized media surrounding the Earth and other planets. Currently, physical models that aim to simulate the solar wind fail to accurately capture this characteristic. Therefore, there's a pressing need for physical models that can properly replicate this property. In addition, we observed that the solar wind's electric fields and the electron heat flux share a similar power spectrum. This shared power spectrum is believed to be a result of the compressive turbulence that exists in the solar wind. Nonetheless, the magnetic field measurements do not follow the same power spectrum as the electric fields. Instead, they are characterized by a more flat distribution. This phenomenon is anticipated to emerge in the solar wind at distances closer to the sun, which are well within the orbit of the terrestrial planets. In effect, this property is likely to have a considerable impact on the solar wind's interaction with other planets. At the same time, it is also believed to play a crucial role in shaping the magnetic field measurements observed in deep space. Finally, it is worth noting that the solar wind's electric fields demonstrate the existence of a nonlinear relationship between electric field and density. This is a property that is thought to exist in other ionized media as well. At the same time, it is also notable that the solar wind's electric fields are correlated with the ion acoustic turbulence. This is a property that is believed to be a fundamental aspect of the solar wind. In contrast, the solar wind's electric fields do not demonstrate any correlation with the transverse magnetic field measurements. Instead, they are primarily determined by the electric conductivity, the electron heat flux, and the scale sizes of the solar wind. In conclusion, comprehensive data obtained from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission provide new insights into the solar wind's electric fields

Notably, this process requires massive energy release on a nanosecond timescale, which in turn necessitates substantial mass loss from near-black-hole systems at roughly the same pace as the black hole's mass growth. In near-fall-in scenarios, this mass loss is linked to a relativistic kinetic energy transfer from a black hole to its surrounding accretion disc, leading to the question: can a Bondi mass loss rate hinged on black hole accretion be a suitable indicator of this energy transfer? Ultimately, this accretion leads to the creation of dark matter candidate particles, which in turn result in neutrino production, giving rise to the observed high-energy signatures in compact object mergers. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games has been their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests involving thousands of players over extended periods of time.
TextWorldExpress maintains the same level of difficulty and engaging gameplay as its original counterparts while employing a combination of sophisticated techniques, including multi-threaded code execution and advanced data structures. 
The performance boost brings text-based games more closely in line with real-time applications, making them more suitable for thorough agent evaluations. 
A comprehensive study demonstrates the effectiveness of a straightforward yet powerful agent strategy called the Exploration-Expansion method, which achieves remarkable success by focusing solely on areas with high potential rewards and taking the shortest paths to reach them. 
To facilitate widespread access to our optimized game challenges, we are releasing a highly versatile and user-friendly visual tool used to create and study text-based games, available under an open-source license. 
This tool allows for seamless integration of various visualization techniques and can handle even the most complex game scenarios, making it ideally suited for testing a wide range of agent strategies. 
The future development pathways for text-based games are also explored to determine how they can continue to utilize emerging technologies to push the limits of what virtual agents can accomplish. 
In particular, two promising avenues for further research are natural language processing and reasoning, which text-based games are well-equipped to exploit. 
Related technical details are discussed in the appendices, and extensive experimental data are provided in a public database for the sake of transparency and replicability of our results. 
An accompanying technical report provides an in-depth review of the underlying research challenges and theoretical frameworks governing text-based games. 
An interactive demonstration of TextWorldExpress is available online at textworldexpress.github.io. 
The source code for TextWorldExpress is openly available on GitHub at textworldexpress.github.io/i6-textworld-express. 
The data collected during our research are publicly accessible on GitHub at textworldexpress.github.io/i6-textworld-data. 
The code used to visualize our results is publicly accessible on GitHub at textworldexpress.github.io/i6-textworld-visualizations

Topological Insulators are insulating phases that exhibit topological invariants being robust against external perturbations and spatial deformations. We introduce a mathematical framework for dealing with defects in Topological Insulators using spectral transformations. We apply this method to study different types of defects in one-dimensional chiral insulators and two-dimensional Topological Insulators under the influence of a Chern number. Our approach allows for the creation of any desired defect spectrum, thereby enabling the realization of any desired transverse current pattern. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various examples, such as merging two Topological Insulators to form a gapped system or introducing a zero-mode in the spectrum for potential technological applications. Additionally, we propose an extension of our method to closed systems by incorporating the study of BPS solitons within the framework of spectral deformations. We anticipate our mathematical framework to contribute significantly to the study of Topological Insulators and Insulators with defects.

The manipulability ellipsoid provides valuable insights into a robot's dexterity, allowing comparisons between human and robot hand configurations. To facilitate meaningful correlations, it is necessary to ensure that these ellipsoids align properly. However, this task is complicated by the lack of a straightforward method to map human hand configurations to robot hand configurations. Since many interaction tasks are contingent on both hands, it becomes crucial to establish a consistent framework that can bridge electronic and human hands. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that utilizes machine learning to predict the manipulability ellipsoid's rotation from one hand to another. Notably, this model relies on data that has been preprocessed using the FastICA method. While efficient, this process can introduce inaccuracies in certain configurations, which we rectify by developing a new algorithm. Inspired by the concept of parallel transport, it uses the Low-Rank Factorization optimization technique to refine the manipulated ellipsoids' rotation over time. To test our model's generalizability, we conducted a series of experiments that involved a diverse range of robotic hands. During these trials, small differences in the manipulated ellipsoids' rotation led to notable performance variations, which prompted us to develop a more robust method to estimate this rotation. By combining the ideas of manifold ICp and parallel transport, we developed a multi-step approach that calculates the optimal rotation, trajectory, and alignment of the manipulated ellipsoids. This technique also enables seamless hand substitutions in tasks such as grasping and manipulation, which we successfully demonstrated in a series of simulated and real-world experiments. To validate our method's efficacy, we conducted a series of robotic hand swap tasks, which involved demonstrating the new dexterity that a low-dexterity robotic hand can achieve after applying the parallel transport algorithm. To accomplish this, we employed a trajectory optimization method that takes into account the manipulability ellipsoids' constraints, which we estimated using a deep learning model that generalizes well to various robotic hands. In the future, we plan to extend this approach to higher-dimensional ellipsoids, which will enable us to compare the dexterity of robotic and human hands in three-dimensional grasping configurations. To achieve this, we will develop a dedicated evaluation platform that can accurately estimate the manipulability ellipsoids' rotation and performance across a wide range of 3D interaction tasks. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite their potential, they are hampered by a 'node issue': too few nodes result in underfitting, while too many nodes lead to overfitting. Existing methods either expand the network uniformly or prioritize data-dense areas. A more effective approach would be to learn from data distribution and adaptively place nodes. This would, however, require learning the nodes, which is computationally intensive and violates the principle of self-consistency. To address this challenge, a residual-based adaptive node creation method (RANG) is proposed. It utilizes the smooth prediction from physics-informed neural networks to estimate the spacing between nodes and adapts the grid based on residual magnitude in each dimension. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding how vulnerabilities spread through a software dependency network. Our research addresses this issue by designing an innovative approach to create a vast knowledge graph about dependency weaknesses. Utilizing this graph, we successfully identified the sources of many vulnerability outbreaks. Our proposed technique not only outperforms existing methods but also offers superior accuracy, boasting a 24.8% improvement in precision and a 99.8% improvement in recall over the benchmark. The substantial gains in recall demonstrate how effectively our approach propagates vulnerabilities, whereas the gains in precision highlight the high precision of our vulnerability source identification method. Composed of extensive bibliographic information, this weakness graph encompasses over 330 million pieces of data, spanning three distinct entities: package managers, dependencies, and vulnerabilities. Our approach is versatile, compatible with various package managers, and showcases the effectiveness of our methodology when applied to Maven, a widely-used package manager. By conducting an in-depth evaluation, we validate the effectiveness of our knowledge graph and underlying algorithms through multiple assessment strategies. Furthermore, our study includes an exploratory analysis, revealing insights into vulnerability dissemination, such as how often a vulnerability remains unpropagated and how often a vulnerability spreads to all dependencies of its parent project. The depth of our findings is a direct result of our knowledge graph's comprehensive design, allowing us to derive so much information from it. Ultimately, our research contributes a valuable knowledge base that can be used for automated vulnerability detection in software dependency systems. With regular updates, our knowledge graph continues to expand, covering an ever-growing percentage of existing Cargo projects. Currently, the graph encompasses over 350,000 projects, a figure expected to double in the near future, thereby further enhancing the accuracy of our vulnerability propagation results. In the future, we intend to expand our research by incorporating additional entities, such as vulnerabilities fixing information, to further broaden the applications of our knowledge graph and weakness propagation technique. By incorporating this additional information, we can determine not only how vulnerabilities propagate but also how they are resolved across a software dependency network. With this expanded capability, our research will have far-reaching implications for the fields of software engineering, vulnerability research, and dependency analysis. To facilitate the development of future research, we are openly providing the underlying technical details, including the used data processing tools, for replicating our results and building upon our research. Additionally, our study includes a detailed assessment of the practical utility of our approach, highlighting numerous applications in vulnerability research and software dependency systems. To foster collaboration, we are inviting researchers to contribute to our research

In this study, we establish minimum order parameters for the power graph of finite nilpotent groups. Specifically, for a finite nilpotent group G, we demonstrate that the power graph's G-simplicial complex has a minimum order given by |G|^2 < |G|^3 < |G|^4, with the upper bound representing the maximum possible order. Furthermore, we prove that if |G| is a perfect square, the order upper bound is |G|^4. Additionally, for a finite nilpotent group G, with the exception of certain cases such as G being abelian or isomorphic to A4, we show that the power graph's G-simplicial complex has a minimum order given by |G|^2. We also explore the minimum order of the square root of the power graph's G-simplicial complex, establishing that if |G| is a perfect square, the order upper bound is |G|^2. For a finite non-abelian nilpotent group G, with the exception of certain cases such as G being isomorphic to A4, A5, A6, A7, A8, or D8, we show that the power graph's G-simplicial complex has a minimum order given by |G|^2. We also provide a join operation implementation on power graphs to facilitate the determination of the order upper bound. Using this implementation, we examine specific examples of finite non-abelian nilpotent groups in various orders and compute the order of the power graph's G-simplicial complex for each. We also investigate the properties of the power graph's G-simplicical complex for certain specific groups. In the course of this research, several new, non-abelian finite nilpotent groups satisfying the order condition |G| <= |G|^2 are discovered and added to the Small Groups Library. We also propose an algorithm to generate all finite non-abelian nilpotent groups meeting the order condition |G| <= |G|^2 and aim to integrate this into the Small Groups Library. We also explore in our research the properties of the square root of the power graph's G-simplicial complex for finite non-abelian nilpotent groups. The HiGRARE project aims to develop an advanced hadron spectrometer with hi-tech features, capable of tackling challenges in several areas, including cosmic ray research, astrophysics, and baryon physics at high energy scales (10 TeV, 50 TeV). The proposed device will address two key problems in cosmic ray research: determining the maximum of the cosmic ray energy spectrum and exploring the characteristics of Grandfather Paradoxes. Furthermore, it will enable the selection of extremely energetic, long-lived particles in atmospheric nuclei interactions, thereby providing crucial data for studying resonances and their decays. Utilizing the LHCb experiment's underground site and refining its detection systems with the latest technologies will facilitate hi-resolution investigations of long-lived particles at 13.6 TeV and their combinations with magnetic fields. Prototypes of key components are being developed with a focus on an R&D period of two years, followed by prototype testing and site integration in 2024-25. The HiGRARE detector will then be ready for operations in 2026 at the LHCb experiment's site, where it will undergo a two-year period of prototyping and testing before an eventual deployment as a portable, ground-based detector for cosmic ray research and astrophysics applications. The detector will feature a 15-degree sector of a Wilson chamber with electron and muon identification capabilities, a 4-sigma top priority magnetic separation of long-lived particles and their combinations with magnetic fields, and a 6-sigma high precision time-stamping system with 100 nanosecond resolutions. Additionally, the HiGRARE detector will benefit from an optional trigger system with deep learning and a high-level data reduction process. The HiGRARE project is a collaborative effort with 20 researchers from Russian and foreign institutions. They will also establish a school for young scientists and researchers, focusing on an interdisciplinary course in cosmic ray research, astrophysics, and baryon physics at high energy scales. The course will feature notable scientists and researchers, including Professor Dr. David Saltz and Professor Dr. Andrew Watson, as guest speakers. The course will enable young scientists and researchers to develop innovative ideas and solutions, thereby stimulating their creativity and potential to become leaders in their respective fields. The HiGRARE project encompasses significant research and development opportunities across three key areas: software, prototyping, and educational initiatives. As a result, the project has secured funding and support from multiple institutions and organizations. Recent breakthroughs from 2D convolutional networks have driven progress in
vision, but research has been limited in utilizing 3D convolutional networks for
image recognition. This paper proposes Direction Convolution Networks (DC-Net), a
new model that leverages 3D convolutional networks for global image recognition. A
novel DC-Net architecture consists of a stack of 3D convolutional layers with
linearly transformed filters, followed by a linear projection, and demonstrates
exemplary classification performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. By
analyzing its generalization capabilities, we find the optimal depth and in-plane
filter rotation range for the DC-Net architecture. Moreover, this study provides a
theoretical basis for the effectiveness of the DC-Net architecture. Through
experiments with cross-domain adaptations and unsupervised domain confusion, we
show the DC-Net architecture can generalize well to unsupervised domain
adaptation tasks. Additionally, the unsupervised domain confusion method proposed
in this study can be applied to various deep network models to improve their
generalization to unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios. The code for this
research is publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/achiaomdc/DC-Net.

This study seeks to enhance the graph convolutional network's capability to propagate information within point clouds, particularly in point cloud learning tasks. We critically examine the traditional graph convolutional network, noting its limitations in point cloud learning due to the use of node features in Euclidean space and the reliance on grid-based methods, which can lead to information loss. To address this issue, we propose the PointGCN network, featuring a graph convolutional layer that combines node feature propagation with spatial propagation. By doing so, we aim to increase the network's capacity to capture high-level features in point cloud learning tasks. Experimental results demonstrate PointGCN's effectiveness, with the model achieving impressive performance in semantic segmentation and classification tasks. Additionally, we introduce a diverse dataset consisting of airfoil shapes, ultimately achieving classification rates of 92% for categories containing 20 objects and 68% for a category with 400 objects. Our findings also show that PointGCN can automatically discover geometric patterns in categories, surpassing current state-of-the-art models. Notably, the proposed method can be integrated into existing deep learning frameworks without the need to use coordinate axis-specific features. We are creating a spatially resolved, on-the-fly (integral field) device for the Magellan IMACS spectrograph on the Lucas Telescope as part of the Research Observations with the Lucas-Astronomer's Integral Field, or ROSIE project. Our device will be a 3x1 or 1x7 array of 2.5 arcsecond cubes with a total field of view of 3-5 arcseconds square, utilizing the IMACS 17.9 degree field of view to facilitate the exploration of extended objects like galaxies, star-forming regions, and nebulae. Our device will feature an e2V 2020 CCD array with high sensitivity and 27 micron pixels, allowing for a 5.1 arcsecond square sparsity grid when observing at a 90 arcsecond height above the lens array. Our team has completed the design, building, and testing of the device, including a fiber-based cross-dispersion along the length of the array and a dichroic that sends blue light to the top of the array and red light to the bottom, with each cube covering a 1.3-2.1 arcsecond height. We have developed an automated controller and a software package for data acquisition, and have successfully tested the device on multiple occasions, including a 5 night run in March 2018 during observations of the M81 Galaxy. Our device will be available for user observation through a proposal process similar to that used by the Lowel Observatory. Our team expects the device to observe a range of objects including galaxies, star-forming regions, and nebulae, with a range of technical papers and research projects in development. This project has provided our team with valuable educational and professional development opportunities, and has strengthened our relationship with the Lowel Observatory and our community, engaging in activities such as science outreach and public education. In the future, our device will be used in studies of the M81 Galaxy, among many other applications. This work is currently cited in a paper by Clemens et al. Deep neural networks (DNN) have become a preferred method for wireless localization using channel state information (CSI), outperforming traditional approaches by leveraging the rich data in CSI. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of DNN depends on the quality and quantity of gathered CSI data, which can be limited by equipment costs and accessible recording duration. This research introduces a novel strategy to augment existing CSI data through attention-based deep learning, allowing previously recorded CSI to be combined with new recordings without requiring a comprehensive dataset rematch. This'memory-based' approach incorporates attention mechanics to selectively gather relevant information from previous recordings, enhancing the localization performance when updating with fresh data. Experimentation on a real indoor dataset reveals that this attention-assisted method achieves superior results compared to standard deep learning and attention-less models. Moreover, the developed network exhibits greater scalability and generalizability when dealing with various dataset scales and non-scale-dependent datasets. Ultimately, this attention-assisted method reaches an accuracy of 0.41 NMAE by utilizing only 40% of the total dataset, demonstrating substantial computational savings of 80% with minimal performance loss. This finding has significant implications for localization systems using CSI, which often face data recording constraints due to equipment limitations. The proposed method offers a promising solution, enabling existing systems to locally store valuable data, support new arrivals, or update outdated information. Additionally, this approach can be adapted to various deep learning models and problems, such as channel estimation and wireless communication systems. Unlike conventional assessments using a single galaxy template or mock observations, our approach utilizes spectra from numerous sources, exploiting variations in star formation rates, metal content, and mass light emission properties. As a key advantage, our method generates vast numbers of "observations," reducing reliance on precise statistical analysis. To validate our approach, we apply it to a well-established template from Ilbert et al. (2013), observing a notable discrepancy in its predicted star formation rates. To improve future SED-fitting templates and calibration methods, we outline potential adjustments and future developments. Ultimately, our new tool facilitates the large-scale evaluation of SED-fitting techniques, such as the one presented in Pacifici et al. (2018), and may be adapted for analyzing other methods with observational data. By implementing this tool, we identify an issue with negative star formation rates at low luminosity thresholds, suggesting two possible corrections for future developments. Additionally, our method is compatible with the use of star formation histories with decreasing rates, despite initial concerns about their applicability, confirming the versatility and utility of our new tool. To capture the intrinsic variability of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) spectral time series, a probabilistic autoencoder called SpecTempAE has been developed. This autoencoder uses a deep neural network to extract essential features from the spectral evolution of SNe Ia over time, while distinguishing between intrinsic and extrinsic factors that contribute to the variability. As a key component of the SpecTempAE model, a normalizing flow-based prior aims to separate the intrinsic characteristics of a SN Ia explosion from other factors that affect its spectral evolution. By applying the SpecTempAE model in a Bayesian framework, the inherent properties of SNe Ia can be accurately estimated, which is crucial for understanding the cosmological distance redshift distribution. Our analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the SpecTempAE model by applying it to a small dataset consisting of 107 SNe Ia observations with 4 epochs and approximately 1200 spectra. However, further testing with a much larger dataset is required to confirm the model's potential to accurately model SNe Ia observations and obtain reliable posterior distributions. Our work represents the first application of an autoencoder to temporal series data in the context of cosmology. As a public repository, the SpecTempAE model and associated code will be made available to allow for replication of our results and testing of our approach on various datasets. Our findings emphasize the importance of validating the model's performance on multiple datasets before employing it for cosmological distance measurements. Our research paves the way for the use of deep learning methods to analyze temporal series data in cosmology and we anticipate that a large-scale demonstration of our approach will significantly contribute to accurate cosmological distance measurements. Our work will be crossed-checked with other deep learning methods such as Transfer Learning and Random Forests to compare their performance in extracting essential features from temporal series data and we expect that a comprehensive comparison will be carried out in a forthcoming paper. It is worth noting that our approach to applying an autoencoder to temporal series data is unique and represents an innovative solution to cosmological distance measurements based on SNe Ia spectral observations. As a testament to the uniqueness of our method, a prior review by the arXiv reviewers noted that "to the best of my knowledge, this is the first publication treating the resolution of this issue [extracting intrinsic properties from temporal series data] with deep learning methods". This process is more significant when the interface contains particles that interfere with it, affecting the dynamics. For this study, we observed the mass transfer process using a vertical column setup where the interface contained particles of different sizes and densities. The results in the form of particle images and velocity measurements helped us understand the role of particles in the mass transfer process. Due to the particles' effect on the interface, the mass transfer process is increased, especially in certain turbulent regimes. This interaction varies depending on the particles' properties. If the particles have a low density relative to the fluid, their presence significantly affects the mass transfer process, whereas if they have a high density, their presence has a minimal impact. This knowledge can be applied to real-world scenarios such as natural phenomena and industrial processes to optimize outcomes. Given the experimental findings, we observed that particles play a crucial role in determining the mass transfer process, and their effect goes beyond their physical characteristics. Instead, their impact is closely tied to the dynamics of the turbulent flow and the process by which energy is transferred within the fluid. From a theoretical standpoint, we analyzed the process and were able to understand and explain the process from a Lagrangian perspective, focusing on trajectories and behavior. Additionally, we were able to understand and explain the process from a Gaussian perspective, focusing on distributions and processes. Ultimately, we were able to develop a model that accurately represents and predicts the mass transfer process when particles are present. This knowledge can be applied to various scenarios, including heat and mass transfer processes in natural and industrial contexts. We investigate the spread of an infectious disease within a network of interconnected relationships, assuming a large population and a relatively low infection rate. By adapting spectral graph theory to analyze this issue, we identify the critical threshold below which an outbreak is likely to fail, given varying contact patterns among individuals. In particular, our research reveals that more complex social connections increase the likelihood of an epidemic, leading to a higher expected number of infected individuals. Furthermore, we demonstrate how different types of disease transmission mechanisms affect this critical threshold, enabling more accurate predictions of an epidemic's outcome. Ultimately, our analysis provides a more robust understanding of how infectious diseases propagate through human relationships. 

In this study, we focus on two types of disease transmission mechanisms, assuming either mutual infection among connected individuals or widespread transmission among all individuals within a given social circle. By considering both cases, we derive the critical threshold for an extinction to occur, along with expected numbers of infected individuals, through an application of spectral graph theory to analyze epidemic dynamics. To validate our theoretical predictions, we simulate an outbreak within various networks, observing close alignment between our calculations and simulation results. When comparing our findings to past research on disease spread, we uncover substantial differences between our expected numbers of infected individuals and estimates from prior studies. Moreover, we show how our theoretical model's estimates are affected by network topology, highlighting the influence of social connections on an epidemic's course. By considering both the girth and connectivity of a network, we analyze how an epidemic unfolds among closely interconnected individuals. In particular, we examine how an epidemic spreads among a tight group of connected individuals, assuming mutual infection within this group, along with transmission mechanisms beyond this group. By combining our theoretical expectations with simulation results, we gain a deeper understanding of how an epidemic, assumed to be a random event, unfolds within a social network. Ultimately, our analysis sheds light on the complex dynamics of disease transmission among socially interconnected individuals. 

We begin our mathematical analysis by defining a hypergraph to represent an interconnected relationship among individuals, along with an epidemic model that spreads an infectious disease within this network, assuming mutual infection among connected individuals. By considering the spectral properties of this network, along with random infections among individuals, we derive the critical threshold below which an outbreak is likely to fail. By applying similar methods to a different disease transmission mechanism, assuming widespread transmission among all individuals within a given social circle, along with mutual infection among all connected individuals, we refine this critical threshold, along with expected numbers of infected individuals, through an adaptation of spectral graph theory to analyze epidemic dynamics.

In an attempt to overcome this restriction, a new deep multimodal model, referred to as the K-fan deep sketch model, is proposed. This model integrates K-fan deep sketch models, which leverage both spatial and temporal information in image and video data, allowing them to be processed in an unsupervised manner. A joint optimization procedure is implemented to shared representations within each layer. As a result, this model demonstrates improved performance on two challenging datasets: static images with labels and labeled videos. Additionally, the proposed model exhibits enhanced state-of-the-art or comparable results on three other datasets: video classification with labels, video captioning, and video retrieval with keywords. Moreover, the resulting model exhibits superior energy minimization properties due to its shared representation property. Consequently, this model has been successfully applied to multiple benchmark datasets, delivering impressive results. In particular, it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on video classification and video retrieval with labeled data. We introduce McMini, a innovative model checker designed for verifying the correctness of multithreaded programs. By leveraging a small set of easily understandable program models and a versatile exploration strategy, McMini achieves high efficiency and versatility. For example, McMini is the first model checker to support McMillan's difference logic on a DPOR platform. Furthermore, McMini outperforms other popular model checkers by handling intricate, multithreaded programs with a high level of efficiency. This has led to a surge in harmful information circulation, prompting concerns among experts. Our investigation highlights the extent of misinformation dissemination, quantifying its transmission range and speed in WhatsApp-enabled groups. We demonstrate that slowing down information dissemination cannot entirely prevent harmful information spread, as it can still reach a substantial number of users within a limited time frame. Consequently, we introduce a metric for assessing effectiveness in combating misinformation and evaluate various strategies for controlling group membership. Notably, introducing a membership verification process requires little additional load on users and significantly limits the spread of misinformation. Ultimately, we suggest practical solutions to minimize the spread of harmful information on WhatsApp-like platforms. These solutions could be implemented by the service providers to mitigate the harm of misinformation spread during crisis situations in the future. Additionally, we outline potential directions for further research in this area. (From the abstract of arXiv:2101.08425)

corrections to be controllable. Researchers have begun analyzing such effective field 
theories, focusing on models like Natural Inflation and Inflatonless Inflation, to 
determine their viability in the context of supergravity. This review will examine the 
ongoing efforts to assess whether these specific types of inflationary models can be 
supported in a supergravity framework. We also investigate the implications of an 
unstable D3-brane on the effectiveness of these models in a string theory context, 
emphasizing the necessity to control supergravity expectations due to brane dynamics. 
The effective field theories studied here lack a specific canonical variable, forcing 
model builders to rely on an unphysical scalar for canonical representation, thus 
highlighting the distinctive characteristics of these inflationary models. The relationship 
between the canonical and non-canonical variables is a crucial aspect of these effective 
field theories, allowing researchers to leverage this relationship to assess model 
viability. Furthermore, the constraint on non-Gaußian corrections within these models 
may limit a model's potential in the supergravity framework, prompting researchers to 
pursue an alternative approach involving an anthropic interpretation of these 
corrections. Ultimately, the distinction between an effective field theory and a full 
supergravity model remains a pressing question, driving researchers to explore an 
unperturbed $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity formulation of these inflationary models to 
investigate whether such an implementation can provide self-consistent, controllable

This achieves an advancement on a long-standing conjecture first presented by Sierpinski in the early 1900s. Our method involves creating two specific subsets of Borel sets, denoted $B$ and $C$, such that both are uncountable but have a cardinality of $2^{\aleph_0},$ yet their union is equal to the real numbers. Additionally, both $B$ and $C$ consist entirely of Borel sets. By applying the continuum hypothesis, which holds in our context due to the choice of $\aleph_2$, we identify that both $B$ and $C$ can be partitioned into $\aleph_2$ distinct Borel sets each. Consequently, this partitioning yields $\aleph_2$ distinct Borel sets, giving us a total count of $\aleph_2$ distinct Borel sets, which is the maximum possible, as demonstrated by a simple embedding of our sets into the Borel sets in the continuum's power set. Finally, we establish that our partitioning method is unaffected by changes in the continuum hypothesis, ensuring the result's validity regardless of the change. Furthermore, this result can be generalized to higher cardinalities and applied to the intervals of the unit interval $[0,1].$ Lastly, we note that our findings contradict a previous result presented by Borel in 1903. $\Box$

Using a dataset of over 1,500 diverse trading approaches, including 18 different time horizons and 10 market conditions, our analysis examines the impact of introducing new strategies on the performance of existing ones. Our results indicate that the new strategies' characteristics have a more substantial effect on their own profitability than on the profitability of the established strategies. Furthermore, the stability of the portfolio's distribution is strongly influenced by the new strategies, yet their introduction does not diminish the return on the initial investment. Our findings are consistent across various time horizons and market conditions, thus offering practical guidance to portfolio managers: can benefit from diversifying their portfolios by incorporating both novel and traditional trading methods. Ultimately, this research contributes to the portfolio management dilemma of 'active vs. passive management,' suggesting a middle-ground approach where existing investment methods are complemented with contemporary analytics to mitigate risks and maximize returns in dynamic markets. Specifically, our study's findings can inform the decision of whether to adopt a purely passive investment philosophy when facing dynamic market conditions. Bloom filters provide quick, memory-efficient assessments of set membership, but their efficiency comes at a cost: they frequently produce false positives. As alternative solutions, cuckoo filters offer fewer false positives but require more computational effort. Both technologies insert multiple elements into fixed-size arrays using hash functions. Insertion in Bloom filters often necessitates writing to multiple, hash-determined array locations, which can lead to conflicts and false positives. In contrast, cuckoo filters utilize separate, hash-determined locations for elements, ensuring no conflicts during insertion. However, this results in underutilized free slots in their arrays. Xor Filters introduce a novel compact hashing approach, inserting elements directly into half-full arrays to minimize conflicts and free slots. This results in performance comparable to Bloom filters with the fewest false positives of cuckoo filters, all without additional overhead. By integrating Bloom and cuckoo filters, Xor Filters offer the best of both worlds, providing an efficient trade-off between false positives, computational cost, and memory usage. Experimental data demonstrates that Xor Filters seamlessly integrate the strengths of existing filtering technologies, making them the most suitable solution for various use cases. In particular, Xor Filters outperform Bloom filters with under 5% more memory and under 2x faster insertion speeds, while offering less than 0.1% additional false positives. We successfully demonstrated the capabilities of a PPO-trained autonomous driving agent in real-world settings, bridging a significant gap between simulated and actual environments. Initially trained in a simulated world and tested on streets in Stuttgart, our agent's performance was enhanced by introducing an image processing step modifying its camera inputs to match real-world image characteristics. This included applying a filter to replicate the distinctiveness of real-world edges, captured through the standard deviation of pixel values within an image. Notably, our findings show that simply converting simulated images to real-world equivalents can yield superior results over directly training in real-world settings. This discovery opens up new possibilities for a streamlined and efficient training protocol, allowing existing models to adapt to real-world conditions with minimal adjustment. Our code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/SebastianSeb/Sim2Real. Additionally, a video showcasing our approach can be found on YouTube at https://youtube.com/seb2709. Significant progress in the field of deepfake research, particularly in the creation and identification of deepfakes, has been made over the past four years. Despite this advancement, detecting deepfakes remains a difficult task, especially in cases where the training data is limited or the images are high-resolution and contain diverse objects. As deepfake generation technology continues to evolve, it is vital to update detection methods to effectively handle high-resolution and diverse objects. In response to these developments, a new and advanced dataset, the Meta-Learning Face Manipulation Dataset, has been created to facilitate the detection of deepfakes in such scenarios. This dataset consists of 2,000 genuine and artificially created images and videos and has been met with positive response from the deepfake research community. A new detection approach using Meta-Learning, a method built on pre-trained CNNs and data augmentation techniques, has been developed to effectively handle low, medium, and high-resolution images. Experimental results reveal that this approach is more accurate than existing methods and demonstrates versatility in various high-resolution and object diversity scenarios. Furthermore, a new deepfake detection method utilizing Wavelet Transform and Domain-CNN has been developed to effectively handle high-resolution images and detect deepfakes in previously unseen categories. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and AUC scores. Ultimately, this research contributes two new methods for deepfake detection: an efficient Meta-Learning technique and a more complex Wavelet-CNN approach that set new benchmarks in deepfake detection. These contributions are anticipated to have a positive impact on the deepfake research community and potentially lead to the detection of deepfakes in everyday life. Finally, comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the resistance of deepfakes to detection through the implementation of resistance metrics including RM, RF, FMI, MMI, MMI2, NCD, and ZCD. The results show that the methods presented in this research are resistant to deepfakes but can be improved using the novel metrics explored in this study. Specifically, the application of RF and ZCD significantly enhances the detection performance of existing methods. In particular, the integration of RF achieves a 0.50 MAE reduction and 0.04 AUC increase, while the incorporation of ZCD results in a 0.42 MAE reduction and 0.05 AUC increase. Ultimately, this research identifies RF and ZCD as valuable metrics for detecting deepfakes and suggests their use in evaluating other deepfake detection methods. Ultimately, this research contributes three new insights

The identification of super-Earths and sub-Neptunes through NASA's Kepler mission led to a significant shift in exoplanet research, and their composition, primarily assuming ocean worlds, remains largely unknown. Oceans on these exoplanets are likely to be hidden from view, but their pressure and temperature conditions can vary greatly, with some reaching the melting point of rocks and others being too hot to support liquid water. This study assesses two distinct composition theories - solubility balances and gas thermochemistry - to better understand the characteristics of these unknown oceans. By analyzing the mass fraction of oxygen, carbon, and silicon in a 1.5 to 1.8 times Earth-radius planet orbiting a G2 star, our findings show that gas thermochemistry would likely introduce carbon and silicon into the overlying atmosphere through the dissolution of minerals, while solubility balances would restrict such release, preserving a higher carbon content in the liquid ocean and resulting in lower atmospheric CO2 levels. Notably, both models predict CO2 levels significantly lower than those expected from geochemical closed-system models, suggesting that CO2 levels in such worlds may largely originate from other sources, such as carbon compounds soluble in water. This characteristic shift in CO2 behavior may serve as a distinct signature in future transmission spectra, as well as in future bio signatures, as these changes could significantly impact the escape of gases from atmospheres back into space. We've developed a novel spiking neural network architecture capable of self-generated sequences, mimicking the sequence learning process observed in biological brains. Our network employs a novel mechanism for synaptic plasticity that combines Hebbian principles with a strict feasibility constraint, ensuring that sequence memorization occurs within a realistic parameter space compatible with biological synapses. This constraint eliminates premature synaptic silencing, giving synapses a prolonged period to develop from initially strong to optimally regulated connections. Our findings indicate that synapses benefit from initial weakness, as this allows for a greater range of exploration in sequence learning before becoming unlearnable. Furthermore, we've integrated our model into a robot navigation task, where the network successfully acquired a spatial memory that facilitated robot navigation within a maze system. This research demonstrates a novel method for biological inspiration in spiking neural networks, enabling them to learn and memorize sequences within a realistic parameter space. You can access the associated code at https://github.com/ChristophDebuysere/Sequence-learning-SNN. This work is based on our previous study on sequence learning in spiking neural networks [Debuysere et al., 2021], where we explored the effects of different synaptic feasibility constraints on sequence memorization. This current research diverges from that previous work by focusing on biological plausibility in spiking neural networks and presents a fresh approach to sequence learning. Unlike our previous research, where we employed an external external noise source to facilitate sequence generation, as well as an 'in-place' learning method where new synapses were added to existing ones. As opposed to external noise, we've now adopted a self-generated sequence approach, where networks learn to produce sequences in response to a single, initial spike. This change arises from our hypothesis that biological brains might utilize inherent spontaneous activity for sequence generation. Moreover, we've integrated our model into a robot navigation task that leverages a biological-plausible spiking neural network, where the network learns to produce relevant sequential codes to guide the robot. This work presents a novel application of our previous research and offers insights into using spiking neural networks, inspired by biological principles, to solve real-world problems. Unlike other studies on sequence learning in spiking neural networks, where either static sequences or sequence generation over a limited time period was achieved, we've successfully developed a spiking neural network capable of both learning static sequences and generating sequences over an extended time period. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with random inputs, but they often struggle with equations that have intricate singular behaviors. To overcome this, researchers have developed an adaptable method for verifying the accuracy of these expansions, even in the presence of singular behaviors. This verification involves comparing the expanded solution with the actual solution in the context of random outcomes. To achieve this, researchers have developed a specialized technique for identifying the singular behaviors in equations and an approach to approximate the expanded solution at specific, unpredictable values. This results in a reliable numerical method that can effectively solve differential equations with complex singular behaviors. Furthermore, this approach does not require any assumptions about the behaviors and can be incorporated into existing numerical methods as an additional validation step. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, researchers have applied it to two distinct generalized polynomial chaos expansions methods for solving differential equations with random inputs. The results show that this verification step significantly impacts the overall error and greatly improves the reliability of these methods. In particular, the overall error can be broken down into two distinct components, one of which is predictable and can be controlled, while another component is difficult to estimate and depends on the specific outcomes. The development of this verification method is crucial for ensuring the reliability of these methods, which is particularly important for ensuring the safety of systems that involve generalized polynomial chaos expansions. The work presented here is an extension of previously published research, but also builds upon other studies in the field. To the best of the researchers' knowledge, this verification method is an innovation in the field of generalized polynomial chaos expansions. We use the latest version of the MOAST/BASS code, a star creation history generator, to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies through their chemical composition. This is achieved by comparing observed abundance ratios with theoretical predictions from different metallicity zones across a range of stellar populations. By optimizing the code to include complex physical processes, we can accurately calculate chemical abundances and understand the star creation histories unique to dwarf galaxies. This unique approach allows us to gather valuable information about the development of these galaxies by leveraging the abundance ratio Z(O/H) versus [alpha/e] from both the metal-rich and metal-poor populations. This method provides insights into the rates of star formation by analyzing the observed spread in abundance ratios, which can also identify potential biases in observations. By applying this analysis to the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Reticulum II, we were able to gather valuable information about its star formation history and chemical composition, which can further our understanding of galaxy evolution. Specifically, we discovered a relatively narrow time frame, approximately 500 million years, in which the star formation rate was consistently high within this galaxy. Additionally, we found that the chemical composition of the galaxy is characterized by a relatively low value of [alpha/e] at low metallicity, which indicates a lack of explosive supernovae during this stage and suggests a high rate of H-fusing stars. Further, we found that the high-velocity stars in Reticulum II share similar chemical properties with stars in other dwarf galaxies, which is also observed in the globular clusters at high Galactic latitudes. These findings are significant in understanding the origin and chemical composition of the metal-poor stars, which is a key area of research in the field of galaxy evolution. By using abundance ratios to investigate the past star formation history and chemical composition of galaxies, we can gain a deeper understanding of dwarf galaxy evolution, which is particularly evident in the analysis of the dwarf galaxy Reticulum II. This research highlights the importance of combining different chemical abundance ratios to accurately describe a galaxy's star formation history and chemical composition, which is particularly effective when utilizing the abundance ratio Z(O/H) versus [alpha/e]. Additionally, we found that the use of abundance ratios is an effective tool for gathering information about a galaxy's past star formation history and chemical composition, which is particularly evident in the analysis of metal-poor and metal-rich stellar populations. A recent surge in document processing through vision has led to a significant need for labeling visually complex documents to generate high-quality training datasets. Unfortunately, manually labeling these documents is often infeasible due to their visually rich content and high data volume. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that leverages a trained vision model to selectively uncover hidden text within documents, pinpointing areas that require human labeling. This groundbreaking method yields exceptional results, revealing that a model can be trained with only 10% of a dataset that was previously required for labeling the entire dataset. Additionally, our model allows for the training of multiple vision models simultaneously, a capability known as multi-task learning. By integrating our approach with multi-task learning, we set a new benchmark in zero-shot annotation auto-generation, achieving nearly full dataset coverage with just 50% of the original data volume. These groundbreaking achievements make it possible for vision models to be trained rapidly and efficiently, especially on datasets that were previously difficult to work with. To showcase the effectiveness of our approach, we tested it on prominent document extraction tasks such as checking account statements, receipts, and flight itineraries. Full details of our methodology can be found on our GitHub repository. It includes a comprehensive step-by-step guide to replicating our findings, along with our code and annotated datasets for repeated use. Several open-source datasets have also been made available for shared research purposes. These datasets include annotated documents in COCO format and the corresponding documentation for running our proposed approach. To support the development of future vision models, we have also made available pre-trained models for common document categories, such as receipts and flight itineraries. These models can be used immediately, saving time and resources that would have been required for model training. In the future, we aim to expand our approach to visually less rich content, such as text conversations and audio recordings. We also plan to explore the use of our approach in semi-automated and interactive modeling scenarios. It is envisioned that our proposed approach will significantly accelerate the training of vision models in numerous document processing applications. A refined hierarchy of classes has been established by combining elements of Wadge and Nash operators. This new classification system includes an efficient set of oracles for each level in the Wadge quantification hierarchy. Additionally, we have developed an algorithm to determine the Wadge degree of any Borel set in $\omega^2$ and any closed subset of the Baire space $\omega^\omega$. This degree determination algorithm works under the assumption of a simple set oracle, which can be obtained by applying a straightforward reduction to any Borel set in $\omega^2$. As a result of this work, every Borel set in $\omega^\omega$ now has a definitive Wadge degree, and this finding resolves a question that had been posed by Satchelan. This paper introduces ClickTrain, a novel efficient training framework that seamlessly integrates end-to-end pruning during deep learning training. By preserving the original network structure through pruned sub-blocks, ClickTrain enhances both inference speed and accuracy without compromising model size. Experimental results reveal the effectiveness of ClickTrain on executing pruned models with minimal loss of accuracy and significant gains in inference speed. Moreover, ClickTrain outperforms current state-of-the-art models both in precision and efficiency. Identifying the types of binary mergers that generate gravitational waves is crucial for understanding high-energy astrophysical phenomena. Although binary black hole mergers have been extensively analyzed, events involving neutron stars or neutron star-black hole mergers remain understudied due to their complex and diverse signal patterns. In this research, we present a new approach based on a multi-layered neural network architecture, which can differentiate between binary black hole and neutron star or neutron star-black hole mergers based on their gravitational wave signals. Utilizing simulated anneal optimization, we generated various binary black hole and neutron star/black hole system models which were used to extract signal patterns. A deep learning method using a 2-layered neural network was applied to these data sets, yielding an accuracy of 95.5% in identifying binary black hole mergers and an accuracy of 94.5% in identifying neutron star/black hole mergers, based on a 1000-fold cross-validation process. When replacing artificial signals with actual events from LIGO/Virginia datasets, our model's accuracy in identifying neutron star/black hole mergers dropped to 72%, while maintaining 95% accuracy in identifying binary black holes. In addition to these findings, we discovered that our model was able to provide more accurate binary black hole merger classifications than the widely used Brookhaven classifier. Supervised reinforcement learning has significant potential in real-world applications but poses a difficult challenge due to the celebrated curse of dimensionality. One strategy to mitigate this difficulty is to incorporate prior knowledge into the modeling. However, adapting actor-critic algorithms in high-dimensional spaces is an unresolved challenge. While they are effective in lower dimensions, they often result in slow convergence in higher dimensions. Despite active research, there is currently no universally effective solution. One promising approach explored in this research is to combine actor-critic algorithms with techniques from Bayesian sampling, specifically Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, for high-dimensional reinforcement learning problems. By leveraging these methods, it has been found that prior knowledge can indeed be utilized to facilitate efficient exploration, thus significantly improving the algorithms' performance. Moreover, prior knowledge can also be utilized to regulate the actor-critic policy optimization, thus resulting in improved stability and faster convergence. Experiments conducted on various high-dimensional reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods, achieving better results than existing benchmark algorithms. Notably, prior knowledge even enables successful training on a control task in a 26-dimensional space, despite theoretical expectations of diminishing returns beyond a dimensionality of about 10. Hence, the developed methods offer novel and effective solutions to actor-critic training in high-dimensional spaces, capitalizing on the benefits of prior knowledge to achieve superior performance. These research findings open up new avenues for incorporating prior knowledge in reinforcement learning tasks with complex dimensions, thereby extending their practical utility. In recent years, presence-absence data has experienced a significant surge in applications across various scientific fields. Despite its widespread use, researchers have given relatively little attention to developing effective clustering methods tailored to this data type. To fill this knowledge gap, we thoroughly examined the performance of eight distinct clustering methods, including three novel approaches, designed specifically for high-dimensional presence-absence data. Our comprehensive evaluation entails analyzing artificial datasets created using simulated species assemblages and comparing the accuracy of these methods when data dimensions vary. Additionally, we applied these clustering methods to a large, annotated bird data set comprising 1,523 samples across 268 dimensions, and validated our findings through careful examination and analysis. Our results indicate that eight out of ten evaluated clustering methods showed improvement when applied to presence-absence data, and surprisingly, the Augment-Means method performed particularly well on this data type, surpassing other competitive methods such as multi-scale hierarchical clustering and random forest. Notably, we discovered a significant correlation between predicted labels and true species assemblages, and through our analysis, we were able to identify various patterns and insights that would have been difficult or impossible to extract using standard clustering methods. Our contributions and findings can be further extended to address challenges in biodiversity research, such as data sparsity, uncertainty associated with species presence-absence information, and the inherent non-stationary nature of species assemblages.
