In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with objects of various shapes and sizes in RGB and RGB-D images remains a complex task. The primary issue lies in the difficulty of accurately capturing object extent information. To address this challenge, we present a novel framework that harmoniously integrates object extent information and semantic cues for salient object detection on RGB and RGB-D images. The proposed framework consists of an object extent estimation module, which employs a self-attention mechanism to extend object regions to a full resolution, and a semantic fusion module that fuses pixel-wise features and semantic cues for salient object detection. By integrating these modules with existing efficient salient object detection networks, we enhance their performance while achieving significant runtime speedup. Notably, our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in F-measure scores on the ADE20K semantic segmentation benchmark by approximately 4%, with a runtime acceleration of around 5 times on the NCLE-SD dataset. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework. The code will be publicly available soon at https://github.com/Chunfanyu/UE-Net.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 Aggressive Speech Classification challenge is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to address the competition, initially utilizing Support Vector Machines as a wrapper for pre-processed text features, and subsequently combining it with BERT-based models leveraging a target word's sentiment and syntactic context. Our final submissions comprised three submissions: two to the English task and a single entry for the Spanish task. For English Subtask A, our top submission showcased an f1-score of 0.7396, whereas in Subtask B we achieved 0.3243. In Spanish Subtask A, our submissions reached f1-scores of 0.6206, and in Subtask B 0.2793. We observed significant room for improvement in Subtask B, implying the significance of word-level context and domain-specific vocabulary. On the other hand, our BERT-based approach excelled in Subtask A by providing more comprehensive context through the addition of target words. Experimental cross-validations on both datasets revealed potential enhancements via model fine-tuning and the incorporation of additional contextual information. Ultimately, our systems' performances in both tasks outpaced the SemEval baseline. We plan to make our code and pre-trained models publicly accessible. 

Keywords: Natural Language Processing, Sentiment Analysis, BERT, Spanish, English, Aggressive Speech Classification.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in radiology for diagnosing tissue abnormalities, also providing information about X-ray interactions with different body tissues through polyenergetic projection data. By supplementing a conventional fan-beam scan, source-motion can be exploited to enhance image quality via system-response compensation and forward-modeling. This study proposes a non-convex variational reconstruction framework that integrates a simplified dual-energy model, noise suppression, and material differentiation. Formulated as an constrained optimization problem, the proposed model relies on an alternating Direction Of Augmentations (ADOA) solver, capable of alternating between image and dual-energy estimates. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in a 16-slice CT scanner, showcasing its ability to produce superior images, dual-energy estimates, and tissue compositions even with noisy data. These results validate the potential of the proposed framework in a research setting. Further development aims to test the framework on a data-set comprising a variety of tissues. However, optimizing memory allocation on GPUs can be complex and inefficient, especially in object-based programming models that involve frequent memory reallocations. To address the memory management challenges in such environments, we have developed DynaSOAr, a highly parallel memory allocator designed for use with CUDA. By introducing an array of memory blocks, each block consisting of multiple objects, DynaSOAr ensures efficient memory access and use, including the ability to optimize memory space within the array. This allows the allocator to automatically compile and merge partially filled memory blocks, thereby reducing memory waste and maximizing memory utilization. Our experimental results demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms other allocators, including the standard GCC allocator, by an average of 12.2% to 57.6%, depending on the specific application. Our findings also show that DynaSOAr's performance stability under various allocation patterns makes it suitable for a wide range of applications. To further validate the efficacy of DynaSOAr, we successfully integrated it into the SOAr memory management framework, which is widely used in scientific simulations and other challenging computational applications. Our experiments using multiple benchmark suites, including BFS and SFolio, reveal that DynaSOAr significantly improves the overall performance of these applications by an average of 10.3% to 52.6%, primarily due to its memory-related optimizations. To ensure the scalability and efficiency of DynaSOAr, we thoroughly analyzed its time complexity, which shows a linear relationship with the number of memory blocks and objects within those blocks. Our analysis predicts a maximum time complexity of O(n), which is confirmed by our experimental results and outperforms the GCC allocator by a factor of up to 57.6%. We've developed a unconventional approach to simulate dynamics in phase space using a lattice of discrete sites, where sites correspond to solutions of Hamilton's equation applied to various initial conditions. Trajectories with lower energies occupy lower sites, eliminating the need to update solutions for higher energy sites. This method requires solving Hamilton's equation for $6N$ dimensions with $N$ representing the number of degrees of freedom. It offers two key benefits: first, it determines trajectories without relying on traditional numerical integration techniques, and second, it provides a straightforward mechanism for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics in complex systems by applying an appropriate Hamiltonian. As a demonstration of its capabilities, we've successfully applied our method to a simple Ising model and observed a break in detailed balance during the free expansion phase. Observations reveal that lower energy states are more likely to occupy lower sites, while higher energy states occupy higher sites. This behavior is consistent with the Boltzmann distribution and confirms that the phase space volume increases during the free expansion phase. Furthermore, we've established a relationship between site indices and energies, allowing us to calculate energy distributions within our method. These findings verify that the system follows a cumulative energy distribution known as the Gaussian thermal distribution. In addition to its applications in simulating dynamics, our method also offers a novel way to measure energy distributions. We encourage other researchers to test our method against their own research questions and explore its potential applications and implications. This description results in the accordion graph construction method. Our research focuses on analyzing properties of accordion graphs, particularly those with a quartic structure. Key findings include the following: (1) If an accordion graph is quartic and connected, it must have a Hamiltonian cycle. (2) In pairs of quartic accordion graphs with distinct parameters, if one graph in the pair is Hamiltonian, the other must also be. (3) A quartic accordion graph can be considered perfect if its parameters meet specific conditions. (4) Isomorphisms between quartic accordion graphs are examined under varying parameter conditions. Specifically, it's established that some quartic accordion graphs are isomorphic to circulant graphs. Ultimately, a method is developed to determine whether an accordion graph is quartic and whether it's isomorphic to a circulant graph. This technique involves analyzing its pairings and Hamiltonian cycle. As a result, distinguishing between certain classes of graphs becomes achievable. Various examples and problems are presented to illustrate the accuracy and potential applications of the developed method. It's shown, for instance, that some quartic accordion graphs have unique properties not exhibited by circulant graphs. Specifically, it's demonstrated that there exist non-circulant and non-isomorphic-to-circulant quartic accordion graphs of any order. Furthermore, it's established that there are pairs of non-isomorphic quartic accordion graphs of any order that are also non-isomorphic to circulant graphs. Additionally, it's shown that there are pairs of non-isomorphic quartic accordion graphs of any even order that are also non-isomorphic to circulant graphs. Lastly, it's proven that there are no accordion graphs of any order that are both circulant and quartic, unless they're also isomorphic to a circulant graph. Specifically, it's established that there are no quartic and circulant accordion graphs on even orders beyond four. Finally, a method is developed to determine whether an accordion graph is quartic and whether it's isomorphic to a circulant graph on a specific even order. This technique involves analyzing its pairings and Hamiltonian cycle. As an example, it's shown that the method accurately distinguishes between the quartic and non-circulant accordion graph on order 58 from the quartic and circulant accordion graph on order 60. This achieves a long-sought solution to Problem 3.2.

We present a simple proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces. This proof doesn't require the use of a specific assumption previously made on the initial data and can be understood through a straightforward manipulation of the equations, resulting in a significant loss of regularity when the data is slightly modified. This approach is different from previous methods that involved constructing a specific type of solution and testing the idea using several variables. Additionally, this proof can be modified to address other similar equations, such as the non-homogeneous incompressible Euler equations, by incorporating a brief 'calculation' that accounts for the initial data's growth. This modified approach is then used to confirm a pre-existing theorem stating the ill-posedness of the equations in question. Furthermore, this paper primarily utilizes basic properties of certain types of function spaces and is written in a accessible style, aiming to make the proof more understandable. We also provide a brief introduction to several key concepts related to function spaces used throughout the paper. Ultimately, we hope that this proof will contribute to a deeper understanding of the function spaces themselves.

Imitation learning in large image spaces poses significant challenges, primarily due to the vast possible action space.  The selection of relevant images by predecessors (as source images for imitation) is crucial in controlling the image space search.  Current approaches rely on manual input to limit the search space, but these methods are impractical on a large scale.  To resolve this issue, we introduce The Stable Creator, an autonomous system that independently discovers and makes use of source images contributed by past agents (as prior knowledge).  By allowing past agents' contributions to be incorporated through identity transformations (adding marks, changing colors etc.), the system learns to steer the image space search towards regions relevant to the task at hand.  Through additions like 'painting tools', the task solver is motivated to mimic actions similar to those of past successful agents, thus leveraging prior knowledge to enhance imitation.  As a result, The Stable Creator improves the quality of learned skills and their autonomous exploration.  Notably, it achieves better performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models in the domain of image diffusion models. Minimal films are an optimal human movement strategy, characterized by the fewest possible movements between two objects. Researchers have two main approaches to understanding this strategy: either they try to find a universal minimum film for all situations, or they analyze specific examples to identify general patterns. This paper takes the second approach, examining a large dataset of hundreds of minimal films in everyday scenes to find recurring movement sequences. Unlike previous models, this research suggests that dynamic recognition models don't always follow a smooth, predictable trajectory, and in fact, can get "stuck" in loops. While optimization models can efficiently generate universal minimum films, this study shows that such models may not adequately capture the complexity of real-world movements, and that dynamic models are needed to fully understand human minimum films. Finally, this paper presents a new challenge: testing whether machine learning algorithms can learn to identify minimal films automatically. Despite recent advances in computer vision, this task remains a significant hurdle, and the proposed dataset, along with human minimum films, can be found at minimalfilms.com. Future work could also use neural networks to identify common patterns in human films and explore the role of attention in dynamic recognition. Additionally, this research raises the possibility of leveraging AI to improve human physical training by identifying the most efficient movement strategies. In the long term, this could lead to new forms of interaction between humans and machines. Finally, this paper suggests that dynamic models can provide fresh perspectives on understanding human cognition and perception. More broadly, this research raises questions about the potential of AI to rediscover human capabilities, and whether machines can ever truly "learn" to move and perceive like humans. We propose a theory in which these dark particles remain stable on a milli-scale due to an inherent symmetry of the dark sector. Upon interacting with regular matter through an electromagnetic field, these dark particles break the magnetic monopole's charge, resulting in a persistent galactic magnetic field that decays over time. Assuming the dark current density is comparable to regular matter's, we simulate magnetic field decay across various scales and find that our model can explain magnetic field strengths observed at specific scales in the Milky Way without violating constraints from cosmic microwave background observations. This unique feature sets our model apart from standard dark matter models and makes it testable through magnetic field measurements at different scales in our galaxy. Additionally, we calculate the dark matter mass range for our model, taking into account observations from the Alpha Gamma telescope and other astrophysical constraints. We discover that our model can accommodate dark matter masses up to approximately 10 picograms. If detected within the next decade, dark matter in this mass range could be directly measured, thereby validating our model. On the other hand, a measurement cap of around 10 nanograms by direct detection experiments would imply that dark matter consists of compositionally identical particles with an inherent stability, marking a significant departure from standard dark matter models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dark matter in our model can be constrained through galaxy cluster observations, particularly by examining the cluster's edge in the Coma cluster using a technique called Faraday Rotation Mapping. This technique yields a mass limit of approximately 36 milligrams, thereby confirming that our model is compatible with observations of magnetic fields at various scales. If future galaxy cluster measurements extend the scale range to around 30 kiloparsecs, they would rule out our model unless specific compact objects are present at the cluster's center, thereby linking cluster observations to magnetic monopole dark matter through the lens of galactic magnetic field persistence. Predicting the future state of the atmosphere is a complex task in various applications such as weather forecasting. Due to the diverse scale and pattern of weather phenomena, it is crucial to consider both spatial and temporal relationships in their prediction. In this paper, a cutting-edge spatiotemporal model is proposed to forecast future weather states by utilizing the integration of current weather conditions, future grid predictions, and incorporating the constraints of weather data with the scaling properties of weather patterns. Experiments on the dataset "intensity" show that the newly suggested model outperforms other state-of-the-art methods with a notable improvement of 4.27% in terms of mean absolute error. Additionally, the proposed model exhibits exceptional scalability and adaptability in various weather forecasting tasks. The model's source code is available at https://github.com/ghulamtariq/SE-WTFA. With its ability to handle intricate weather data, this model has numerous applications such as weather forecasting, climate modeling, and atmospheric research. In the context of resource theory of quantum channels, we examine the self-dual family of protocols formed by PPT (positive semi-definite) channels. Focusing on the PPT Quadrilateral Conjecture, which would imply that any PPT box can be converted into a PPT box with only one non-PPT input, we investigate its local equivalents but find them to be invalid. Furthermore, we look into the optimality of PPT boxes and show that, under specific conditions, the PPT boxes are not only optimal but also unique in a specific context. Finally, we explore the relationship between PPT boxes and convex polygons with rational vertices, particularly examining if the completion of such a polygon with rational vertices is also a convex rational polygon after applying a local PPT protocol. Our analysis yields a positive result for certain specific local PPT protocols but leaves the question unresolved for all local PPT protocols. To prove our findings, we derive various geometric and algebraic properties of the sets defining PPT boxes, including the closure of the set after taking a local PPT protocol. Our analysis also reveals that the local PPT protocols can be represented through a finite collection of rational numbers, and we establish a relationship between PPT boxes and convex polygons with rational vertices, along with their complements under a local PPT protocol. Along the way, we prove a local version of the PPT Quadrilateral Conjecture, which is more general and applies not only to PPT boxes but also to other boxes defined by specific local PPT protocols. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that PPT boxes possess numerous optimal and unique properties across a wide range of scenarios. These findings provide significant evidence supporting the PPT Quadrilateral Conjecture. To make our analysis more accessible, we include a detailed appendix that summarizes our methods, provides additional technical details, and explores potential future research avenues. Modern single-image de-blurring methods primarily rely on convolutional neural networks.  However, they fail to differentiate between motion blur caused by objects and the still background.  As a result, previously frozen frames in an image sequence can appear as a single blurred image, with both moving and stationary objects looking similarly blurred.  This paper proposes an innovative approach where a separate module is trained to generate motion blur effects on given frames, allowing a subsequent de-blurring network to distinguish between moving and stationary objects.  This novel synthesis-de-blurring pipeline is the first of its kind in the field.  As a result, our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in blurring caused by objects, demonstrating superior performance on challenging synthetic and real-world blurred image sequences.  Notably, our method is the first to apply image segmentation techniques to blur-causing objects, enabling more accurate restoration of both moving and stationary regions.  In a notable achievement, our method also surpasses state-of-the-art standards for general de-blurring tasks, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness. The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered relationships, regardless of the rules used. Surprisingly, the resulting refined set has a maximum number of levels within its hierarchical structure. We aim to understand and determine the maximum capacity of this refined structure for any given ordered set. In particular, we focus on a specific type of hierarchical structure known as a tree and establish a key criterion for determining when a tree is complete in the refined set. This involves relating a particular sequence of numbers derived from the tree to the tree's height and ranking system. We demonstrate that a tree has a complete structure if and only if a specific property applies uniformly across all elements of a particular sequence, which relates to a fundamental concept in modern set theory known as continuity. As a result, a tree's completeness is certain if it meets a specific condition analogous to being compact in traditional set theory topologies. We demonstrate that a refined structure is "entire" if and only if a particular fundamental concept in modern set theory known as "mixing" applies to its level tracking sequence. Finally, we delve into the relationship between a refined structure's "entirety" and its hierarchical ranking system, examining how a particular sequence of numbers that assign ranks to elements in a refined structure are affected by a refined structure's levels over time as distinct from its local ranking system. Profiling a dataset is now an essential step in machine learning, as it enables
choices to be made about model architecture, training parameters, and other
options.  However, current profiling methods use general, universal metrics that
don't account for the characteristics of individual datasets, leading to the
selection of suboptimal model architectures and parameters.  Instead, we
propose that dataset-specific profiling be utilized, as varying datasets have
different relationships between interdependent features.  For instance, while
self-similarity is a key property of music, inter-dataset similarity is minimal.
  In contrast, face images exhibit strong inter-dataset connections.  By
investigating the relationships between features in datasets, such as inter-modal
connections, self-similarity, and inter-dataset similarity, our aim is to
understand how these relationships affect model generalization.  To that end, we
introduce the concept of dataset particularity - a measure of the diversity
between datasets.  Our research demonstrates that dataset particularity correlates
negatively with non-local, self-attention based models, as well as other
universal models.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of
dataset-specific profiling in model selection.  Ultimately, our work serves as
a foundation for future research into dataset particularity and its effects on

This research introduces an advanced generalized correntropy-based smoothing algorithm for graph signal reconstruction, capable of mitigating noisy and interfered signals. Building on the original work in [Reference], we extend the method to accommodate variable kernel width, derived from the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which is then numerically optimized through a gradient-based approach. As its original counterpart, our proposed method exhibits superior robustness against malicious interference while providing better accuracy in reconstructing smooth signals. Moreover, computational efficiency is significantly enhanced by converting the optimization problem into a convex form. Experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world data validate the robustness and effectiveness of our proposed method. A significant improvement in reconstruction quality is observed, particularly for large-scale datasets, where reconstruction time is notably reduced. For example, reconstructing the EU-HABs dataset using our proposed method yields an average PSNR of 34.72 dB with an average reconstruction time of 0.019 seconds, compared to 2.65 seconds using the original algorithm. Furthermore, our method consistently outperforms conventional smoothing methods, such as the Fourier smoothing technique, in both signal reconstruction and kernel parameter optimization aspects. Additionally, we demonstrate the robustness of our method against hyperparameter errors, where reconstruction quality remains nearly unchanged even with large deviations in kernel width. For instance, the average relative decline in our method's reconstruction quality (PSNR) is approximately 0.12%, whereas the original algorithm's quality (MSSE) declines around 30% under similar conditions. Lastly, we successfully apply our generalized correntropy-based smoothing algorithm to various tasks, such as denoising and porto-channel estimation, where signal characteristics are known in advance, allowing for optimized kernel parameter determination. In other cases, such as graph signal classification, kernel width is treated as an unknown variable, effectively learned through our algorithm's adaptive capability. Consequently, our generalized correntropy-based smoothing algorithm produces satisfactory results in these tasks. For denoising, a PSNR of 18.35 dB is achieved, surpassing the 16.23 dB achieved by the Fourier smoothing technique. Furthermore, in porto-channel estimation, an accuracy of 89% is reached, surpassing the 84% accuracy achieved with the Fourier smoothing technique. Lastly, in graph signal classification, an accuracy of 90% is reached, comparable to the 91% accuracy achieved using the Fourier smoothing technique. The first eigenvalue of this problem converges to $\frac{N(1+L)}{2}$ as $\delta$ tends to a positive limit $\delta_*$. Furthermore, we derive an optimal symmetrization inequality for this problem. Utilizing this inequality, we demonstrate that the first eigenvalue is bounded below by a constant times $\delta$ in the case where $\Omega$ is a unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Deep Learning techniques, particularly Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), have seen widespread success across various domains. However, some architectures, such as Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), remain relatively underrepresented in terms of their theoretical foundations. This lack of understanding regarding GCNNs' working principle limits their utilization in challenging graph-related tasks. To fill this gap, we present a study that sheds new light on the GCNNs' operation mechanism, casting it in an equivalent form that is easier to comprehend. In doing so, we propose introducing a new concept, referred to as 'Graph Filtering Neural Networks' (GFNNs), which serves as an intermediate representation bridging traditional CNNs and GCNNs. By examining the properties of linear transformations within graphs, we identify a specific pattern that GFNNs, including GCNNs, aim to detect and emphasize. This detection aligns with the idea of matched filtering, a fundamental concept that shares analogies with radar signal processing. This study offers a novel perspective on GCNNs, rendering their operation more intuitive and understandable, even for those unfamiliar with DNNs. Additionally, this study provides insights into the role of convolutional layers in DNNs, offering a simplified explanation of their functioning through a simplified example in Section 5. Moreover, this study introduces an innovative application of GCNNs in retro-radiative imaging (RRI), a field that exploits radar signal processing principles, thereby facilitating data exchange between radar and medical communities. A comprehensive numerical evaluation, accompanied by a developed open-source code, is also presented in this study. The proposed GCNN implementation exhibits superior performance when compared to existing RRI methods, thereby validating its efficacy and demonstrating its potential to succeed in various graph-related tasks. Furthermore, this study provides a comprehensive review of GCNNs, covering fundamental aspects, and offering insights into their history, evolution, and applications. Ultimately, this study aims to establish a lasting impact on the understanding of GCNNs, paving the way for their increased adoption in graph-related tasks. The introduced GFNNs concept may also contribute to exchanging knowledge between radar and deep learning communities, as they may find useful insights in this study, enabling a deeper comprehension of DNNs, particularly those involving convolutional layers. Similarly, this study may inspire data scientists working on radar data to leverage DNNs, as their counterparts in this study. Moreover, this study may aid researchers in exploring the potential of GCNNs to solve challenging graph-related tasks, as demonstrated in the RRI example

However, the method's effectiveness is largely contingent upon the quality of the pseudo annotations, which presents a challenging task, particularly in dependency parsing, due to the need for accurate annotation of complex syntactic structures. Furthermore, this finding implies the existence of a linear-time obstruction to equivalent problems in P and CP on unit-width SMH graphs. In an effort to build on this discovery, researchers developed a method for converting a CP-broken circuit within an SMH graph of width k into a CP-broken circuit within an SMH graph of width 2, using a description of k and poly(n) operations. This new approach led to the creation of a 2^O(n) time algorithm for determining if a given SMH graph of width k contains a CP-broken circuit. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition when replaced with Ir ions by smaller Eu ions. To explore the nature of this transition and delocalization of Ir 5d electrons, a series of (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 samples with varying Bi content were studied using HXPES, complementing earlier findings from resistivity, Hall, and NIXSW measurements. Bioxygen exposure led to a noticeable reduction in the energy spacing between Ir 5d bands in Bi-rich samples, resulting in a 0.5 eV shift towards lower binding energies as Bi content increases. This observation is consistent with the phenomenon of chemical doping in this system. Moreover, our data indicate that the degree of Ir 5d delocalization and electron correlation increase as Bi content grows. A comparison of our data with those from magnetization and Hall effect measurements reveals that the insulator-to-metal transition and the resulting emergence of metallic behavior in this series coincides with the onset of long-range magnetic order and increased electron correlation, suggesting that the metal-like behavior in this series is likely the result of opposing effects counterbalanced by each other. Finally, our findings in this study offer fresh insights into the control of electron correlation in this system through 5d electron delocalization. [Figure: See the attached graphics]

By leveraging this framework, we are able to prove the existence of highly unlikely distributions that are both cyclic and non-transitive. 1. The second-order likelihood ratio is positive for any three random variables.
2. There exists a set of four random variables where the first- and second-order likelihood ratios are positive for any combination of three of these variables.

Furthermore, our work lays the groundwork for studying higher-order likelihood ratios and their properties. Finally, we illustrate the practical applications of these highly unlikely probability distributions by designing games of chance and create a task that is both mentally challenging and rewarding to solve. Additionally, we provide a mathematical problem that is currently unsolved and offer a significant prize for its resolution. Lastly, we make a statement about the inherent nature of likelihood ratios, particularly in relation to our findings.

This paper explores the behavior of non-linear phenomena in a two-level system connected to a bosonic mode through the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. Unlike the standard Jaynes-Cummings model, where the system and bosonic mode become entangled, the opposite occurs in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. We investigate the system's transmission, entanglement, and Rabi oscillations without and with dissipation. Notably, although entanglement in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model does not meet the criteria for quantum memory, other non-linear features can still benefit its operation. Ultimately, we identify specific conditions under which the system's ability to transmit quantum information exceeds that of a pure dephasing system. Moreover, a particular anti-Jaynes-Cummings mode exhibits an increased probability of flipping compared to its Jaynes-Cummings counterpart. Lastly, although dissipation negatively impacts the system, certain parameters can still optimize the system's transmission and flipping probabilities. These findings align with experimental observations of a similar system using ultra-cold atoms. Ultimately, understanding these results could facilitate the development of quantum keys using the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model for quantum information processing. Additionally, the observed non-linear behaviors have potential applications beyond quantum information processing, such as generating controlled quantum states and exploring the connection between light-matter interactions and botanical growth. In particular, the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model can mimic the dynamics of botanical growth, including the phenomenon of van der Waals, for a system consisting of a spinning atom and a saturable jet boiler. Measuring inter-beat intervals in electrocardiograms is crucial, but the common method employed by cardiologists is prone to significant errors due to noisy recordings. Researchers have proposed various signal processing techniques, such as the Fourier Transform combined with frequency peak detection, to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio and locate the frequency peak, but these methods remain theoretical and have not been tested on a dedicated deep learning framework. We have developed a deep learning-based approach, specifically the Tiramisu network, to measure IBIs from low-frequency components of ECG signals, and our results show that IBI estimates are nearly error-free, outperforming traditional signal processing methods. Additionally, our work has implications for using deep learning models to correct existing measurement errors and providing baseline values for comparing measurement accuracy. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abdulrazzaqkt/IWI_CVC. Additionally, the pre-trained model can be downloaded from HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/dlktir. This model has been successfully tested on datasets from public domains, specifically the MIT-BIH arrhythmia database, and produced outstanding results, with an average IBI error of 0.02 beats-per-minute. Specifically, it achieved IBIs with error rates of 0.01, 0.02, and 0.04 bpm for lead I, II, and III, respectively. The error rates for the frequency peak detection method using the Fourier Transform were 2, 4, and 6 bpm. The outstanding performance of our approach is due to its use of deep learning models, specifically the Tiramisu network, to measure IBI error rates. Similarly, the Fourier Transform is used in other methods to estimate frequency peak locations. We have demonstrated the error-correcting capabilities of our deep learning model and shown that, in comparison to the Fourier Transform, it produces significantly lower IBI error rates. The Tiramisu network's ability to learn and represent complex data distributions has contributed to its use in measuring IBI error rates. Furthermore, our work in measuring IBI error rates may have implications for evaluating other measurement accuracy in various domains. We investigate the fluctuations of a active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOP) that exhibits active movement while being subjected to a constant external force. The particle's active movement causes asymmetry in energy consumption, which is quantified by converting the stochastic dynamics into a generalized star-shaped model. By mapping the AOP to this model, we are able to generalize the work distribution of this particle, which varies depending on the type and duration of the external force applied. These investigations provide insight into how non-uniform energy usage affects fluctuation dynamics in self-propelled cells and microorganisms. The generalized work distribution could be applied to other stochastic movement models that exhibit active movement. Furthermore, we observe that applying an external force that causes the particle to move in the direction of its self-propulsion leads to reduced fluctuations in work compared to an equivalent passive particle. On the other hand, opposing the particle and applying a constant external force result in increased fluctuations of work. When the duration of the external force exceeds the active relaxation time, these fluctuations demonstrate non-Gaussian behavior and can be characterized using specific probability distribution functions. Notably, the nature of these fluctuations depends on whether the external force assists or opposes the particle's movement, in which case the distribution functions display opposing signs. Additionally, we derive expressions for key statistical properties of work, such as the mean, variance, and skewness in various scenarios. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the work distribution and the particle's motion, where we observe a transition from small to large work values. On the other hand, we examine the work distribution in a scenario where the external force oscillates in direction and magnitude at a constant amplitude, which causes the particle to exhibit periodic motion. In this scenario, we identify the conditions under which the work distribution is bimodal or uniform. Lastly, we investigate how one specific statistical property of work, the third moment or skewness, responds to variations in active movement strength, where we observe a transition from a specific statistical property of a passive particle to another based on movement type. All of these findings provide insight into how non-uniform energy usage affects the fluctuation dynamics of self-propelled cells and microorganisms. Moreover, we generalize the work distribution in a specific statistical property, which could be applied to other active movement models. Lastly, we explore the relationship between the work distribution and the movement of the particle. This investigation provides insight into active movement in biology, which could also be applied to other stochastic movement models that exhibit active movement. This paper introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset containing colorful markers on subjects to record various everyday situations from multiple viewpoints.  
The primary objective of HUMBI is to track a subject's movement using 2D and 3D data, leveraging 14 distinct camera views to capture a person's gestures in a simulated environment.  
To facilitate markerless person tracking, the dataset excludes individuals wearing regular clothing, focusing instead on subjects dressed in colorful, tightly-fitting outfits to ensure optimal marker visibility.  
Permutations of 10 diverse individuals are incorporated within the dataset, along with 184 unique poses captured from a total of 340 minutes of video footage, totalling 1.26TB of information.  
To test the accuracy of our tracking system, a gold standard model-derived method is applied, then contrasted with a contemporary 2D and 3D human body model, along with the integration of PASCAL VOC 2009+challenge for inter-dataset consistency assessment.  
Ultimately, the main contribution of HUMBI lies in its multifaceted dataset design, aiming to improve monocular and multiview human body gesture recognition, along with a proposed benchmark challenge based on the dataset to foster innovative algorithm development.  
The HUMBI dataset is accessible at https://github.com/fatemehkarim/HUMBI and under review at https://papersonline.org/.

Despite the growing need for multilingual models, many current systems are limited to a single language due to high development costs and the challenges of transferring models across languages. In response, researchers have explored automatic and semi-automatic methods for creating multilingual models, but these approaches often rely on sophisticated annotations and are difficult to scale. This work instead focuses on leveraging plain text task descriptions to facilitate language transfer, requiring only that task descriptions and data are available in one language and the task itself can be defined through input-output pairs. To achieve this, we first developed a neural network that can encode task descriptions and use this representation to guide cross-language model training. In various experiments, our system showed promising results, with task success rates of up to 80% without requiring annotations in the target language. When annotations are available in the target language, our system achieves near-full performance with only slight improvement. Due to its reliance on plain text task descriptions, our method is highly adaptable and can be used to create multilingual models for a wide range of tasks. Moreover, it does not require task-specific knowledge and can be applied to unfamiliar tasks through supervised or unsupervised learning. As such, we believe this approach holds significant potential for reducing the development costs of multilingual models. A task dataset, along with language pairs and task examples, is available at https://github.com/johnrysa/neural-task-cross-lingual-transfer. investigates the potential benefits and limitations in model-based methods. Our
results show that using a single network for multiple tasks in model-based

catastrophic interference, which hinders learning across distinct tasks. To

This research introduces a method to assess the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on high-voltage power grids. A spatial modeling framework is presented to simulate the physical interactions between hurricanes, storm surges, and transmission lines. The proposed approach utilizes established hurricane and storm surge models to estimate spatially-resolved wind and water levels affecting transmission components. A detailed line model is then applied to calculate system impedance as wind speeds and distances from the center of the hurricane vary. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through case studies analyzing a 3000-MVA test system in the presence of hurricanes and storm surges. The outcomes show that high storm surges can cause widespread power outages extending far beyond the directly affected area. The proposed spatial model offers a more accurate representation of power system behavior under extreme weather conditions, revealing valuable insights for grid operators and planners. The model can support operations in the short term and planning in the long term by providing estimates of wind speeds and distances from the center of the hurricane. The study validates the importance of effectively communicating storm surge warnings to ensure smooth power system operations during hurricanes. The model can be utilized by utilities to develop contingency plans, set safety standards, and identify areas requiring upgrade or reinforcement to maintain reliable grid operations. The outcomes of this research can guide experts in modeling and analyzing transmission systems for the sake of improving grid resilience. Future developments of this research will involve collaboration with meteorologists to refine the estimation of wind speeds and storm surges in conjunction with numerical weather prediction models. Additionally, the integration of load modeling and customer behavior under extreme weather conditions will be explored in the future. We leverage Clifford algebra and the monotonicity formula derived by V. Monclair to develop a new approach for proving the Three Balls Conjecture in this context. We directly utilize an expression for the monotone quantity $\rho(x)=\left|\Phi(x)\right|^2+\left|\nabla_\Lambda \Phi(x)\right|^2$, without introducing additional subharmonic functions. This methodology allows us to obtain a highly optimized version of the conjecture, along with sharp constants. We also provide a detailed geometric interpretation of the method's core challenge. Furthermore, we derive a relevant extension of the monotone quantity expression, which has significant implications for the field of Clifford analysis. We then employ these results to address an alternative formulation of the Three Balls Conjecture, which initially emerged during a stimulating conversation with M. Abughazaleh and P. Bogdan. The conversation took place during the 13th ISAAC Conference held at the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania. We successfully generalize the optimized conjecture to the setting of bounded domains that are mean convex. We also make notable observations regarding the behavior of eigenfunctions near the boundary of these domains. We anticipate that this generalization will play a significant role in the broader field of differential equations. Additionally, we directly address the eigenvalue component, $\lambda$, and establish a refined version of the Three Balls Conjecture that incorporates this component. The resulting inequality exhibits an intriguing proportionality similar to that seen in the Heisenberg formula. We anticipate that further research will yield even more striking connections between these two expressions. WaveNet is a highly realistic generative model, but its scalability is limited due to its complex structure. To overcome this, we introduced two novel techniques: Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution Neural Network (PCENet) and Hierarchical Fusion (HF). PCENet was designed to learn speech features at different frequency ranges and can be applied to various speech synthesis tasks. HF was developed to improve the efficiency of WaveNet by merging sub-networks at different pitch levels. The results show that QPNet outperforms the state-of-the-art speech synthesis systems in terms of mean opinion score and metric learning. TOSSP was based on the popular Tacotron system and was used to conduct the experiments in this study. TOSSP is now available for public use. The extensive research in collaborative filtering aims to address the issue of recommending personalized items to users based on aggregated global patterns in a sparse user-item rating matrix. However, this approach overlooks the inherent groupings within the matrix, which can provide more refined and accurate personalization. Our proposed bicluster-based collaborative filtering method delves into these sub-matrix patterns to uncover fine-grained preferences, thereby leveraging the inherent structure in the data. Utilizing the concept of differential evolution for parameter optimization, our approach demonstrates exceptional performance compared to state-of-the-art recommender systems in a range of real-world scenarios. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis highlights the benefits of incorporating bicluster patterns into collaborative filtering systems. Despite its promising results, our approach still relies on aggregate patterns, which may lead to a limited understanding of individual preferences. Conversely, models focusing solely on user-specific models often struggle to capture global patterns, compromising their accuracy. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel combination of collaborative filtering systems that integrate the best of both approaches. By synergistically merging the bicluster-based method with individual latent factor models, our proposed architecture achieves superior performance while maintaining interpretability. Thorough experimentation in multiple settings validates the efficacy of our combined strategy. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the fundamental differences between user and bicluster models highlights the unique characteristics and capabilities of each. To further empower researchers and developers, we publicly disclose our code, data sets, and evaluation results. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of the biases in the widely-used MovieLens dataset is provided, including an in-depth examination of the causes and consequences of these biases, along with proposed solutions to mitigate their impact on recommender system evaluation. Ultimately, our study contributes to the body of knowledge in recommender systems by addressing various challenges highlighted throughout the manuscript. To achieve this, we draw from diverse domains including machine learning, data mining, and information retrieval to name a few. In particular, under-studied aspects of sparse data, differential evolution, and bias in rating datasets are explored. Magnetic activity is a critical factor affecting the spectral properties of solar spectra, especially at low-frequency endpoints, which can impact exoplanet detection and characterization. By analyzing solar spectra from the HARPS-N instrument at the Canary Islands' 3.6-meter telescope, we investigated the spectral features of active stars and their impact on observations of solar-like stars. We identified and tested new activity indicators in addition to evaluating established ones. We also examined the frequency limitations of these indicators and the variations in spectral features throughout the observation period. The most suitable indicators for ground-based observations appear to be the S-index, R'$_{CK}$ index, and a specific absorption at 785.5 nm, all of which exhibit a consistent relationship with observations of solar spectra. Notably, the 450-day R'$_{CK}$ index displayed the least influence on observed spectral features among all options. Understanding the spectral features of active stars and incorporating activity indicators in data processing can help reduce systematic noise in solar and astronomical spectra, ultimately improving exoplanet detection and characterization efforts. We recommend incorporating the 450-day R'$_{CK}$ index and other activity indicators into the HARPS-N pipeline for data calibration. Moreover, integrating activity indicators into the analysis of solar spectra may help mitigate systematic noise in asteroseismology and gyrochronology applications. Based on our findings, the 785.5 nm absorption feature appears to be linked to fast-moving stellar shells with short lifetimes, which could pose a significant challenge in accurately measuring stellar rotation periods in ancient stars. Quick incorporation of these features in various astronomical observations and stellar analyses is essential to minimize systematic noise, which may cause biases in results. On the other hand, integrating activity indicators into the analysis of solar spectra may help eliminate systematic noise, which could lead to valuable insights in asteroseismology and gyrochronology. Additionally, we observed that the spectral features of active stars are largely unaffected by Earth's rotation, which might be attributed to the instrument's broad field of view capturing a combination of stellar features and Earth's atmospheric variability. Lastly, the spectral features of active stars are not influenced by Earth's obliquity, which could be an interesting area of investigation in the future. We provided readers with essential information regarding spectral features of active stars, which might be helpful in understanding these features on exoplanets and other stars with their own magnetic activity. The increased current it supports, however, remains within the same threshold as before. Furthermore, our model displays this phenomenon the same way in numerical data as in theoretical predictions, using a set of specific equations we've developed. According to our theory, the number of quasiparticles that can easily move through the system should remain the same when using a dissipative lead versus a normal lead. However, the increased current allowed by a dissipative lead can distinguish Majorana peaks from others, which may change with varying temperatures. The concept of shadows has emerged as a potent tool in bicategorical research. This paper aims to deepen understanding of shadows by establishing them as manifestations of Bimodules. Through this new perspective, we demonstrate the equivalence between shadows and Bimodules, opening doors to applications in categories like algebraic and topological K-theory. As a initial application, we build upon existing results by showing that extended modules, which serve as the foundation for the homotopy category of modules, can indeed be seen as a type of shadow, effectively generalizing the idea of projective resolutions. This new understanding also allows us to reinterpret Khovanov and Sem seminctor's discovery that homotopy categories of modules are categorically equivalent to the category of shadows. By replacing the concept of homotopy categories of modules with Bimodules, we are able to extend this result to all modules within the underlying category. This extension has further implications, such as allowing us to conclude that stable homotopy categories of commutative algebra are categorically equivalent to the category of shadows. This discovery is notably broad in scope and can be translated to other theories, such as topological K-theory. Additionally, we show that Khovanov and Seminctor's result can be extended to any subcategory with a module coverage, such as the category of graded vector spaces. This extension has further implications, such as allowing us to conclude that homotopy categories of graded vector spaces are categorically equivalent to the category of shadows. This discovery has further applications in algebraic research and can be translated to other theories, such as stable homotopy theory of spectra. Furthermore, we show that Khovanov and Seminctor's result can be extended to any category with a module coverage that is also monoidal closed, such as the category of graded vector spaces, yielding a broader generalization of the result. This discovery has further applications in algebraic research and can be translated to other theories, such as stable homotopy theory of spectra. This work presents a novel understanding of Khovanov and Seminctor's result and reveals a deeper underlying relationship between the homotopy category of algebraic K-theory and the category of shadows. A variety of image enhancement tasks rely on color style transfer between two images,  achieving notable results in existing research, yet these methods often ignore the complex semantic connections between images, reducing their transfer outcomes to basic color adjustments. To overcome these limitations, we present a new neural network, the Style Distillation Network (SDN), which captures a style from one image and applies it to another image while maintaining the original image's semantics. While existing methods only perform forward style transfer, our SDN can be trained for both forward and inverse style transfer, a capability few models have demonstrated. By incorporating a semantic-aware loss function, SDN ensures accurate transfer of image semantics, and its ability to perform cross-domain style transfer is unparalleled, outperforming existing models in extensive experiments. SDN's source code and demo are available online at https://github.com/IndigoPhoton/Style-Distillation-Network. 
With vast applications in image enhancement, our proposed method aims to contribute to the advancement of style transfer research. 
In specific, SDN has been successfully applied to image enhancement, colorization, and picture matte generation tasks, delivering superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models. This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts faced significant challenges in processing multi-step responses, multiple modalities, and dynamic button representations within video content. Our video understanding module leverages a pre-trained video transformer to extract relevant spatio-temporal features from video clips, which are then embedded and combined with the text and temperature features. A specially designed optical sensor, precision-crafted for long-range detection, is employed to track the movement of snowflakes at a distance of around 10 meters. This extensive research gathers a substantial quantity of data, amounting to nearly 400,000 individual snowflake trajectories. This data is then used to model the velocity distributions of the snowflakes as they move through the turbulent air. Interestingly, the results reveal two distinct states of the snowflakes' movements - one that closely follows the general velocity patterns of the air and another that exhibits unusually high velocities, far exceeding those typically found in the air. A sophisticated analysis framework suggests that the high-velocity movements can be attributed to a process known as "sweeping," where the air currents within the atmosphere carry the snowflakes at remarkable speeds many times greater than usual. This process is found to significantly impact the global velocity distribution of the snowflakes, and is hypothesized to be a common phenomenon not just limited to snowflakes but also other atmospheric particles and the clouds that form the basis of the weather. A major discovery of this study is the significant role that turbulent air currents play in the settlement of snowflakes, and it is proposed that future studies of atmospheric particles should take into account this sweeping phenomenon. We initially demonstrate that by using a specific type of solution, referred to as a soliton, it is possible to achieve an infinite maximum value for the reflection coefficient when considering an infinite plane filled with vortex structures of only one sign. Notably, the contribution to the reflection coefficient comes primarily from a very narrow area along the axis of the soliton, and the depth of this contribution is directly related to the local rate of change of the soliton's strength at a specific point. Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of binary black hole inspirals, employing post-Newtonian theory up to the third order, reveal that late-time residual eccentricities exhibit a uniform pattern regardless of mass ratio. Specifically, these findings align with predictions from semi-analytical models, and by analyzing straddling configurations, we identify critical thresholds for late-time residual eccentricities in terms of gravitational-wave detection boundaries and mass ratios. To further refine accuracy, we developed and implemented a novel numerical approach, precise to a level of five significant figures, to determine residual eccentricities at late times. Our work demonstrates that high-accuracy computations of residual eccentricities can inform semi-analytical models, thereby enhancing their underlying equations. Consequently, this improves the reliability of semi-analytical models as approximations at the threshold of gravitational-wave detection. Additionally, our findings suggest that late-time residual eccentricities will not solely depend on the final gravitational-wave detection frequency but also on the binary system's mass ratio, particularly in scenarios involving unequal masses. Given these considerations, we suggest revising the frequently used "standard" model, known as the "standard template bank," to account for late-time residual eccentricities and, by extension, post-Newtonian corrections in extra binary parameters. Our work has implications for the calculation of late-time merger properties such as final orbital separation, closing angle, and final black hole eccentricity, and could aid in the estimation of binary inspiral durations when subject to late-gravitational-wave detection signals. Our analysis code, specifically designed for the calculation of post-Newtonian corrections to binary inspiral properties, is fully publicly available through the GitHub platform under the label "pnc-inspiral-catalogue." Furthermore, we outline a proposed plan for generating a detailed, high-accuracy catalog of binary inspiral properties, thereby serving as a reference point for future theoretical and numerical work in the field of binary black hole studies. Specifically, we suggest that theoretical and numerical investigations should focus on achieving a precision of at least a level of ten in key binary inspiral properties when straddling critical thresholds for gravitational-wave detection. In turn, this precise knowledge will, in turn, inform and enhance the accuracy of semi-analytical models, thereby contributing to a more refined understanding of late-inspiral binary black holes. To achieve this goal, we propose a multi-step approach, and specifically identify areas where future advancements in numerical modeling, particularly through the application of higher-order numerical methods, could significantly contribute to the growth of precision in binary inspiral property calculations.

Dynamic graphs represent evolving relationships between graph nodes over time, with frequent edge addition and removal, vertex inclusion, and attribute updates. Real-world applications of these graphs cover critical surveillance purposes such as analyzing a city's traffic patterns or detecting anomalies in network security. Our work focuses on incident detection in dynamic graphs using a novel approach that combines the advantages of both sparse subspace modeling and deep learning. Specifically, we proposed an method that automatically detects anomalies in traffic graphs, revealing incidents like road closures and accidents. Our approach involves transforming the graph incident data into a numerical format through sparse subspace modeling and then using a deep learning technique to classify the resulting data into distinct categories. Our experiments, involving real-world data from New York City, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in detecting incidents from dynamic graph data. Our code is available on GitHub for public access.

The growing presence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in daily life is undeniable, 
with a significant proportion of AI systems emerging in various settings, 
including industry, healthcare, and transportation. As AI systems' influence 
continues to expand, ensuring they remain understandable and reliable is becoming 
the focus. While software engineering and requirements engineering have long 
acknowledged the significance of transparency and accountability, specifically 
in the context of user-centered design, the reverse is not always the case. 
This study aims to bridge this gap by exploring the connection between requirements 
engineering and the explainability of AI systems. First, we establish the link 
between requirements engineering, user experience, and explainability. Next, we 
outline the key areas that explainability requirements should address, drawing on 
relevant research and real-world examples. Finally, we highlight promising areas 
for further research, such as developing the full spectrum of explainability requirements 
and creating standardized taxonomies and guidelines for explainability requirements 
engineering practices. By promoting a user-centric approach, we hope to enhance 
explainability in AI systems, ultimately leading to more people-friendly AI. 

Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Explainability, Requirements Engineering, User-Centric 
Approach, Understandability. 

This work is inspired by the SE4X initiative and is a preliminary outcome, 
separating explainability requirements from other aspects of AI systems' 
functionality and user experience. As such, it does not comprehensive cover 
explainability in AI, but rather focuses on requirements from a user-centered 
perspective. We aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on explainability 
in AI and hope to receive feedback and input from interested parties.

Focusing on zero-error compression, we investigate the maximum amount of information an adversary can obtain from the communication with high confidence. Although they offer several advantages, SAR images often exhibit speckle noise that hinders their interpretation. Numerous existing enhancement methods have addressed this issue, but the optimal solutions depend on specific assumptions regarding the underlying data distributions. A recent development in the literature suggests using generative models as prior distributions in Bayesian approaches to image enhancement. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates QAOA's variational principles into diverse quantum optimization techniques.  To increase its success rate, researchers employ extensive numerical testing to determine optimal variational parameter values, although these often struggle to perform well in similar problems.  We develop and evaluate an alternative approach, where Bayesian analysis determines variational parameter values, yielding consistent improvements in QAOA's capacity to solve specific problems.  From a theoretical standpoint, our method's performance in finding global maxima in combinatorial optimization problems, like MAX-cut on a complete graph of 200 vertices, surpasses variational tuning via reinforcement learning and often achieves better results than classical approximate algorithms.  From a practical perspective, our method proves adaptable to various quantum hardware platforms and is typically faster than tuning via reinforcement learning.  We open-source our code, allowing others to reproduce our findings and apply our approach to a wide range of applications.  Our results serve as a general framework for variational quantum algorithms, suggesting that Bayesian analysis could improve the performance of numerous QAOA-like methods.  We also investigate the relationship between variational parameter values and the resulting QAOA energies, revealing that our Bayesian approach often selects parameter values resulting in global energy minima, despite these typically lying near the classical boundary, suggesting a need for future research into QAOA's inner workings.  To bridge the gap between current variational quantum algorithms and the ideal quantum circuits of Grover's algorithm, we propose an alternative analysis, where the short, noisy circuits of quantum algorithms are evaluated based solely on their ability to approximate the ideal circuits, rather than their current behavior.  This model presents a challenging open mathematical problem.  Without this challenging analysis, our numerical testing reveals that the short, noisy circuits of QAOA can efficiently approximate the ideal circuits of Grover's algorithm, resisting noise through the accumulation of phase shifts and allowing it to perform better than classical algorithms even in noisy environments.  This concept could be widely applicable to diverse quantum algorithms, where we hypothesize that the short, noisy circuits of any variational quantum algorithm may efficiently approximate the ideal circuits of their classical counterparts.  This challenging analysis may hold the key to overcoming noise's detrimental effect on quantum circuits and could enable a wide range of quantum circuits to operate reliably in delicate quantum hardware.  This principle could potentially be incorporated into diverse variational quantum algorithms, allowing them to function robustly in delicate quantum hardware and remains an open research area. In a recent study, researchers used the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to investigate magnetic excitations in a model Hubbard model on a triangular lattice. This lattice-based quantum system has multiple low-lying phases, which were mapped out by solving the associated DMFT problem. The findings reveal that, in the region of a specific phase transition (from nematic to valence bond solid), magnon behavior is dominant at the zone boundary, but at a nearby critical point (between valence bond solid and polar phases) a new phase emerges where magnons are suppressed and excitations with fractional charge predominate. The researchers used a specialized computational method to verify the emergence of a new type of order, known as order-by-disorder, which is typically seen in systems exhibiting magnon behavior. The study's phase diagram prediction shows good agreement with results from numerical cluster methods and presents a potential pathway to experimental verification of the new phase through the use of neutron scattering. The newly discovered phase is characterized to have excitations with fractional charge, which are robust against thermal fluctuations. Furthermore, the breakage of symmetries in the system was investigated in detail. Finally, the researchers explored the relationship between a proxy variable, used to describe the system's behavior in a simplified manner, and the true variable, which governs the system's behavior. The proxy variable was found to be a reliable descriptor of the system's behavior and that its dynamics can be solved analytically. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification in CT scans are crucial for various clinical tasks but are often challenging due to difficulties arising from, for instance, poor imaging quality, anatomical variation, or anatomically based models that necessitate initial localization as a starting point. To tackle these problems, this paper introduces an end-to-end solution that incorporates vertebrae alignment to serve as a reference point for identification. Specifically, the proposed method involves adjusting and transforming a L-shaped CT scan template to fit a given CT scan, taking into consideration anatomical constraints such as spatial relationships, sizes, and sequences to ensure a single, unique solution. Once the template is aligned, the method applies an optimization technique to determine the optimal vertebrae locations, with an emphasis on maintaining anatomical relationships among the vertebrae, rib cages, and skulls to prevent deviations in identification. To evaluate the method, this paper compares it with two other state-of-the-art approaches on a large CT dataset containing 12,052 pairs, revealing superior performance with the following results: the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for the detection task increased by 0.10 to 0.995, and identification accuracy rose by 0.40% to 99.70%, with average processing time decreasing from 170 seconds to 72 seconds. Furthermore, the method was successfully tested on CT data without segmentation labels, demonstrating excellent reliability with accuracy above 98% for vertebrae localization and identification. The proposed method using L-shaped templates has shown superior performance and efficiency, making it a viable option for clinical use. The associated code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/pkchang12/VertebralLocalizationIdentification. By making this connection, we explore an extension of standard stochastic thermodynamics to accommodate arbitrary Markovian dynamics, encompassing both ergodic and non-ergodic cases. Our quantum geometry is based on a noncommutative Poisson algebra called relative quantum geometry. We demonstrated the self-consistency of this framework by showing that certain key properties remain unchanged across a full set of transformations. In our research, we identified specific characteristics of quantum geometry and studied quantum Poisson brackets under transformation. Furthermore, we examined an explicit example involving a del Pezzo surface of order four. We also found that quantum geometry is fully described by certain discrete data, similar to the case of toric noncommutative projective spaces. In a broader sense, our findings generalize existing theories on quantum toric varieties, noncommutative U(1)-invariant Poisson toric varieties, and Cox rings. Our work also has broader applications and offers new directions for research in the field. Ultimately, our goal is to use the algebraic structure of relative quantum geometry to study quantum invariants, such as quantum invariants recently described for smooth del Pezzo surfaces. In future work, we plan to extend our research to conic del Pezzo surfaces, surfaces of type K3^*, and other related surfaces. We anticipate that the results of our research will have significant implications for the field of low-dimensional topological quantum information and coding theory. Specific predictions derive from our findings regarding discrete data and quantum algebraic structure, which we believe will prove particularly significant. We derive a novel condition of coherence for the Milnor fiber of a isolated hypersurface singularity using cohomology and the flatness of the critical locus. Furthermore, we establish that the topological Milnor number computes the dimension of the Milnor fiber when the base field is perfect, essentially relying on Goresky-MacPherson's lemma. Additionally, we compute the Milnor fiber cohomology ring in the case of a quadratic monomial surface singularity. The proposed coherence condition has implications in the context of vanishing cycles and weighted homogeneous singularities, where we demonstrate the dimension of the Milnor fiber can be determined through explicit calculations. The calculations not only show the Milnor fiber Coherence but also illustrate how the structure of the singularity is reflected in the differential form $\frac{\omega}{\lambda}$, with $\omega$ being a regular differential form on the Milnor fiber and $\lambda$ being a linear form on the normal space. Lastly, we provide an example illustrating that the condition of coherence does not necessarily apply to all regular singularities on surfaces. The presented results are part of the doctoral work in mathematics of the author.

Galileo's rejection of scholastic methodology was based on an ardent belief in the necessity of experimental evidence, prompting him to denounce conventional reasoning as invalid and unimportant. This paper seeks to refine Galileo's stance by differentiating between uninspired reasoning and valid mathematical demonstration, contending that the former is indeed ineffective, whereas the latter remains a reliable method for acquiring knowledge. Moreover, I argue that scholastic reasoning, though flawed in Galileo's view, is not entirely without value and that Ignoramus should not be seen as a total rejection but rather a targeted critique of specific scholastic practices. Ultimately, I suggest that Galileo's thoughts on methodology can be read as a call for a more nuanced balance between reasoning and observation, rather than an emphatic indictment of all rational inquiry. In contrast to popular historical narratives, I maintain that Galileo's views on methodology were not uniquely revolutionary and that predecessors such as Menaechius and Polycarp had already advocated for a more observational approach, one that Galileo would later adopt and modify for himself. In the course of this work, I also examine the intellectual heritage of early modern scholastic mathematics, revealing that mainstream scholastic thinkers had little understanding of mathematical concepts and had instead developed their own unique interpretations of mathematical demonstrations. In contrast to conventional historical accounts, I contend that early modern scholastic mathematics was not merely a matter of borrowing from Aristotle but rather an complex and multifaceted tradition that merited further study. In the course of this research, I discovered that the early modern scholastic mathematical tradition had given rise to a range of distinct concepts and problems, including the demonstration of inevitability in coin-tossing outcomes and the derivation of the price of a loaf of bread from the price of rye. In exploring these early modern scholastic mathematical themes, I draw on a range of sources from the Paduan school to the Cistercian Order and examine the relationship between mathematics and society in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italy. In particular, I examine the ways in which early modern scholastic mathematics engaged with issues of usury, trade, and finance, revealing a range of views on these topics that are at odds with conventional historical narratives. In this work, I also contend that the distinct concepts and problems of early modern scholastic mathematics remained a living part of the intellectual heritage of Galileo and his contemporaries, one that continues to shape the relationship between mathematics and society in the modern world.
